NAMES.name: equilibrium_weight_of_flux_loop
NAMES.short: Nonnegative factor that sets the relative contribution of an individual flux-loop poloidal-flux residual to an equilibrium objective function.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the nonnegative relative weight assigned to the residual of one flux loop’s measured and equilibrium poloidal magnetic flux. It controls how strongly that individual constraint influences the equilibrium objective, rather than defining a magnetic flux itself.

The contribution associated with one flux-loop constraint is defined by

$$
J_{\mathrm{FL}} = \frac{1}{2} w_{\mathrm{FL}}^2 \frac{(\psi_{\mathrm{rec}}-\psi_{\mathrm{meas}})^2}{\sigma_{\mathrm{FL}}^2}
$$

where $J_{\mathrm{FL}}$ is the objective-function contribution of the flux-loop constraint, $w_{\mathrm{FL}}$ is this equilibrium weight, $\psi_{\mathrm{rec}}$ is the equilibrium poloidal magnetic flux at the constraint location, $\psi_{\mathrm{meas}}$ is the corresponding measured poloidal magnetic flux, and $\sigma_{\mathrm{FL}}$ is the standard deviation assigned to that measurement error.

The weight applies to one flux-loop poloidal-flux constraint and is not itself summed over sensors; the objective function aggregates the separate contributions from individual constraints. It excludes the flux value, the residual, and the measurement-error standard deviation, which are distinct physical or statistical quantities.

The constrained flux is the [poloidal magnetic flux at the constraint position](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_constraint_position), while the sensor-specific weighting convention parallels the [equilibrium weight of a poloidal magnetic-field probe](name:equilibrium_weight_of_poloidal_magnetic_field_probe) with a different sensor object.

NAMES.name: equilibrium_weight_of_poloidal_magnetic_field_probe
NAMES.short: Dimensionless factor that controls the relative contribution of a poloidal magnetic-field probe residual to the equilibrium objective function.
NAMES.long:
The equilibrium weight of a poloidal magnetic-field probe is a dimensionless factor assigned to the residual of one probe constraint in an equilibrium reconstruction objective.

For constraint index $i$, the objective contribution is defined through

$$
J = \frac{1}{2}\sum_i w_i^2\frac{(q_i^{\mathrm{rec}}-q_i^{\mathrm{meas}})^2}{\sigma_i^2}
$$

where $J$ is the equilibrium objective function, $w_i$ is the weight of constraint $i$, $q_i^{\mathrm{rec}}$ is its reconstructed poloidal magnetic-field value, $q_i^{\mathrm{meas}}$ is its measured value, and $\sigma_i$ is the standard deviation of its measurement error.

This quantity applies to a single poloidal magnetic-field probe constraint and does not represent the probe field, its residual, or the measurement uncertainty. It is not an aggregate over multiple probes; the objective function aggregates the individually weighted constraint contributions. The analogous [equilibrium weight of an interferometer beam](name:equilibrium_weight_of_interferometer_beam) applies the same weighting role to a different constraint observable.

NAMES.name: faraday_angle
NAMES.short: Faraday rotation of a probing wave’s polarization plane caused by electron density and the magnetic-field component along its plasma path.
NAMES.long:
The Faraday angle is the signed rotation of a probing electromagnetic wave’s polarization plane caused by propagation through magnetized plasma. For an equilibrium state, it is the angle predicted from the electron density and magnetic field encountered along the beam path.

In the cold, weakly dispersive magnetoionic approximation, the plasma-induced rotation is defined by

$$
\theta_F = \frac{e^3\lambda^2}{8\pi^2\epsilon_0 m_e^2 c^3} \int_{\mathcal{L}} n_e(\ell) B_{\parallel}(\ell)\,d\ell
$$

where $\theta_F$ is the Faraday rotation angle, $e$ is the elementary-charge magnitude, $\lambda$ is the probing-wave vacuum wavelength, $\pi$ is the circle constant, $\epsilon_0$ is the vacuum permittivity, $m_e$ is the electron mass, $c$ is the speed of light, $\mathcal{L}$ is the segment of the beam path crossing the plasma, $\ell$ is distance along that path, $n_e(\ell)$ is the local electron number density, and $B_{\parallel}(\ell)$ is the signed magnetic-field component along the beam direction.

The quantity applies to the electron contribution accumulated along one probing beam through the plasma. Its aggregation is a line integral along that path, not a local rotation rate, flux-surface average, or sum over multiple beams; optical rotation produced outside the plasma is excluded. The equilibrium-derived value is the rotation predicted by the reconstructed plasma state and is distinct from a directly observed angle or from a residual between prediction and observation.

Faraday angle describes rotation of the polarization plane, whereas [polarization ellipticity of a polarimeter beam](name:polarization_ellipticity_of_polarimeter_beam) describes the signed shape of the polarization ellipse through its axis ratio; the two quantities are not interchangeable.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the polarization plane rotates according to the right-hand rule about the beam propagation direction from its incident reference orientation.

NAMES.name: flux_surface_averaged_inverse_of_square_of_magnetic_field_magnitude
NAMES.short: Flux-surface average of the reciprocal square of total magnetic-field strength, a geometric coefficient in neoclassical and flux-surface-averaged transport relations.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the flux-surface average of the reciprocal square of the total magnetic-field strength on a nested magnetic surface. It captures field-strength geometry independently of the magnetic-field direction.

The defining relation is

$$
\left\langle \frac{1}{|\mathbf{B}|^2} \right\rangle_\psi
=
\frac{\displaystyle \int_{S(\psi)} |\mathbf{B}|^{-2}\,\frac{dS}{|\nabla\psi|}}
{\displaystyle \int_{S(\psi)} \frac{dS}{|\nabla\psi|}}
$$

where $\mathbf{B}$ is the total magnetic-field vector, $|\mathbf{B}|$ is its magnitude, $\psi$ is the flux-surface label, $S(\psi)$ is the magnetic surface labeled by $\psi$, $dS$ is its surface-area element, and $\nabla\psi$ is the spatial gradient of the flux-surface label.

The quantity applies to the complete magnetic flux surface and uses the inverse-$|\nabla\psi|$ weighting shown in the defining relation. It is not a pointwise inverse-square field value and has no selection by magnetic-field direction, component, species, or source.

It is the flux-surface-averaged transformation of the parent [inverse square of magnetic-field magnitude](name:inverse_of_square_of_magnetic_field_magnitude), with the reciprocal square formed locally before averaging. It is distinct from [flux-surface-averaged magnetic-field magnitude](name:flux_surface_averaged_magnetic_field_magnitude) and [flux-surface-averaged square of magnetic-field magnitude](name:flux_surface_averaged_square_of_magnetic_field_magnitude), because nonlinear inversion and squaring do not commute with surface averaging.

NAMES.name: flux_surface_averaged_inverse_of_square_of_major_radius
NAMES.short: Flux-surface average of reciprocal squared major radius, providing a geometric metric coefficient for parallel-gradient and neoclassical transport calculations.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the flux-surface average of the reciprocal square of the major radius on a nested equilibrium magnetic flux surface. It is a positive geometric metric coefficient used in parallel-gradient operators and neoclassical and gyrokinetic transport equations.

It is defined by

$$
g_{m1}(\psi)=\left\langle \frac{1}{R^2}\right\rangle_{\psi}
$$

where $g_{m1}$ denotes this metric coefficient, $R$ is the major radius measured from the toroidal symmetry axis, $\psi$ is the poloidal magnetic flux labeling the surface, and $\langle\cdot\rangle_{\psi}$ denotes the flux-surface average on that surface.

The quantity applies to the entire magnetic flux surface and has no species, field-component, or source-process restriction. Its aggregation convention is a flux-surface average of the local reciprocal-square geometric factor; it is not the reciprocal square of a flux-surface-averaged major radius.

It is the flux-surface-averaged form of the pointwise [inverse of square of major radius](name:inverse_of_square_of_major_radius). It differs from the related [flux-surface-averaged inverse of major radius](name:flux_surface_averaged_inverse_of_major_radius), which averages the first reciprocal power of $R$ rather than its reciprocal square.

NAMES.name: flux_surface_averaged_major_radius
NAMES.short: Flux-surface-averaged nonnegative perpendicular distance from the toroidal symmetry axis to points on a nested magnetic flux surface, giving the mean major-radius coordinate in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
Major radius is the nonnegative perpendicular distance from the toroidal symmetry axis to a geometric point or specified location. For this flux-surface-averaged quantity, that distance is averaged over each nested magnetic flux surface in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

The flux-surface average of major radius is defined by

$$
\langle R\rangle_\psi = \frac{\oint_\psi R\,dl/B_p}{\oint_\psi dl/B_p}
$$

where $\langle R\rangle_\psi$ is the averaged major-radius coordinate, $\psi$ is the magnetic-flux label identifying the surface, $l$ is poloidal arc length along that surface, and $B_p$ is the magnitude of the poloidal magnetic field. The contour integral extends around the complete poloidal intersection of the nested magnetic flux surface.

This quantity applies to a complete magnetic flux surface and aggregates the local [major radius] using the flux-surface weighting defined by the inverse poloidal-field magnitude. It is therefore distinct from pointwise major radius and contains no point-specific or localized evaluation.

The quantity is the flux-surface-averaged counterpart of [major radius]. It must not be confused with [flux-surface-averaged inverse of major radius](name:flux_surface_averaged_inverse_of_major_radius), which averages the reciprocal $1/R$ rather than averaging $R$ itself; consequently, it is not generally the reciprocal of that neighboring average.

NAMES.name: flux_surface_averaged_ratio_of_square_of_toroidal_flux_coordinate_gradient_magnitude_to_square_of_magnetic_field_magnitude
NAMES.short: Flux-surface average of the squared toroidal-flux-coordinate gradient magnitude divided by the squared local magnetic-field magnitude, a metric coefficient for equilibrium geometry.
NAMES.long:
This coefficient describes the flux-surface-averaged geometric weighting of a toroidal-flux radial coordinate by the inverse square of the local magnetic-field magnitude.

The defining relation is

$$
\mathcal{G}_B = \left\langle \frac{|\nabla \rho_{\mathrm{tor}}|^2}{|\mathbf{B}|^2} \right\rangle_{\mathrm{FS}}
$$

where $\mathcal{G}_B$ is the averaged metric coefficient, $\rho_{\mathrm{tor}}$ is the toroidal-flux radial coordinate, $\nabla$ is the spatial gradient, $\mathbf{B}$ is the magnetic-field vector, and $\langle\cdot\rangle_{\mathrm{FS}}$ denotes the average over a magnetic flux surface.

The quantity applies to nested equilibrium magnetic flux surfaces and uses the average of the pointwise ratio, not the ratio of separately averaged numerator and denominator. It is nonnegative because both the gradient magnitude and magnetic-field magnitude are squared.

It is the flux-surface-averaged form of the local [ratio of squared toroidal-flux-coordinate gradient magnitude to squared magnetic-field magnitude](name:ratio_of_square_of_toroidal_flux_coordinate_gradient_magnitude_to_square_of_magnetic_field_magnitude). It shares the gradient-squared geometric factor with the [flux-surface-averaged squared toroidal-flux-coordinate gradient magnitude](name:flux_surface_averaged_square_of_toroidal_flux_coordinate_gradient_magnitude), but additionally applies the pointwise inverse-square magnetic-field weighting before averaging. It is distinct from the corresponding major-radius denominator variant, [flux-surface-averaged ratio of squared toroidal-flux-coordinate gradient magnitude to squared major radius](name:flux_surface_averaged_ratio_of_square_of_toroidal_flux_coordinate_gradient_magnitude_to_square_of_major_radius).

NAMES.name: flux_surface_averaged_ratio_of_square_of_toroidal_flux_coordinate_gradient_magnitude_to_square_of_major_radius
NAMES.short: Flux-surface-averaged magnetic-geometry coefficient measuring the squared toroidal-flux-coordinate gradient relative to the squared major radius.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is a magnetic-geometry metric coefficient that characterizes how a toroidal-flux radial coordinate varies across nested magnetic surfaces, with the variation weighted by inverse squared major radius.

It is defined by

$$
g_2 = \left\langle \frac{|\nabla \rho|^2}{R^2} \right\rangle_{\mathrm{FS}}
$$

where $g_2$ is the flux-surface-averaged metric coefficient, $\rho$ is the toroidal-flux radial coordinate, $\nabla\rho$ is its spatial gradient, $|\nabla\rho|$ is the gradient magnitude, $R$ is the major radius, and the subscript $\mathrm{FS}$ denotes the prescribed average over a complete magnetic flux surface.

The quantity applies to an equilibrium magnetic flux surface and represents an aggregate over that surface rather than a pointwise local value. It has no species, population, or transport-channel restriction.

It is the flux-surface average of the local ratio defined by [ratio of square of toroidal flux coordinate gradient magnitude to square of major radius](name:ratio_of_square_of_toroidal_flux_coordinate_gradient_magnitude_to_square_of_major_radius). Unlike [flux-surface-averaged square of toroidal flux coordinate gradient magnitude](name:flux_surface_averaged_square_of_toroidal_flux_coordinate_gradient_magnitude), it retains the inverse-square-major-radius weighting; the numerator is constructed from the [toroidal flux coordinate gradient magnitude](name:toroidal_flux_coordinate_gradient_magnitude).

NAMES.name: flux_surface_averaged_square_of_magnetic_field_magnitude
NAMES.short: Flux-surface average of the squared magnitude of the total equilibrium magnetic field, providing a geometric coefficient for equilibrium and neoclassical transport relations.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the surface-averaged squared strength of the total magnetic field on a nested magnetic flux surface. It is a geometric metric coefficient used in equilibrium descriptions and in bounce-averaged and neoclassical transport relations.

The flux-surface average is defined by

$$
\left\langle B^2 \right\rangle_\psi = \frac{\displaystyle\oint_{S(\psi)} \frac{B^2}{\lvert\nabla\psi\rvert}\,dS}{\displaystyle\oint_{S(\psi)} \frac{1}{\lvert\nabla\psi\rvert}\,dS}
$$

where $B^2$ is the [square of the magnetic-field magnitude](name:square_of_magnetic_field_magnitude), $\psi$ is the poloidal magnetic-flux label of the surface, $S(\psi)$ is the closed magnetic flux surface with that label, $\nabla\psi$ is the gradient of the flux label, and $dS$ is the surface-area element.

The quantity applies to the total equilibrium magnetic field, including all of its components, and is aggregated over each closed flux surface with the inverse-$\lvert\nabla\psi\rvert$ weighting shown above. It is not the pointwise value of $B^2$, the square of a flux-surface-averaged magnetic-field magnitude, or a single magnetic-field component.

It is the flux-surface-averaged form of [square_of_magnetic_field_magnitude](name:square_of_magnetic_field_magnitude). It differs from [flux_surface_averaged_magnetic_field_magnitude](name:flux_surface_averaged_magnetic_field_magnitude), which averages the field magnitude before squaring, and from [flux_surface_averaged_inverse_of_square_of_magnetic_field_magnitude](name:flux_surface_averaged_inverse_of_square_of_magnetic_field_magnitude), which averages its reciprocal.

NAMES.name: flux_surface_averaged_square_of_toroidal_flux_coordinate_gradient_magnitude
NAMES.short: Flux-surface average of the squared magnitude of the gradient of the normalized toroidal-flux radius. It is the averaged contravariant radial metric coefficient for the flux coordinate rho_tor.
NAMES.long:
Flux-surface average of the squared magnitude of the gradient of the toroidal flux coordinate is the average, over one magnetic flux surface, of the squared norm of $\nabla \rho_\mathrm{tor}$. It is the flux-surface-averaged contravariant radial metric coefficient associated with the radial coordinate in the flux-coordinate system $(\rho_\mathrm{tor}, \theta, \phi)$, where $\theta$ is a poloidal angle label and $\phi$ is the toroidal angle.

The quantity is defined by the flux-surface average of the local radial metric component:

$$
G_{\rho\rho}(\rho_\mathrm{tor}) = \left\langle |\nabla \rho_\mathrm{tor}|^2 \right\rangle_{\rho_\mathrm{tor}} = \frac{\int_{S(\rho_\mathrm{tor})} |\nabla \rho_\mathrm{tor}|^2\, dA / |\nabla \rho_\mathrm{tor}|}{\int_{S(\rho_\mathrm{tor})} dA / |\nabla \rho_\mathrm{tor}|}
$$

where $G_{\rho\rho}$ denotes this flux-surface-averaged metric coefficient, $\rho_\mathrm{tor}$ is the normalized toroidal-flux radius, $S(\rho_\mathrm{tor})$ is the magnetic flux surface with that label, $\nabla$ is the spatial gradient operator, $dA$ is the surface-area element, and $\langle\cdot\rangle_{\rho_\mathrm{tor}}$ denotes averaging over that flux surface.

The coordinate $\rho_\mathrm{tor}$ is constituted by $\rho_\mathrm{tor}=\sqrt{\Phi/\Phi_b}$, where $\Phi$ is the toroidal magnetic flux enclosed by the flux surface and $\Phi_b$ is its value at the plasma boundary. The scope is closed nested equilibrium flux surfaces; the aggregation convention is an average over the entire surface at fixed $\rho_\mathrm{tor}$.

This is not the pointwise quantity $|\nabla \rho_\mathrm{tor}|^2$, not the flux-surface average of $|\nabla \rho_\mathrm{tor}|$, and not a volume or time average. It belongs to the same flux-surface-averaged geometric-metric family as the [flux-surface-averaged inverse major radius](name:flux_surface_averaged_inverse_of_major_radius), but it characterizes the radial metric of the normalized toroidal-flux radius rather than a major-radius factor.

NAMES.name: flux_surface_averaged_toroidal_flux_coordinate_gradient_magnitude
NAMES.short: Geometric metric coefficient formed by averaging the local magnitude of the toroidal-flux-coordinate gradient over each nested magnetic flux surface.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the flux-surface average of the local geometric rate at which the toroidal flux coordinate changes through physical space. It is a scalar metric coefficient associated with nested magnetic surfaces.

The defining relation is

$$
\mathcal{G}(\mathcal{S}) = \left\langle \left|\nabla \rho_{\mathrm{tor}}\right| \right\rangle_{\mathcal{S}}
$$

where $\mathcal{G}(\mathcal{S})$ is the averaged metric coefficient, $\mathcal{S}$ is a magnetic flux surface, $\rho_{\mathrm{tor}}$ is the toroidal flux coordinate labeling nested magnetic surfaces, $\nabla$ is the spatial gradient, and the angle brackets with subscript $\mathcal{S}$ denote averaging over that surface.

The quantity applies to the complete nested magnetic flux surface and is aggregated over the surface rather than evaluated at a point, along a line, or over a volume. It represents the average of the gradient magnitude, not a directional component and not the local unaveraged value.

It is obtained by applying flux-surface averaging to the local [toroidal flux coordinate gradient magnitude](name:toroidal_flux_coordinate_gradient_magnitude). Unlike [flux-surface-averaged square of toroidal flux coordinate gradient magnitude](name:flux_surface_averaged_square_of_toroidal_flux_coordinate_gradient_magnitude), it averages the magnitude itself rather than its square.

NAMES.name: gap_at_outboard_midplane
NAMES.short: Signed major-radius separation between a measurement position and the magnetic separatrix, mapped along its flux surface to the outboard midplane; positive outside the separatrix.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the signed major-radius separation between a measurement position and the magnetic separatrix after the position is mapped along its flux surface to the outboard midplane. It applies pointwise to the selected position and separatrix rather than to an average or to the separation between two separatrices.

With the mapped position and separatrix evaluated at the outboard midplane, the separation is defined by

$$
\Delta R_{\mathrm{sep,mid}} = R_{\mathrm{pos,mid}} - R_{\mathrm{sep,mid}}
$$

where $\Delta R_{\mathrm{sep,mid}}$ is the mapped separatrix distance, $R_{\mathrm{pos,mid}}$ is the major-radius coordinate of the mapped measurement position, and $R_{\mathrm{sep,mid}}$ is the major-radius coordinate of the separatrix at the outboard midplane.

The quantity refers to one measurement position, its associated magnetic flux surface, and one selected separatrix. It is a signed major-radius separation in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, with no flux-surface, spatial, species, or time aggregation. It is not the shortest geometric distance, a plasma-wall clearance, or the distance between inner and outer separatrices.

The flux-surface assignment can be expressed through the [normalized poloidal flux coordinate at measurement position](name:normalized_poloidal_flux_coordinate_at_measurement_position), while the two terms in the difference are outboard-midplane radial coordinates of the type defined by [radial coordinate at outboard midplane](name:radial_coordinate_at_outboard_midplane). The mapping therefore converts the original position into a common outboard-midplane comparison before the major-radius difference is taken.

NAMES.name: lower_triangularity_of_flux_surface
NAMES.short: Dimensionless lower triangularity shape parameter for a nested magnetic flux surface, given by the normalized inward radial displacement of its lower vertical extremum.
NAMES.long:
Lower triangularity of a flux surface is the dimensionless triangularity shape parameter defined at the lower vertical extremum of a nested magnetic flux surface. It is the normalized inward displacement in major radius $R$ of that lower extremum relative to the magnetic-axis reference.

For the lower vertical extremum, the defining relation is:

$$
\delta_{\mathrm{lower}} = \frac{R_{\mathrm{axis}} - R_{\mathrm{lower}}}{a}
$$

where $\delta_{\mathrm{lower}}$ is lower triangularity, $R_{\mathrm{axis}}$ is the major-radius coordinate of the magnetic axis, $R_{\mathrm{lower}}$ is the major-radius coordinate of the lower vertical extremum, and $a$ is the minor radius of the same flux surface. These coordinates are defined in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius measured from the machine symmetry axis, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

This quantity applies independently to each nested magnetic flux surface and is a geometrical property of the surface rather than a plasma-population quantity. It resolves the lower vertical extremum only; it is not averaged over flux surfaces or combined with the upper extremum. It is distinct from [lower triangularity of a flux surface boundary](name:lower_triangularity_of_plasma_boundary), which describes the outer plasma boundary rather than an arbitrary nested surface.

It is the lower-extremum branch of [triangularity of a flux surface](name:triangularity_of_flux_surface), whose parent quantity permits the relevant upper or lower vertical extremum. The corresponding [upper triangularity of a flux surface](name:upper_triangularity_of_flux_surface) uses the upper vertical extremum, while [elongation of a flux surface](name:elongation_of_flux_surface) describes vertical-to-horizontal shaping rather than triangular displacement.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the lower vertical extremum lies at smaller major radius $R$ than the magnetic-axis reference, corresponding to an inward displacement.

NAMES.name: magnetic_shear_at_flux_surface
NAMES.short: Dimensionless logarithmic radial gradient of the safety factor on a magnetic flux surface, measuring how magnetic-field-line pitch changes across neighboring surfaces.
NAMES.long:
Magnetic shear at a magnetic flux surface is the local logarithmic radial variation of the safety factor, expressing the change in magnetic-field-line pitch between neighboring nested surfaces.

It is defined by

$$
s(\rho_\mathrm{tor}) = \frac{\rho_\mathrm{tor}}{q(\rho_\mathrm{tor})}\frac{dq(\rho_\mathrm{tor})}{d\rho_\mathrm{tor}}
$$

where $s$ is magnetic shear, $\rho_\mathrm{tor}$ is the toroidal-flux radial coordinate labeling the magnetic flux surface, and $q$ is the safety factor on that surface.

The quantity applies to the equilibrium magnetic geometry of the specified magnetic flux surface without restricting the surface to a particular plasma region, species, or particle population. It is a local value associated with one surface, not a sum, volume integral, or average over multiple surfaces.

It is distinct from the corresponding values at special loci such as the [magnetic axis](name:magnetic_shear_at_magnetic_axis), [plasma boundary](name:magnetic_shear_at_plasma_boundary), or [internal transport barrier](name:magnetic_shear_at_internal_transport_barrier). The expression relates magnetic shear directly to the logarithmic derivative of the safety factor with respect to the toroidal-flux radial coordinate.

NAMES.name: maximum_magnetic_field_magnitude
NAMES.short: Largest magnitude of the magnetic-field vector over a specified evaluation domain, distinguishing total field strength from any signed field component.
NAMES.long:
The maximum magnetic-field magnitude is the greatest total field strength attained within the physical evaluation domain associated with the quantity.

The defining extremum is

$$
B_{\max} = \max_{\mathbf{x}\in D} \left\lVert \mathbf{B}(\mathbf{x}) \right\rVert
$$

where $B_{\max}$ is the maximum magnetic-field magnitude, $\mathbf{B}(\mathbf{x})$ is the magnetic-field vector at spatial point $\mathbf{x}$, and $D$ is the specified evaluation domain.

The domain may be a nested magnetic flux surface or a coil-conductor surface, as established by the physical context. The maximum operation aggregates the field magnitude over all points in $D$ and returns its largest value; it does not represent a spatial average or a particular field component.

This quantity selects the modulus of the magnetic-field vector before applying the maximum operation. It is therefore the magnitude-specific child of [maximum magnetic field](name:maximum_magnetic_field), whose parent concept leaves the scalar field being maximized unspecified. It excludes maxima of signed toroidal, poloidal, radial, or other individual magnetic-field components.

NAMES.name: mhd_energy
NAMES.short: Global plasma stored energy obtained from the volume integral of total kinetic pressure, including thermal and fast-particle pressure contributions.
NAMES.long:
MHD plasma stored energy is the global energy content assigned to the plasma by integrating its equilibrium-reconstructed total kinetic pressure over the full plasma volume. It includes thermal and fast-particle contributions rather than representing only one pressure population.

The defining relation is

$$
W_{\mathrm{MHD}} = \frac{3}{2}\int_{V_{\mathrm{plasma}}} p_{\mathrm{tot}}\,dV
$$

where $W_{\mathrm{MHD}}$ is the MHD plasma stored energy, $p_{\mathrm{tot}}$ is the total kinetic pressure determined by the equilibrium reconstruction, $V_{\mathrm{plasma}}$ is the complete plasma volume, and $dV$ is the differential volume element.

This is a global volume-integrated quantity over all included plasma populations. It is distinct from [thermal plasma energy](name:thermal_plasma_energy), which integrates thermal pressure only, and from [diamagnetic energy](name:diamagnetic_energy), which is restricted to pressure perpendicular to the local magnetic field. The factor $3/2$ defines the stored-energy convention used for the total kinetic-pressure integral.

NAMES.name: minor_radius_of_plasma_boundary
NAMES.short: Half the difference between the maximum and minimum major-radius coordinates of the last closed plasma-boundary contour, defining its horizontal cross-sectional size.
NAMES.long:
The minor radius is the effective horizontal semi-axis of the last closed plasma-boundary contour and characterizes the radial extent of the plasma cross-section.

The minor radius $a$ is defined by

$$
a = \frac{R_{\max} - R_{\min}}{2}
$$

where $a$ is the minor radius, $R_{\max}$ is the maximum major-radius coordinate on the boundary contour, and $R_{\min}$ is the minimum major-radius coordinate on that contour.

This quantity applies to the complete last closed plasma-boundary contour and is determined from its global major-radius extrema. It is a nonnegative geometric size parameter, not a local major-radius coordinate such as the [radial coordinate at the outboard midplane](name:radial_coordinate_at_outboard_midplane) and not a flux-surface average.

The [elongation of the plasma boundary](name:elongation_of_plasma_boundary) uses this minor radius as the horizontal reference semi-axis when forming the boundary's vertical-to-horizontal shape ratio.

NAMES.name: normalized_plasma_internal_inductance
NAMES.short: Dimensionless li_3 parameter measuring poloidal magnetic-field peaking through a plasma-volume integral normalized by total plasma current and a reference major radius.
NAMES.long:
The quantity is the normalized internal inductance of the plasma current distribution. It characterizes the peaking of the poloidal magnetic field generated by the total plasma current, rather than a ratio formed only from a boundary field.

Under the li_3 definition,

$$
l_i = \frac{2}{R_0\mu_0^2 I_p^2} \int_{V_p} B_p^2\,dV
$$

where $l_i$ is the normalized internal inductance, $R_0$ is the reference major radius, $\mu_0$ is the vacuum permeability, $I_p$ is the total signed plasma current, $B_p$ is the magnitude of the poloidal magnetic field, $V_p$ is the plasma volume, and $dV$ is a differential volume element.

This is a global equilibrium quantity. The aggregation is a volume integral of the squared poloidal-field magnitude over the entire plasma volume, normalized by the square of the total plasma current; it does not select a separate species, charge state, orbit class, or localized position.

It is distinct from the dimensional [plasma inductance]: the present quantity includes the reference-radius and vacuum-permeability normalization in the defining expression and is not a local inductance, a flux-surface average, or a boundary-field ratio.

If $L_p$ denotes the [plasma inductance], the normalized quantity is related by $l_i = 2L_p/(R_0\mu_0)$. Thus, under the same reference normalization, a larger value indicates a more strongly concentrated poloidal-field energy distribution associated with the plasma current.

NAMES.name: normalized_toroidal_flux_coordinate
NAMES.short: Dimensionless radial label equal to the square root of toroidal magnetic flux normalized between the magnetic axis and equilibrium boundary.
NAMES.long:
The normalized toroidal flux coordinate is a dimensionless label for nested magnetic surfaces, increasing outward from the magnetic axis toward the equilibrium boundary. It is a magnetic-surface coordinate, not a cylindrical distance or a local vector component.

$$
\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}} = \left(\frac{\Phi_{\mathrm{tor}} - \Phi_{\mathrm{tor,axis}}}{\Phi_{\mathrm{tor,boundary}} - \Phi_{\mathrm{tor,axis}}}\right)^{1/2}
$$

where $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}$ is the normalized toroidal flux coordinate, $\Phi_{\mathrm{tor}}$ is the toroidal magnetic flux enclosed by the labeled surface, $\Phi_{\mathrm{tor,axis}}$ is its value at the magnetic axis, and $\Phi_{\mathrm{tor,boundary}}$ is its value at the equilibrium boundary used for normalization.

The coordinate applies to nested magnetic surfaces and to mapped physical locations assigned to those surfaces. It is zero at the magnetic axis and one at the chosen equilibrium boundary; each value is a single surface label, with no summation, averaging, species aggregation, or mode aggregation. Locus-specific quantities such as the [normalized toroidal flux coordinate at a beam-tracing point](name:normalized_toroidal_flux_coordinate_at_beam_tracing_point) and the [normalized toroidal flux coordinate at a measurement position](name:normalized_toroidal_flux_coordinate_at_measurement_position) are evaluations of this same coordinate.

This quantity is distinct from the dimensionful [toroidal flux coordinate](name:toroidal_flux_coordinate), because it is normalized to the axis-to-boundary interval and transformed by a square root. It also differs from the [normalized poloidal flux coordinate](name:normalized_poloidal_flux_coordinate), which uses poloidal rather than toroidal magnetic flux, and from the [normalized minor radius of a flux surface](name:normalized_minor_radius_of_flux_surface), which is based on geometric extent rather than enclosed toroidal flux.

NAMES.name: normalized_toroidal_flux_coordinate_at_constraint_position
NAMES.short: Dimensionless radial label locating an equilibrium constraint on a nested magnetic surface, normalized from the magnetic axis to the last closed flux surface.
NAMES.long:
This quantity assigns the radial magnetic-surface coordinate of an equilibrium constraint position. It identifies the nested flux surface passing through that position rather than the physical quantity being constrained.

The normalized toroidal flux label is defined by

$$
\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}} = \left(\frac{\Phi_{\mathrm{tor}} - \Phi_{\mathrm{tor,axis}}}{\Phi_{\mathrm{tor,LCFS}} - \Phi_{\mathrm{tor,axis}}}\right)^{1/2}
$$

where $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}$ is the normalized toroidal flux coordinate, $\Phi_{\mathrm{tor}}$ is the toroidal magnetic flux enclosed by the surface through the constraint position, $\Phi_{\mathrm{tor,axis}}$ is its value at the magnetic axis, and $\Phi_{\mathrm{tor,LCFS}}$ is its value at the last closed flux surface (LCFS).

The quantity is evaluated pointwise at one equilibrium constraint position within the nested closed-flux-surface region. With this normalization, it is zero at the magnetic axis and one at the LCFS; it is not a flux-surface average, volume average, integral, or value of the constrained current, density, pressure, or safety factor.

This entry is the locus-specific evaluation of the parent [normalized toroidal flux coordinate](name:normalized_toroidal_flux_coordinate). It differs from [normalized toroidal flux coordinate at measurement position](name:normalized_toroidal_flux_coordinate_at_measurement_position) because its locus is an equilibrium constraint position rather than a diagnostic measurement location.

NAMES.name: parallel_flux_surface_averaged_current_density_due_to_wave_driven_current_drive
NAMES.short: Flux-surface-averaged field-aligned conventional plasma current density generated non-inductively by electromagnetic-wave–particle interactions.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the scalar field-aligned component of the conventional plasma current generated by electromagnetic-wave–particle interactions. It represents the wave-driven contribution to current flowing along the magnetic field on a magnetic flux surface.

For a magnetic flux surface labeled by the poloidal flux coordinate $\psi$, the flux-surface-averaged parallel current density is defined by

$$
j_{\parallel,\mathrm{FSA}}(\psi) = \frac{\left\langle \mathbf{J}_{\mathrm{wave}} \cdot \mathbf{B} \right\rangle_{\psi}}{B_0(\psi)}
$$

where $j_{\parallel,\mathrm{FSA}}$ is this scalar current-density quantity, $\mathbf{J}_{\mathrm{wave}}$ is the conventional current-density contribution generated by wave–particle interactions, $\mathbf{B}$ is the magnetic-field vector, $\langle\cdot\rangle_{\psi}$ denotes averaging over the flux surface labeled by $\psi$, and $B_0(\psi)$ is the reference magnetic-field magnitude used for the parallel-current normalization.

The quantity applies to the wave-driven current contribution from the plasma populations participating in the electromagnetic-wave interaction and uses a flux-surface average rather than a local value. It excludes inductive current and current contributions from non-wave mechanisms, and it is distinct from the full vector [flux-surface-averaged wave-driven current density](name:flux_surface_averaged_current_density_due_to_wave_driven_current_drive).

It is the magnetic-field-aligned scalar projection of that vector parent, retaining only the component parallel to the local magnetic field; [parallel current density due to ohmic current drive](name:parallel_current_density_due_to_ohmic_current_drive) instead represents the inductive resistive contribution.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the wave-driven conventional current flows in the direction of the magnetic field, so that $\mathbf{J}_{\mathrm{wave}} \cdot \mathbf{B} > 0$.

NAMES.name: plasma_beta
NAMES.short: Plasma beta is a dimensionless measure of total plasma pressure relative to a magnetic-pressure scale, with the pressure aggregation, field reference, and any additional normalization supplied by each specialized plasma-beta definition.
NAMES.long:
Plasma beta is a dimensionless equilibrium measure of the total pressure content of the confined plasma relative to a magnetic-pressure scale. It names the common plasma-pressure-to-magnetic-pressure concept without selecting a particular magnetic-field reference, pressure aggregation, or additional normalization.

The generic specialization relation is

$$
\beta_\star = \mathcal{N}_\star\!\left(\frac{2\mu_0\,p_{\mathrm{plasma},\star}}{B_{\mathrm{ref},\star}^{2}}\right)
$$

where $\beta_\star$ is a specialized plasma beta, $\star$ labels the specialized definition, $p_{\mathrm{plasma},\star}$ is the plasma-pressure measure prescribed by that definition, $B_{\mathrm{ref},\star}$ is the corresponding magnetic-field reference, $\mu_0$ is the vacuum permeability, and $\mathcal{N}_\star$ is any additional normalization operation prescribed by that definition. Where no additional normalization is prescribed, $\mathcal{N}_\star$ is the identity operation.

The scope is the confined plasma in an equilibrium state. Its aggregation convention is not fixed at the parent level: each specialized plasma-beta name supplies the pressure aggregate, the included plasma populations, and the plasma region over which that aggregate is formed. This parent excludes species-resolved pressure measures, local beta values, and any fixed choice of toroidal, poloidal, vacuum, or total magnetic-field reference unless that choice is made by a specialized name.

Concrete plasma-beta names specialize this parent by fixing $p_{\mathrm{plasma},\star}$, $B_{\mathrm{ref},\star}$, and $\mathcal{N}_\star$. The child [normalized toroidal plasma beta](name:normalized_toroidal_plasma_beta) is a specialized plasma beta with a toroidal-field pressure scale and an additional normalization; related axis-specific beta quantities such as [poloidal beta](name:poloidal_beta) and [toroidal beta](name:toroidal_beta) fix their magnetic-pressure scale according to their own definitions.

NAMES.name: normalized_toroidal_plasma_beta
NAMES.short: Normalized toroidal plasma beta, conventionally denoted β_N, is the ratio of toroidal plasma beta times plasma minor radius and reference toroidal magnetic field to total plasma current, including the conventional factor 100.
NAMES.long:
Normalized toroidal plasma beta, conventionally denoted $\beta_N$, is the ratio of toroidal plasma beta times plasma minor radius and reference toroidal magnetic field to total plasma current, including the conventional factor 100. It is a whole-plasma equilibrium beta metric based on the volume-averaged total perpendicular plasma pressure entering toroidal beta.

The defining relation is:

$$
\beta_N = 100\,\beta_{\mathrm{tor}}\,\frac{a B_0}{I_p}
$$

where $\beta_{\mathrm{tor}}$ is [beta](name:beta), the unnormalized toroidal plasma beta; $a$ is the plasma minor radius; $B_0$ is the reference toroidal magnetic field; and $I_p$ is the total plasma current. The factor $100$ and the prescribed numerical normalization of $a$, $B_0$, and $I_p$ are part of the definition.

The scope is the whole plasma. The pressure population is the total perpendicular plasma pressure represented by $\beta_{\mathrm{tor}}$, with the volume averaging inherited from [beta](name:beta); it is not restricted to thermal pressure.

This quantity is distinct from [beta](name:beta), which is the unnormalized toroidal pressure ratio, and from a thermal-pressure-only normalized toroidal beta. Within the global beta-metric family, $\beta_N$ rescales [beta](name:beta) by plasma size, reference-field, and current factors, whereas [poloidal_beta](name:poloidal_beta) uses a poloidal-field/current normalization.

NAMES.name: plasma_current
NAMES.short: Net toroidal electric current carried by the entire plasma column, obtained by integrating toroidal current density over its enclosed poloidal cross-section.
NAMES.long:
Plasma current is the net electric current carried by the full plasma population, represented as the toroidal current crossing a poloidal cross-section in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

$$
I_p = \int_{A_p} j_\phi\,\mathrm{d}A
$$

where $I_p$ is the total plasma current, $A_p$ is the enclosed poloidal cross-sectional area, $j_\phi$ is the toroidal component of the electric current density, and $\mathrm{d}A$ is the differential area element.

The quantity includes the algebraic sum of toroidal currents from all charged plasma species and charge states over the complete enclosed plasma cross-section. It is a global total rather than a local current density, a species-resolved contribution, or a current restricted to a particular physical mechanism.

It is the area integral of the toroidal projection of [current density](name:current_density). The narrower [toroidal total runaway-electron current](name:toroidal_total_runaway_electron_current) represents only the runaway-electron contribution and is not the full plasma current.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the net plasma current flows in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: plasma_pressure
NAMES.short: Plasma pressure is the isotropic kinetic pressure of the plasma, the scalar part of the kinetic pressure tensor used in equilibrium force balance. The unqualified quantity denotes an equilibrium scalar pressure, not a first-order pressure perturbation.
NAMES.long:
Plasma pressure is the isotropic kinetic pressure of the plasma, the scalar part of the kinetic pressure tensor in a fluid or magnetohydrodynamic description. It represents equilibrium mechanical stress from the plasma populations included in the pressure model and is not a perturbation amplitude.

The scalar pressure is the one-third trace of the kinetic pressure tensor:

$$
p = \frac{1}{3}\operatorname{tr}\mathbf{P}
$$

where $p$ is the plasma pressure, $\mathbf{P}$ is the kinetic pressure tensor, and $\operatorname{tr}$ denotes the tensor trace. For locally isotropic Maxwellian populations, an included population $s$ contributes $n_s k_B T_s$, where $n_s$ is the number density of population $s$, $T_s$ is its temperature, and $k_B$ is the Boltzmann constant.

The unqualified quantity applies to equilibrium scalar kinetic pressure; it is additive over the included plasma populations and does not imply normalization, volume integration, or selection of only a bulk-thermal, fast-particle, or perturbed population subset. It excludes magnetic pressure, dynamic ram pressure, anisotropic pressure components, and any individual component of the pressure tensor.

[Total plasma pressure](name:total_plasma_pressure) is the specialization in which all represented equilibrium kinetic pressure contributions are included, while [thermal plasma pressure](name:thermal_plasma_pressure) is restricted to bulk thermal electron and ion populations. [Perturbed plasma pressure](name:perturbed_plasma_pressure) denotes a first-order variation about an equilibrium pressure and is not part of the equilibrium quantity defined here. In magnetohydrostatic equilibrium, the pressure gradient satisfies $\nabla p = \mathbf{j} \times \mathbf{B}$, where $\nabla p$ is the spatial gradient of plasma pressure, $\mathbf{j}$ is the electric current density, and $\mathbf{B}$ is the magnetic field; on nested magnetic flux surfaces this pressure may be expressed as a function of the [poloidal magnetic flux](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux) $\psi$, where $\psi$ is the poloidal magnetic flux.

NAMES.name: poloidal_angle_of_flux_surface
NAMES.short: Pointwise geometric angle locating a position around a magnetic flux-surface cross-section, measured clockwise from its low-field-side midplane.
NAMES.long:
Poloidal angle is the geometric angular coordinate assigned pointwise to each position on the poloidal cross-section of a specified magnetic flux surface. It is measured from the geometric center of that cross-section rather than from magnetic-field-line distance.

At a point on the surface, the angle $\theta$ is defined by

$$
\theta = \operatorname{atan2}\!\left(-(Z-Z_0),\,R-R_0\right)
$$

where $\theta$ is the poloidal angle, $\operatorname{atan2}$ returns the signed principal angle, $R$ is the major-radius coordinate, $Z$ is the vertical coordinate, and $(R_0,Z_0)$ is the geometric center of the flux-surface cross-section. These coordinates belong to the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $\phi$ is the toroidal angle.

The quantity applies to individual points on one magnetic flux surface and has no averaging or summation over the surface. The surface is identified by a constant [poloidal magnetic flux at a flux surface](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_flux_surface) value; the angle therefore parameterizes position around that surface rather than assigning one unique angle to the entire surface. It is a geometric angle, distinct from a straight-field-line poloidal angle.

This quantity specializes [poloidal angle](name:poloidal_angle_of_flux_surface) by making the flux-surface locus explicit and provides the angular coordinate used to distinguish positions around the surface's poloidal cross-section.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the point advances clockwise from the low-field-side midplane in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: poloidal_beta
NAMES.short: Poloidal beta is a dimensionless measure of total plasma pressure relative to the magnetic-pressure scale of the plasma-current-generated poloidal field.
NAMES.long:
Poloidal beta is a dimensionless equilibrium measure of the total pressure content of the confined plasma relative to the magnetic-pressure scale generated by the plasma current. It characterizes pressure relative to the poloidal magnetic field rather than the toroidal magnetic field.

The defining relation is

$$
\beta_p = \frac{4\int_V p\,dV}{R_0\,\mu_0\,I_p^2}
$$

where $\beta_p$ is poloidal beta, $p$ is the total plasma pressure, $V$ is the confined plasma volume, $dV$ is a differential volume element, $R_0$ is the reference major radius, $\mu_0$ is the vacuum permeability, and $I_p$ is the total toroidal plasma current.

The pressure integral extends over the entire confined plasma volume and aggregates the pressure of all included plasma populations, so this quantity is global rather than local or species-resolved. It excludes any separate normalization based on minor radius or reference toroidal magnetic-field strength.

As the poloidal-field member of the [beta](name:beta) family, poloidal beta uses a current- and major-radius-based poloidal magnetic-pressure scale. It is distinct from [toroidal_beta](name:toroidal_beta), which normalizes pressure to a toroidal magnetic-field scale, and from [normalized_toroidal_plasma_beta](name:normalized_toroidal_plasma_beta), which applies an additional engineering normalization.

NAMES.name: poloidal_current_function
NAMES.short: Major-radius-weighted toroidal magnetic-field function used in axisymmetric equilibria and vacuum fields; in ideal-MHD plasma it is constant on each magnetic flux surface.
NAMES.long:
The poloidal current function is the major-radius-weighted toroidal magnetic field that defines the equilibrium $F$-function. It provides a common description for the toroidal field in axisymmetric plasma equilibria and in current-free vacuum magnetic fields.

In the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, the defining relation is

$$
F(R,Z) = R B_\phi(R,Z)
$$

where $F$ is the poloidal current function, $R$ is major radius measured from the machine symmetry axis, $B_\phi$ is the toroidal component of the magnetic field, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

For an axisymmetric ideal-MHD plasma equilibrium, $F$ is a flux function: it is constant on each nested magnetic flux surface and can therefore be expressed as a function of the poloidal magnetic-flux coordinate. The quantity describes the full toroidal magnetic field represented by the equilibrium; it is not a surface or volume integral, an average, or a restriction to a particular current source.

The [vacuum poloidal current function](name:vacuum_poloidal_current_function) is the corresponding external-coil contribution in a current-free vacuum region, whereas the unqualified quantity denotes the general $F$-function. The [product of the poloidal current function and its derivative with respect to the poloidal magnetic flux coordinate](name:product_of_poloidal_current_function_and_derivative_with_respect_to_poloidal_magnetic_flux_coordinate_of_poloidal_current_function) is a distinct Grad–Shafranov source term formed from $F$ and its flux derivative.

NAMES.name: poloidal_length_of_flux_surface
NAMES.short: Poloidal arc length of a closed magnetic-flux-surface contour in an equilibrium poloidal cross-section, measuring the perimeter of that selected surface.
NAMES.long:
The poloidal length is the perimeter of the closed contour formed by one selected magnetic flux surface in a poloidal cross-section. It is a geometric property of the surface boundary, rather than its enclosed area, volume, or toroidal circumference.

The contour length is defined in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height:

$$
L_{\mathrm{pol}} = \int_{\theta_a}^{\theta_b} \sqrt{\left(\frac{dR(\theta)}{d\theta}\right)^2 + \left(\frac{dZ(\theta)}{d\theta}\right)^2}\,d\theta
$$

Here $L_{\mathrm{pol}}$ is the poloidal length, $\theta$ is any smooth parameter along the contour, $R(\theta)$ and $Z(\theta)$ are its cylindrical coordinate functions, and $\theta_a$ and $\theta_b$ are parameter values at the same contour point after one complete circuit. The contour is taken at fixed toroidal angle $\phi$.

The quantity applies to one magnetic flux surface and includes the complete closed poloidal contour, with no averaging or summation over multiple surfaces. It excludes local arc segments and geometric quantities associated with the enclosed region. The selected surface may be labeled by the [normalized poloidal flux coordinate](name:normalized_poloidal_flux_coordinate).

Unlike [elongation of a flux surface](name:elongation_of_flux_surface), which describes a scale-independent cross-sectional shape ratio, the poloidal length retains the absolute geometric scale of the contour.

NAMES.name: poloidal_magnetic_field
NAMES.short: Poloidal magnetic-field strength of the local total induction, formed from radial and vertical components in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
Local total poloidal magnetic induction is the magnitude of the total magnetic-field vector projected into the poloidal plane spanned by the radial and vertical directions. It represents the local poloidal field strength without selecting a source contribution, perturbation state, or named evaluation locus.

In the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height, the defining relation is

$$
B_p = \sqrt{B_R^2 + B_Z^2}
$$

where $B_p$ is the poloidal magnetic-field strength, $B_R$ is the radial component of the local total [magnetic induction](name:magnetic_field), and $B_Z$ is its vertical component. The radial direction follows increasing $R$, and the vertical direction follows increasing $Z$.

The quantity is pointwise and applies wherever the local total magnetic induction is defined, including confined plasma and surrounding vacuum. It has no particle-species or population aggregation and is not spatially averaged, integrated, or summed over a region. When associated with a field-sensing location, it denotes the local measured field strength rather than a value defined as a reconstructed equilibrium estimate.

Unlike the signed [radial magnetic-field component](name:radial_magnetic_field) and [vertical magnetic-field component](name:vertical_magnetic_field), this quantity is the nonnegative magnitude of their combined poloidal projection. Together with the [toroidal magnetic-field component](name:toroidal_magnetic_field), it specifies the decomposition of the local total magnetic induction into poloidal and toroidal parts.

NAMES.name: poloidal_magnetic_flux
NAMES.short: Poloidal magnetic flux is the signed surface integral of the magnetic field over a surface bounded by a closed toroidal contour of a nested magnetic flux surface. It labels nested magnetic flux surfaces and is complementary to toroidal magnetic flux.
NAMES.long:
Poloidal magnetic flux is the signed surface integral of the magnetic field over a surface bounded by a closed toroidal contour of a nested magnetic flux surface. It is the poloidal member of the [magnetic flux](name:magnetic_flux) family and is the flux function used to label nested magnetic flux surfaces in an axisymmetric equilibrium.

The poloidal magnetic flux $\psi$ associated with a closed toroidal contour $C$ is defined by the magnetic-flux integral over an oriented surface $S_C$ whose boundary is $C$:

$$
\psi(C) = \int_{S_C} \mathbf{B} \cdot d\mathbf{A}
$$

where $\psi(C)$ is the poloidal magnetic flux associated with $C$, $C$ is the closed toroidal contour, $S_C$ is the oriented surface with $\partial S_C=C$, $\mathbf{B}$ is the [magnetic-field vector](name:magnetic_field), $d\mathbf{A}=\hat{\mathbf{n}}\,dA$ is the oriented area element, $\hat{\mathbf{n}}$ is the unit normal set by the surface orientation, and $dA$ is the scalar surface-area element.

The unqualified quantity denotes the net integral over the whole chosen toroidal-boundary surface, including all magnetic-field contributions, with no source separation, weighting, or averaging. It applies to the equilibrium magnetic configuration wherever the scalar flux function is defined; on nested closed magnetic flux surfaces, all points on the same surface share the same $\psi$ value.

Poloidal magnetic flux is distinct from the local magnetic field, from magnetic-field components or magnitudes, from a normalized flux coordinate derived from $\psi$, and from a time derivative such as loop voltage. It is complementary to [toroidal magnetic flux](name:toroidal_magnetic_flux), which uses the poloidal cross-section enclosed by a flux surface rather than a toroidal-boundary surface; [poloidal magnetic flux at flux surface](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_flux_surface) is the evaluation of $\psi$ on a specified flux surface.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the net magnetic-field projection through the toroidal-boundary surface is along the right-hand-rule area orientation for a boundary contour directed toward increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_flux_surface
NAMES.short: Signed poloidal magnetic flux assigned to a nested magnetic surface, serving as the equilibrium label for its position in the plasma.
NAMES.long:
Poloidal magnetic flux at a flux surface is the signed magnetic flux through a horizontal disk centered on the toroidal symmetry axis and bounded by that surface. In an axisymmetric equilibrium, it is constant over each nested magnetic surface and provides its absolute, unnormalized flux label.

The poloidal flux at cylindrical coordinates $(R,Z)$ is defined by

$$
\psi(R,Z) = \int_0^R B_Z(R',Z)\,2\pi R'\,dR'
$$

where $\psi$ is the poloidal magnetic flux, $R$ is major radius, $Z$ is vertical height, $R'$ is the integration radius, and $B_Z$ is the vertical magnetic-field component, all expressed in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

This quantity applies to nested equilibrium magnetic surfaces within the plasma and represents the signed physical flux itself, not a flux-surface average, species sum, or normalized radial coordinate. It is distinct from the magnetic flux linked by a [poloidal magnetic flux of a flux loop](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux_of_flux_loop), which is defined by an oriented diagnostic-loop surface rather than by an equilibrium flux surface.

The [normalized poloidal flux coordinate](name:normalized_poloidal_flux_coordinate) is obtained by shifting and scaling this poloidal-flux label between its magnetic-axis and plasma-boundary values; the present quantity retains the absolute label.
NAMES.sign: Positive when $B_Z$ points in the $+Z$ direction through the integration disk.

NAMES.name: poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_magnetic_axis
NAMES.short: Signed poloidal magnetic flux evaluated at the magnetic axis, providing the inner reference value for normalized poloidal-flux coordinates.
NAMES.long:
Poloidal magnetic flux at the magnetic axis is the signed value of the poloidal flux function at the central extremum associated with nested magnetic surfaces.

The defining evaluation is

$$
\psi_\mathrm{axis} = \psi(R_\mathrm{axis}, Z_\mathrm{axis})
$$

where $\psi_\mathrm{axis}$ is the poloidal magnetic flux at the magnetic axis, $\psi$ is the poloidal magnetic-flux function, $R_\mathrm{axis}$ is the major-radius coordinate of the magnetic axis, and $Z_\mathrm{axis}$ is its vertical coordinate. The coordinates are expressed in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height; $Z_\mathrm{axis}$ is the [vertical coordinate of the magnetic axis](name:vertical_coordinate_of_magnetic_axis).

This quantity applies specifically to the equilibrium magnetic field at the magnetic axis rather than to an arbitrary point or a plasma region. It is a single point evaluation with no species selection, regional aggregation, or flux-surface averaging.

The value is an unnormalized flux reference and is distinct from [poloidal magnetic flux at the plasma boundary](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_plasma_boundary), which supplies the outer reference value. Together, these two endpoint values define the flux interval used by the [normalized poloidal flux coordinate](name:normalized_poloidal_flux_coordinate).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the poloidal flux is oriented so that the vertical magnetic field through the defining horizontal disk points in the $+Z$ direction.

NAMES.name: poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_plasma_boundary
NAMES.short: Signed poloidal magnetic flux evaluated on the last closed flux surface, providing the outer reference for normalized poloidal-flux coordinates.
NAMES.long:
The poloidal magnetic flux at the plasma boundary is the signed magnetic flux through a horizontal disk whose edge lies on the last closed flux surface. It is the outer boundary value of the poloidal magnetic-flux function for the confined plasma.

In the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height, the boundary value for an axisymmetric equilibrium is

$$
\psi_b = \psi(R_b,Z_b) = \int_0^{R_b} B_Z(R',Z_b)\,2\pi R'\,dR'
$$

where $\psi_b$ is the poloidal magnetic flux at the plasma boundary, $\psi(R_b,Z_b)$ is the poloidal magnetic-flux function at a selected boundary point, $(R_b,Z_b)$ are that point's cylindrical coordinates, $B_Z$ is the vertical magnetic-field component, $R'$ is the integration variable representing major radius, and $\pi$ is the circle constant.

This quantity applies specifically to the last closed flux surface bounding the confined plasma. It is a single boundary value of the flux function, with no averaging over the boundary or enclosed plasma implied; it is distinct from the value at the magnetic axis given by [poloidal magnetic flux at the magnetic axis](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_magnetic_axis).

The boundary value supplies the outer endpoint for [normalized poloidal flux coordinate](name:normalized_poloidal_flux_coordinate), while the magnetic-axis value supplies the corresponding inner endpoint. The poloidal flux function is constant along a given closed flux surface in the axisymmetric equilibrium description.
NAMES.sign: Positive when $B_Z$ on the defining horizontal disk points in the $+Z$ direction.

NAMES.name: poloidal_magnetic_flux_of_flux_loop
NAMES.short: Signed poloidal magnetic flux linked by an individual flux loop, defined by the magnetic field threading an oriented surface bounded by that loop.
NAMES.long:
Signed poloidal magnetic flux of a flux loop is the magnetic flux linked by an individual flux loop and threading an oriented surface whose boundary is that loop. It is the finite-surface flux linkage associated with the loop as a whole, not a local magnetic-field component.

The loop-linked flux is defined by the surface integral of the magnetic-field vector over a spanning surface of the loop:

$$
\Phi_{\mathrm{loop}} = \int_{S_{\mathrm{loop}}} \mathbf{B} \cdot d\mathbf{S}
$$

where $\Phi_{\mathrm{loop}}$ is the signed poloidal magnetic flux of the flux loop, $S_{\mathrm{loop}}$ is an oriented spanning surface bounded by the flux loop, $\mathbf{B}$ is the magnetic-field vector, and $d\mathbf{S}$ is the directed surface element on that surface.

The scope is one specified flux loop and the total flux through its complete spanning surface; no averaging over multiple loops or loop segments is implied. The quantity is distinct from a point-locus evaluation such as [poloidal magnetic flux at a sensor attachment point](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux_of_flux_loop), which evaluates a flux function at a specified position rather than integrating over a finite loop-bounded surface.

The defining surface is any oriented spanning surface with the same loop boundary and orientation; the absence of magnetic monopoles makes the linked flux independent of the particular spanning surface. This quantity is related to [poloidal magnetic flux](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux) as a loop-bounded flux linkage, and it must not be identified with [toroidal magnetic flux](name:toroidal_magnetic_flux), which uses a different flux-surface geometry; a reconstructed counterpart, [reconstructed poloidal magnetic flux of flux loop], shares the same magnetic quantity but represents a distinct value type when that distinction is made.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the magnetic-field vector has a positive net projection on the oriented surface element selected as positive for the flux loop.

NAMES.name: poloidal_plane_cross_sectional_area_of_flux_surface
NAMES.short: Geometric area enclosed by a closed magnetic-flux-surface contour in a fixed-toroidal-angle poloidal plane of the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
Geometric area enclosed by a closed magnetic-flux-surface contour in a fixed-toroidal-angle poloidal plane of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame is the poloidal-plane cross-sectional area of that flux surface. It characterizes the planar section enclosed by one closed magnetic flux surface.

The area is defined by the planar contour integral

$$
A_{\mathrm{pol}} = \frac{1}{2}\left|\oint_{\mathcal{C}} \left(R\,dZ - Z\,dR\right)\right|
$$

where $A_{\mathrm{pol}}$ is the poloidal-plane cross-sectional area, $\mathcal{C}$ is the closed poloidal contour of the flux surface at fixed toroidal angle $\phi$, $R$ is major radius measured from the toroidal symmetry axis, $Z$ is vertical height, $\phi$ is the toroidal angle in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, and $dR$ and $dZ$ are differentials along the contour. The absolute value makes the area independent of the contour traversal orientation.

This quantity applies to the nested family of closed magnetic flux surfaces from the magnetic axis to the plasma boundary; its limiting value at the magnetic axis is zero. It is an individual-surface geometric measure at fixed toroidal angle, not an average over toroidal angle, not an aggregate over multiple flux surfaces, and not a measure of open field-line regions.

It is distinct from the [surface area of flux surface](name:surface_area_of_flux_surface), which is the area of the toroidal surface generated by the flux-surface contour. At the last closed flux surface, the corresponding boundary quantity is the [poloidal-plane cross-sectional area of plasma boundary](name:poloidal_plane_cross_sectional_area_of_plasma_boundary); it is also distinct from the [volume of flux surface](name:volume_of_flux_surface), which measures the toroidal volume enclosed by the same nested surface.

NAMES.name: poloidal_plane_cross_sectional_area_of_plasma_boundary
NAMES.short: Area enclosed by the last closed magnetic flux surface in a poloidal plane, defining the equilibrium plasma cross-sectional size at the plasma boundary.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the geometric area enclosed by the last closed magnetic flux surface (LCFS), which forms the plasma boundary, in a poloidal cross-section.

In the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, the enclosed area is defined by

$$
A_{\rm LCFS} = \iint_{\mathcal{S}_{\rm LCFS}} dR\,dZ
$$

where $A_{\rm LCFS}$ is the LCFS cross-sectional area, $\mathcal{S}_{\rm LCFS}$ is the region enclosed by the LCFS contour at fixed toroidal angle $\phi$, $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, $Z$ is vertical height, and $dR\,dZ$ is the poloidal-plane area element.

This is a global equilibrium quantity for the complete plasma-boundary contour. It is not a local surface element, a flux-surface average, or the area of a toroidal surface formed by revolving the contour.

It is the plasma-boundary specialization of [poloidal plane cross-sectional area of a flux surface](name:poloidal_plane_cross_sectional_area_of_flux_surface), whose corresponding area is defined for an arbitrary closed magnetic flux surface; the LCFS is the outermost such surface enclosing the plasma.

NAMES.name: product_of_poloidal_current_function_and_derivative_with_respect_to_poloidal_magnetic_flux_coordinate_of_poloidal_current_function
NAMES.short: Grad–Shafranov equilibrium source term equal to the poloidal current function multiplied by its derivative with respect to poloidal magnetic flux.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the flux-function product that represents the toroidal-field contribution to the Grad–Shafranov equilibrium balance. It is formed from the poloidal current function and its variation across nested magnetic flux surfaces.

The defining expression is

$$
F\,\frac{dF}{d\psi}
$$

where $F$ is the [poloidal current function](name:poloidal_current_function), equal to the major-radius-weighted toroidal magnetic field, and $\psi$ is the signed [poloidal magnetic flux](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux) labeling the nested equilibrium flux surfaces.

This quantity applies to an axisymmetric equilibrium and is evaluated as a function of the poloidal-flux label. It has no species, population, region, or mechanism restriction, and its aggregation convention is the direct product of two flux-function quantities: it is neither a flux-surface average nor a sum over surfaces. It is distinct from the undifferentiated poloidal current function and from the product $F^2$.

Within the Grad–Shafranov equation, this term supplies the magnetic contribution associated with the variation of the poloidal current function and therefore participates in the balance determining toroidal current density and plasma pressure. The derivative factor distinguishes it from the parent [poloidal current function](name:poloidal_current_function) itself.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the poloidal current function and its derivative with respect to signed poloidal magnetic flux have the same sign; the poloidal current function is positive when the toroidal magnetic field points toward increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: radial_coordinate_at_inboard_midplane
NAMES.short: Major-radius coordinate of a magnetic flux surface at its inboard midplane intersection, locating the high-field-side point relative to the toroidal symmetry axis.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the major-radius coordinate of the point where a magnetic flux surface intersects the inboard midplane, identifying the high-field-side location of that surface relative to the toroidal symmetry axis. It is a locus-specific form of the [radial coordinate](name:radial_coordinate).

For a magnetic flux surface $\mathcal{S}$, the inboard-midplane radial coordinate is defined by

$$
R_{\mathrm{in}}(\mathcal{S}) = R\!\left(\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{in}}(\mathcal{S})\right)
$$

where $R_{\mathrm{in}}(\mathcal{S})$ is the quantity defined here, $R(\mathbf{x})$ is the major-radius coordinate of spatial position $\mathbf{x}$, $\mathcal{S}$ is the specified magnetic flux surface, and $\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{in}}(\mathcal{S})$ is its inboard midplane intersection. The coordinates are expressed in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

The scope is one coordinate value for each specified magnetic flux surface at its inboard, high-field-side midplane intersection. It is not a flux-surface average, a poloidal or toroidal average, or the corresponding outboard-midplane coordinate; the latter is represented by [radial coordinate at outboard midplane](name:radial_coordinate_at_outboard_midplane). Unlike [radial magnetic field](name:radial_magnetic_field), this quantity describes the location of a surface and not a magnetic-field component.

This quantity specializes [radial coordinate](name:radial_coordinate) by fixing the evaluation locus to the inboard midplane. Comparing it with the outboard-midplane value characterizes the horizontal extent and radial placement of the same magnetic flux surface.

NAMES.name: radial_coordinate_at_outboard_midplane
NAMES.short: Major-radius coordinate of the low-field-side intersection between a magnetic flux surface and the equatorial midplane.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the major-radius coordinate $R$ of the point where a specified magnetic flux surface intersects the equatorial midplane on its outboard, low-field side. It gives the outboard radial extent of that surface rather than a distance across the plasma or an average over the surface.

In the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, with unit-vector basis $(\hat{R},\hat{\phi},\hat{Z})$, the major-radius coordinate is related to the right-handed Cartesian basis $(\hat{x},\hat{y},\hat{z})$ by:

$$
R = \sqrt{x^2+y^2}
$$

Here $R$ is the perpendicular distance from the toroidal symmetry axis, $\phi$ is the toroidal angle, $Z$ is the vertical coordinate, and $x$ and $y$ are the horizontal Cartesian coordinates measured from that axis.

The quantity applies to one specified magnetic flux surface, identified by its poloidal magnetic-flux label $\psi$, where $\psi$ denotes the flux function labeling nested magnetic surfaces. It is evaluated only at the outboard intersection with the equatorial midplane; it excludes the inboard intersection and any flux-surface average.

It is a locus-specific specialization of the [radial coordinate](name:radial_coordinate), obtained by evaluating $R$ at the outboard midplane. The corresponding [inboard-midplane radial coordinate](name:radial_coordinate_at_inboard_midplane) describes the distinct high-field-side intersection of the same type of magnetic surface.

NAMES.name: radial_coordinate_of_closest_wall_point
NAMES.short: Major-radius coordinate R of the first-wall point nearest the plasma boundary, measured from the toroidal symmetry axis in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The quantity is the major-radius coordinate of the wall point selected as closest to the plasma boundary. It identifies that point’s perpendicular distance from the toroidal symmetry axis in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, phi, Z)$ frame.

The defining geometric relation is

$$
R_{\mathrm{cw}} = \left\lVert \mathbf{r}_{\mathrm{cw},\perp} \right\rVert
$$

where $R_{\mathrm{cw}}$ is the radial coordinate of the closest wall point and $\mathbf{r}_{\mathrm{cw},\perp}$ is the perpendicular displacement vector from the toroidal symmetry axis to that point.

The scope is the single wall point selected by its minimum proximity to the plasma boundary. This is a pointwise geometric coordinate with no plasma-population dependence and no averaging, summation, or integration. It is not the wall-to-boundary separation distance, nor is “closest” a statement that the point has the smallest major radius among all wall points.

This quantity is a locus-specific instance of [radial coordinate](name:radial_coordinate), restricted to the closest wall point rather than an arbitrary geometric reference position.

sources.leaf_definition: Major radius
sources.parent_definition: Position and distance to the plasma boundary of the point of the first wall which is the closest to plasma boundary

NAMES.name: radial_coordinate_of_conductor_cross_section
NAMES.short: Major-radius coordinate of the designated reference point associated with a conductor cross-section, measured from the toroidal symmetry axis.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the major-radius coordinate $R$ assigned to the designated reference point of a conductor cross-section. It locates the cross-section in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame without describing the cross-section's shape or extent.

The coordinate is defined from the horizontal Cartesian coordinates of the reference point:

$$
R = \sqrt{x^2+y^2}
$$

where $R$ is the perpendicular distance from the toroidal symmetry axis, and $x$ and $y$ are the horizontal coordinates in the right-handed Cartesian $(\hat{x},\hat{y},\hat{z})$ basis, with $\hat{z}$ aligned with the vertical direction.

The quantity applies to one conductor cross-section and represents one designated reference location for that cross-section. It is not summed over conductors, averaged over the cross-sectional area, or resolved pointwise along the cross-sectional outline.

Unlike the [radial outline of a coil conductor element](name:radial_outline_of_coil_conductor_element), which assigns radial coordinates to outline points, this quantity identifies the cross-section's reference geometry. It does not specify the reference point's vertical coordinate, toroidal angle, dimensions, or outline shape.

This is a conductor-cross-section specialization of the parent [radial coordinate](name:radial_coordinate); the parent definition supplies the general major-radius meaning, while this name fixes the locus to a conductor cross-section.

NAMES.name: radial_coordinate_of_control_surface
NAMES.short: Major-radius coordinate of each point on a control-surface outline, measured as perpendicular distance from the toroidal symmetry axis in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The radial coordinate of a control-surface outline point is its major-radius location, measured as perpendicular distance from the toroidal symmetry axis. It identifies the point's position in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

The defining geometric relation is

$$
R = \sqrt{X^2 + Y^2}
$$

where $R$ is the major-radius coordinate, and $X$ and $Y$ are the Cartesian coordinates perpendicular to the toroidal symmetry axis in the right-handed Cartesian $(\hat{x},\hat{y},\hat{z})$ basis. The cylindrical angle $\phi$ is the toroidal angular coordinate and $Z$ is the vertical coordinate of the same point.

This quantity applies to each point defining the control-surface outline. The control surface is defined by an outline in a poloidal plane and extends in the toroidal direction with axisymmetric geometry; this quantity is the local coordinate of an outline point, not a surface average or an integrated surface property. It is distinct from displacement along a flux-surface normal, which describes a different geometric direction.

This entry specializes [radial coordinate](name:radial_coordinate) by restricting its locus to a point on a control-surface outline while retaining the same major-radius definition.

NAMES.name: radial_coordinate_of_current_center
NAMES.short: Major-radius coordinate of the plasma-current centroid, obtained by normalizing the toroidal-current first moment over the poloidal plasma cross-section by total plasma current.
NAMES.long:
The radial coordinate of the current center is the major-radius location of the centroid of the toroidal plasma-current distribution. It identifies a current-weighted position and is distinct from the geometric centroid or the magnetic axis.

The coordinate is defined by the toroidal-current first moment:

$$
R_c = \frac{\displaystyle\int_{D_p} R\,j_\phi\,dS}{I_p}
$$

where $R_c$ is the major-radius coordinate of the current center, $R$ is the major-radius coordinate in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, $j_\phi$ is the toroidal component of the plasma [current density](name:current_density), $dS$ is an element of poloidal cross-sectional area, $D_p$ is the plasma current-carrying poloidal cross-section, and $I_p$ is the total toroidal plasma current, equal to the corresponding integral of $j_\phi$ over $D_p$.

The quantity applies to the full plasma-current distribution and uses a current-weighted first-moment aggregation over the poloidal cross-section. It excludes weighting by particle density, pressure, magnetic-field strength, or geometric area alone; the resulting position is therefore not a generic geometric center.

This quantity is a locus-specific instance of the general [radial coordinate](name:radial_coordinate), evaluated at the current center. Its vertical counterpart, [vertical coordinate of the current center](name:vertical_coordinate_of_current_center), supplies the corresponding vertical position needed to locate the current centroid in the cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.
