sources.parent_definition: Position and vertical velocity of the current centre

NAMES.name: radial_coordinate_of_dr_dz_zero_point
NAMES.short: Radial coordinate of the dR/dZ zero point is the R coordinate, in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame, of a plasma-boundary or separatrix point where R is locally stationary with respect to Z.
NAMES.long:
Radial coordinate of the dR/dZ zero point is the $R$ coordinate, in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, of a specified point on a plasma-boundary or separatrix contour where $R$ is locally stationary with respect to $Z$. In this frame, $R$ is major radius measured from the toroidal symmetry axis, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

The coordinate is defined by the stationary-radius condition on the specified contour:

$$
R_{\mathrm{dR/dZ=0}} = R(P_0), \qquad \left.\frac{dR}{dZ}\right|_{C,P_0} = 0
$$

where $R_{\mathrm{dR/dZ=0}}$ is the radial coordinate of the dR/dZ zero point, $P_0$ is the specified dR/dZ zero point, $C$ is the plasma-boundary or separatrix contour on which $P_0$ lies, $R(P_0)$ is the major-radius coordinate of $P_0$, $Z$ is the vertical-height coordinate, and $dR/dZ$ is the derivative of the contour coordinate $R$ with respect to $Z$ along $C$.

The scope is a single specified geometric point on the contour; the value is not an average over the contour, over toroidal angle $\phi$, or over all stationary points. If several points on the contour satisfy $dR/dZ=0$, the definition does not by itself impose an inboard, outboard, upper, or lower selection rule; each specified zero point has its own radial-coordinate value.

This quantity is only the cylindrical $R$ coordinate of the point, not a flux-surface-normal displacement or a flux-label coordinate. Together with the [vertical coordinate of the dR/dZ zero point], it locates the point in the poloidal $(R, Z)$ cross-section at fixed $\phi$ of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. It is distinct from the [radial coordinate of an X-point](name:radial_coordinate_of_x_point), which locates a magnetic null on a separatrix rather than a radial extremum of a boundary or separatrix contour.

NAMES.name: radial_coordinate_of_geometric_axis
NAMES.short: Major-radius coordinate locating the midpoint of the plasma boundary's radial extrema, thereby specifying the horizontal position of its geometric axis.
NAMES.long:
The radial coordinate of the geometric axis is the major-radius position of the plasma cross-section's geometric center, defined from the extrema of the plasma boundary in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

The geometric-axis coordinate is defined by

$$
R_{\mathrm{geo}} = \frac{R_{\max} + R_{\min}}{2}
$$

where $R_{\mathrm{geo}}$ is the major-radius coordinate of the geometric axis, and $R_{\max}$ and $R_{\min}$ are the maximum and minimum major-radius coordinates of the plasma boundary, respectively.

This quantity applies specifically to the geometric axis of the plasma cross-section and uses the midpoint aggregation of the boundary's radial extrema. It is distinct from the [radial_coordinate](name:radial_coordinate) of an arbitrary point or reference position and from the radial coordinate of the magnetic axis; its vertical counterpart is the [vertical coordinate of the geometric axis](name:vertical_coordinate_of_geometric_axis).

NAMES.name: radial_coordinate_of_magnetic_axis
NAMES.short: Major-radius coordinate locating the magnetic-axis O-point in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame around which nested closed flux surfaces are organized.
NAMES.long:
The radial coordinate of the magnetic axis is the major-radius location of the O-point, the local extremum of the poloidal magnetic flux around which nested closed magnetic flux surfaces are organized.

In terms of a right-handed Cartesian basis $(\hat{x},\hat{y},\hat{z})$ with $\hat{z}$ vertical, its major-radius coordinate is defined by

$$
R = \sqrt{x^2+y^2}
$$

where $R$ is the major-radius coordinate in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, and $x$ and $y$ are the Cartesian coordinates perpendicular to the toroidal symmetry axis.

This is a point value evaluated at the magnetic axis in the plasma poloidal cross-section; it is not a flux-surface average, region integral, or coordinate of an arbitrary magnetic or physical contour. It is distinct from [radial_coordinate_at_inboard_midplane](name:radial_coordinate_at_inboard_midplane), which locates a flux-surface intersection with the inboard midplane.

This quantity is the magnetic-axis specialization of [radial_coordinate](name:radial_coordinate): the parent applies to general points or reference positions, whereas this quantity fixes the locus to the magnetic-axis O-point.

NAMES.name: radial_coordinate_of_measurement_position
NAMES.short: Major-radius coordinate locating a measurement position by perpendicular distance from the toroidal symmetry axis in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The radial coordinate of a measurement position is the major-radius location of that position, defined by its perpendicular separation from the toroidal symmetry axis. It identifies a single generic measurement location, independent of the instrument or plasma quantity associated with that location.

The defining geometric relation is

$$
R_{\mathrm{meas}} = \left|\mathbf{r}_{\perp,\mathrm{meas}}\right|
$$

where $R_{\mathrm{meas}}$ is the major-radius coordinate of the measurement position, $\mathbf{r}_{\perp,\mathrm{meas}}$ is its perpendicular displacement from the toroidal symmetry axis, and the vertical bars denote the magnitude of that displacement. The coordinate is expressed in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

The scope is one measurement position; no averaging, summation, or integration over positions is implied. This quantity applies to a generic measurement position and does not identify a particular diagnostic object, line of sight, toroidal angle, or vertical coordinate. Unlike [radial_coordinate_of_line_of_sight](name:radial_coordinate_of_line_of_sight), it is not restricted to a line-of-sight reference point.

This quantity is the measurement-position specialization of the broader [radial_coordinate](name:radial_coordinate); the same perpendicular-distance definition is used, with the locus narrowed to a measurement position.

NAMES.name: radial_coordinate_of_strike_point
NAMES.short: Major-radius location of an individual magnetic strike point where a separatrix leg intersects a divertor target, expressed in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The radial coordinate of a strike point is its major-radius location relative to the toroidal symmetry axis, at the intersection of a separatrix leg with a divertor target.

The major-radius coordinate is defined from the strike point's horizontal Cartesian position by

$$
R_{\mathrm{sp}}=\sqrt{x_{\mathrm{sp}}^2+y_{\mathrm{sp}}^2}
$$

where $R_{\mathrm{sp}}$ is the strike-point major-radius coordinate, and $x_{\mathrm{sp}}$ and $y_{\mathrm{sp}}$ are its horizontal Cartesian coordinates in the right-handed Cartesian $(\hat{x},\hat{y},\hat{z})$ basis, with $\hat{z}$ vertical and coincident with $\hat{Z}$.

This quantity applies to one specified magnetic strike point at a time, with no summation, averaging, or other aggregation. The same definition covers inner and outer divertor strike points without combining them or selecting one branch by the name alone.

It excludes the vertical location of the strike point, which is given by the [vertical coordinate of the strike point](name:vertical_coordinate_of_strike_point). As a component of [radial_coordinate](name:radial_coordinate), it supplies the major-radius coordinate needed with the vertical coordinate to locate the strike point in the poloidal $(R,Z)$ plane. The related [radial coordinate of the X-point](name:radial_coordinate_of_x_point) instead identifies the separatrix's magnetic null rather than its divertor intersection.

NAMES.name: radial_coordinate_of_x_point
NAMES.short: Major-radius coordinate locating the main X-point, the poloidal magnetic-field null that defines the separatrix in an equilibrium.
NAMES.long:
The major-radius coordinate of the main X-point is the perpendicular distance from the toroidal symmetry axis to the poloidal magnetic-field null that defines the separatrix. It identifies the radial location of this specific equilibrium feature in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

The coordinate is defined geometrically by

$$
R_{\mathrm{X}} = \sqrt{x_{\mathrm{X}}^2 + y_{\mathrm{X}}^2}
$$

where $R_{\mathrm{X}}$ is the major-radius coordinate of the main X-point, and $x_{\mathrm{X}}$ and $y_{\mathrm{X}}$ are its horizontal Cartesian coordinates in the right-handed $(\hat{x}, \hat{y}, \hat{z})$ basis, with $\hat{z}$ aligned with the vertical direction $\hat{Z}$. The subscript $\mathrm{X}$ identifies the main X-point.

This quantity applies specifically to the main X-point and represents one coordinate of that point rather than its complete position. It is a single geometric value, not an average, integral, or sum over a flux surface or region; it excludes coordinates of secondary X-points and other equilibrium features.

It is a locus-specific specialization of the [radial coordinate](name:radial_coordinate), which assigns the same major-radius concept to arbitrary geometric positions. The X-point condition distinguishes it from the [radial coordinate of the magnetic axis](name:radial_coordinate_of_magnetic_axis), which locates the poloidal-field O-point rather than the separatrix-defining null.

NAMES.name: radial_derivative_of_poloidal_magnetic_flux
NAMES.short: Rate of change of signed poloidal magnetic flux with the dimensionful toroidal-flux radius labeling nested equilibrium flux surfaces.
NAMES.long:
The radial derivative of poloidal magnetic flux is the rate at which the signed poloidal magnetic flux changes across nested equilibrium magnetic flux surfaces. It is a metric coefficient relating the poloidal-flux and toroidal-flux coordinate descriptions.

The defining relation is

$$
\frac{d\psi}{d\rho_{\mathrm{tor}}}
$$

where $\psi$ is the [poloidal magnetic flux](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux), and $\rho_{\mathrm{tor}}$ is the dimensionful toroidal-flux radius that labels the nested surfaces.

This quantity is evaluated as a function of the toroidal-flux radius, with one derivative value associated with each nested equilibrium surface. It is not a surface integral or average, and it is distinct from a derivative with respect to the cylindrical major radius, minor radius, or a normalized flux coordinate.

Relative to [poloidal magnetic flux](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux), this quantity describes how the flux label changes in the outward toroidal-flux-radial direction. It has the same independent coordinate as the [derivative with respect to toroidal flux coordinate of area of flux surface](name:derivative_with_respect_to_toroidal_flux_coordinate_of_area_of_flux_surface), but differentiates poloidal magnetic flux rather than enclosed surface area.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the poloidal magnetic flux increases as $\rho_{\mathrm{tor}}$ increases outward from the magnetic axis toward the plasma boundary.

NAMES.name: radial_magnetic_field
NAMES.short: Radial magnetic-field component of the local total induction, resolved along increasing major radius in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The radial magnetic field $B_R$ is the signed component of the local total [magnetic induction](name:magnetic_field) resolved along the radial direction. It represents directional field strength rather than the full magnetic-induction vector or its magnitude.

The radial component is defined by

$$
B_R = \mathbf{B} \cdot \hat{R}
$$

where $\mathbf{B}$ is the local total magnetic induction, $\hat{R}$ is the unit vector in the direction of increasing major radius, and $B_R$ is the resulting radial component.

This quantity is defined locally in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. It does not select a plasma, vacuum, perturbed, or other source contribution, and it has no restriction to a particular region or species. The named quantity is the local projection, not a spatial average; any finite-volume average is a separate aggregation.

The radial direction is the cylindrical $\hat{R}$ direction and is distinct from the normal to a magnetic flux surface and from the direction perpendicular to the magnetic field. It is distinct from the [toroidal magnetic field](name:toroidal_magnetic_field) and [vertical magnetic field](name:vertical_magnetic_field), which are projections onto the other cylindrical directions. Together with those components, it resolves the local magnetic induction; its radial and vertical components form the [poloidal magnetic field](name:poloidal_magnetic_field).
NAMES.sign: Positive when $B_R$ points in the direction of increasing major radius $R$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: reference_major_radius
NAMES.short: Nonnegative perpendicular distance from the toroidal symmetry axis to a designated reference location, serving as the major-radius coordinate where the vacuum toroidal magnetic field is specified in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
Major radius is the nonnegative perpendicular distance from the toroidal symmetry axis to a geometric point or specified location. For this reference quantity, the designated location is the radius at which the vacuum toroidal magnetic field is specified, making it the reference specialization of major_radius.

At the designated reference location, the major radius is defined geometrically by:

$$
R_0 = \sqrt{X_0^2 + Y_0^2}
$$

where $R_0$ is the reference major radius, and $X_0$ and $Y_0$ are the Cartesian coordinates of the reference location perpendicular to the toroidal symmetry axis. The Cartesian basis is right-handed $(\hat{x},\hat{y},\hat{z})$ with $\hat{z}=\hat{Z}$; the corresponding cylindrical frame is right-handed $(R,\phi,Z)$ with $\hat{R}\times\hat{\phi}=\hat{Z}$.

This quantity is a single designated geometric reference value associated with the vacuum toroidal magnetic field, represented by [toroidal vacuum magnetic field](name:toroidal_vacuum_magnetic_field). It is not a pointwise plasma-radius field, a flux-surface average, or a region integral, and it has no species or plasma-population scope.

Unlike [flux-surface-averaged major radius](name:flux_surface_averaged_major_radius), which averages the radius over a nested magnetic flux surface, this quantity identifies one reference radius. It is also distinct from a [radial coordinate](name:radial_coordinate) assigned to an arbitrary geometric point or measurement location.

The reference radius and the vacuum toroidal magnetic field form the reference pair $R_0$ and $B_0$, where $B_0$ is the vacuum toroidal magnetic field specified at the reference radius. Their product $R_0B_0$ supplies the geometric-field scale used in normalized toroidal-flux and current-density definitions.

NAMES.name: surface_area_of_flux_surface
NAMES.short: Geometric area of a closed toroidal magnetic flux surface formed by revolving its poloidal contour through one complete toroidal revolution in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the geometric area of a complete closed toroidal magnetic flux surface. It includes the full surface swept out by the corresponding poloidal contour during one toroidal revolution.

For an axisymmetric surface, the area is defined by

$$
A_{\mathrm{surf}}(\xi) = \oint_{C(\xi)} 2\pi R\,dl_p
$$

where $A_{\mathrm{surf}}(\xi)$ is the toroidal-surface area, $\xi$ is the magnetic flux-surface label, $C(\xi)$ is the closed poloidal contour for that surface, $R$ is the major radius, $dl_p$ is differential arc length along the contour, and $\pi$ is the circular constant. The contour is expressed in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

The scope is one selected nested magnetic flux surface, with local surface elements aggregated over the complete toroidal revolution. This is distinct from the area enclosed by a poloidal contour, represented by the [poloidal-plane cross-sectional area of a flux surface](name:poloidal_plane_cross_sectional_area_of_flux_surface), and from the enclosed [volume of a flux surface](name:volume_of_flux_surface).

As a specialization of the broader [area measure associated with a flux surface], this quantity selects the total toroidal-surface area rather than a poloidal cross-sectional area or an area derivative with respect to a flux coordinate.

NAMES.name: toroidal_angle_of_measurement_position
NAMES.short: Toroidal angular coordinate locating a measurement position around the machine symmetry axis in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The toroidal angle is the azimuthal coordinate of a geometric point designated as a measurement position, locating that point around the machine symmetry axis in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

The angle may be defined from the transverse Cartesian coordinates by:

$$
\phi = \operatorname{atan2}(y,x)
$$

where $\phi$ is the toroidal angle, $x$ and $y$ are the transverse Cartesian coordinates in the right-handed $(\hat{x}, \hat{y}, \hat{z})$ basis, and $\operatorname{atan2}$ returns the oriented azimuth relative to the defined zero-angle direction. In the cylindrical frame, $R$ is major radius and $Z$ is vertical height.

This quantity applies to one geometric measurement position and has no plasma-population, field, or region weighting. It is a point coordinate rather than a line-of-sight integral, spatial average, or toroidal displacement from a reference position.

The absolute angular coordinate differs from the signed displacement represented by [toroidal offset at measurement position](name:toroidal_offset_at_measurement_position). The same toroidal-coordinate concept applied to another geometric locus is represented by [toroidal coordinate of aperture](name:toroidal_coordinate_of_aperture).
NAMES.sign: Positive when measured counter-clockwise from the defined zero-toroidal-angle half-plane when viewed from above along $+\hat{Z}$.

NAMES.name: toroidal_flux_coordinate
NAMES.short: Non-negative, radius-like label of a nested magnetic flux surface, derived from enclosed toroidal magnetic flux using a positive reference vacuum toroidal field.
NAMES.long:
The toroidal flux coordinate is a non-negative, radius-like label assigned to each nested magnetic flux surface. It orders surfaces outward from the magnetic axis and approximates an effective minor radius without being a geometric distance.

The coordinate is defined from the enclosed toroidal magnetic flux:

$$
\rho_{\rm tor} = \sqrt{\frac{\Phi_{\rm tor}}{\pi B_0}}
$$

where $\rho_{\rm tor}$ is the toroidal flux coordinate, $\Phi_{\rm tor}$ is the toroidal magnetic flux enclosed by the surface relative to the magnetic axis, $B_0$ is the positive reference vacuum toroidal magnetic field, and $\pi$ is the circle constant.

The quantity applies to arbitrary nested magnetic flux surfaces, including the magnetic axis, internal characteristic surfaces, and the plasma boundary. Each value labels one surface; it has no species or population scope and involves no population summation, charge-state aggregation, or averaging convention. It is a flux-derived coordinate rather than a direct geometric minor-radius measurement.

At the magnetic axis, the enclosed relative toroidal flux vanishes and the coordinate is zero. Evaluations at particular loci, such as the [toroidal flux coordinate at the plasma boundary](name:toroidal_flux_coordinate_at_plasma_boundary) and the [toroidal flux coordinate of the magnetic axis](name:toroidal_flux_coordinate_of_magnetic_axis), are instances of this same surface-labeling quantity. A [normalized toroidal flux coordinate at a measurement position](name:normalized_toroidal_flux_coordinate_at_measurement_position) is a dimensionless rescaling of a toroidal-flux label and is distinct from this dimensional coordinate.

NAMES.name: toroidal_flux_coordinate_at_plasma_boundary
NAMES.short: Dimensionful toroidal-flux radius labeling the outermost closed magnetic flux surface and setting the boundary value for this radial coordinate.
NAMES.long:
The toroidal flux coordinate at the plasma boundary is the non-negative, radius-like label assigned to the outermost closed magnetic flux surface. It represents an effective flux radius rather than a geometric minor-radius measurement.

At the plasma boundary, the coordinate is defined by

$$
\rho_{\mathrm{tor,b}} = \sqrt{\frac{\Phi_{\mathrm{tor,b}}}{\pi B_0}}
$$

where $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,b}}$ is the toroidal flux coordinate at the boundary, $\Phi_{\mathrm{tor,b}}$ is the toroidal magnetic flux enclosed by the boundary, $B_0$ is the positive reference vacuum toroidal magnetic field, and $\pi$ is the mathematical constant.

The quantity applies specifically to the plasma boundary, identified with the outermost closed magnetic flux surface or last-closed flux surface in a closed-boundary equilibrium. It is a single evaluation at that locus; no spatial averaging, boundary integration, or summation over particle populations is implied.

This boundary value is distinct from the [normalized toroidal flux coordinate at the plasma boundary](name:normalized_toroidal_flux_coordinate_at_plasma_boundary), which is dimensionless, and from the [toroidal magnetic flux at the plasma boundary](name:toroidal_magnetic_flux_at_plasma_boundary), which is the enclosed flux rather than its radius-like transformation.

The quantity is the boundary evaluation of the parent [toroidal flux coordinate](name:toroidal_flux_coordinate) and supplies the outer radial reference for flux-coordinate labels based on toroidal magnetic flux.

NAMES.name: toroidal_flux_coordinate_of_magnetic_axis
NAMES.short: Value of the radius-like toroidal-flux label on the magnetic surface passing through the magnetic axis; it is zero because enclosed toroidal flux vanishes there.
NAMES.long:
The toroidal flux coordinate at the magnetic axis is the value of the radius-like flux-surface label on the magnetic-axis reference surface. It identifies the origin of the toroidal-flux radial coordinate and is not a geometric distance from the machine symmetry axis.

The coordinate is defined by

$$
\rho_{\mathrm{tor}} = \sqrt{\frac{\Phi_{\mathrm{tor}}}{\pi B_0}}
$$

where $\rho_{\mathrm{tor}}$ is the toroidal flux coordinate, $\Phi_{\mathrm{tor}}$ is the toroidal magnetic flux enclosed by the magnetic surface, and $B_0$ is the positive reference vacuum toroidal magnetic-field strength. At the magnetic axis, the enclosed toroidal flux is zero, so this value is zero.

The quantity applies to the single magnetic-axis locus and is neither a flux-surface average nor an integral over a finite region. It is the axis value of the parent [toroidal flux coordinate](name:toroidal_flux_coordinate), not the coordinate of an arbitrary flux surface or a geometric major- or minor-radius measurement.

The [toroidal magnetic flux](name:toroidal_magnetic_flux) supplies the enclosed-flux quantity in the defining relation, while the corresponding normalized toroidal-flux coordinate uses axis and boundary values to form a dimensionless radial label.

NAMES.name: toroidal_flux_surface_averaged_current_density
NAMES.short: Flux-surface-averaged toroidal current density is the toroidal conventional current density assigned to a closed magnetic-flux surface. It is the geometry-weighted total toroidal current-density component that acts as the effective toroidal current source for the equilibrium poloidal magnetic-flux distribution.
NAMES.long:
Flux-surface-averaged toroidal current density is the toroidal conventional current density assigned to a closed magnetic-flux surface. It represents the total toroidal current-density component on that surface, expressed with the geometry weighting that provides the effective toroidal current source for the equilibrium poloidal magnetic-flux distribution.

The defining flux-surface average is

$$
j_{\phi,\mathrm{FSA}} = \frac{\left\langle j_\phi/R \right\rangle}{\left\langle 1/R \right\rangle}
$$

where $j_{\phi,\mathrm{FSA}}$ is the flux-surface-averaged toroidal current density, $j_\phi$ is the local toroidal component of the conventional current-density vector projected on $\hat{\phi}$, $R$ is the major-radius coordinate in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, and $\langle \cdot \rangle$ denotes an average over the closed magnetic-flux surface.

The scope is closed magnetic-flux surfaces in an axisymmetric equilibrium, and the aggregation is over the total conventional current carried by the plasma unless a population-specific qualifier is present. This quantity is not the unweighted flux-surface average of $j_\phi$, not a local current-density component at a point, and not a field-aligned or parallel current density.

It is the toroidal counterpart of the [parallel flux-surface-averaged current density](name:parallel_flux_surface_averaged_current_density_due_to_wave_driven_current_drive) and a member of the [flux-surface-averaged current density](name:parallel_flux_surface_averaged_current_density_due_to_wave_driven_current_drive) family. In equilibrium, this weighted toroidal average is the scalar source coupled to the [poloidal magnetic flux](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux) in the Grad-Shafranov balance.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the conventional current-density vector has a positive projection on $\hat{\phi}$, the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: toroidal_magnetic_field
NAMES.short: Signed toroidal component of the local total magnetic induction, resolved along increasing toroidal angle in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The toroidal magnetic field $B_\\phi$ is the signed component of the local total [magnetic induction](name:magnetic_field) resolved along the toroidal direction. It represents directional field strength at a point before any source selection, perturbation selection, spatial aggregation, magnitude reduction, or locus restriction.

In the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \\phi, Z)$ frame, the component is defined by

$$
B_\\phi = \\mathbf{B} \\cdot \\hat{\\boldsymbol{\\phi}}
$$

where $B_\\phi$ is the toroidal magnetic-field component, $\\mathbf{B}$ is the local total magnetic-induction vector, and $\\hat{\\boldsymbol{\\phi}}$ is the toroidal unit vector. Here, $R$ is major radius measured from the symmetry axis, $\\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height; the basis is right-handed with $\\hat{\\mathbf{R}} \\times \\hat{\\boldsymbol{\\phi}} = \\hat{\\mathbf{Z}}$.

The quantity applies pointwise wherever the local total magnetic induction is defined, including plasma and surrounding vacuum regions. It includes all represented magnetic-field contributions and is neither a source-specific field nor a perturbation-only field; it is also distinct from the unsigned [poloidal magnetic-field strength](name:poloidal_magnetic_field).

Together with the [radial magnetic-field component](name:radial_magnetic_field) and vertical component, $B_\\phi$ determines the local magnetic-induction vector in the cylindrical frame. The toroidal component is one directional projection of the parent [magnetic field](name:magnetic_field), not its full vector or magnitude.
NAMES.sign: Positive when $B_\\phi$ points in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\\phi`.

NAMES.name: toroidal_magnetic_field_at_magnetic_axis
NAMES.short: Toroidal magnetic field at the magnetic axis is the signed toroidal component of the total equilibrium magnetic field at the magnetic axis in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame. It includes externally applied vacuum-field and plasma-current-generated contributions.
NAMES.long:
Toroidal magnetic field at the magnetic axis is the signed toroidal component of the total equilibrium magnetic field evaluated at the magnetic axis in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. The magnetic axis is the locus of the equilibrium flux surface with the magnetic-axis value of poloidal magnetic flux. The total field includes externally produced vacuum-field and plasma-current-generated contributions.

In an axisymmetric equilibrium, using the poloidal-current function $F(\psi)=R B_\phi$, the defining relation is

$$
B_{\phi,\mathrm{axis}} = \mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{total}}(R_{\mathrm{axis}}, Z_{\mathrm{axis}}) \cdot \hat{\phi} = B_\phi(R_{\mathrm{axis}}, Z_{\mathrm{axis}}) = \frac{F(\psi_0)}{R_{\mathrm{axis}}}
$$

where $B_{\phi,\mathrm{axis}}$ is this quantity, $\mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{total}}$ is the total equilibrium magnetic field, $B_\phi$ is the [toroidal magnetic field](name:toroidal_magnetic_field), $\hat{\phi}$ is the unit vector in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$, $R_{\mathrm{axis}}$ and $Z_{\mathrm{axis}}$ are the major-radius and vertical coordinates of the magnetic axis, $F(\psi)$ is the [poloidal-current function](name:poloidal_current_function), and $\psi_0$ is the [poloidal magnetic flux at the magnetic axis](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_magnetic_axis).

The scope is the local magnetic-axis value for the equilibrium state; it is not an average over a flux surface, poloidal angle, toroidal angle, or plasma volume. Because it is a component, not a magnitude, it retains the sign of the toroidal projection and does not represent the absolute magnetic-field strength.

This quantity is the on-axis specialization of [toroidal magnetic field](name:toroidal_magnetic_field). It is distinct from [toroidal vacuum magnetic field](name:toroidal_vacuum_magnetic_field), which excludes plasma-current-generated contributions, and from [toroidal reference magnetic field](name:toroidal_reference_magnetic_field), which denotes a prescribed reference field rather than the local total field at the magnetic axis even when numerical values coincide.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the total magnetic field at the magnetic axis has a toroidal component in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: toroidal_magnetic_flux
NAMES.short: Toroidal magnetic flux is the signed surface integral of the magnetic field over the poloidal cross-section enclosed by a nested magnetic flux surface.
NAMES.long:
Toroidal magnetic flux is the signed surface integral of the magnetic field over the poloidal cross-section enclosed by a nested magnetic flux surface. It is the toroidal member of the [magnetic flux](name:magnetic_flux) family and is defined as a function of nested magnetic surfaces in axisymmetric equilibrium.

The defining surface integral is:

$$
\Phi_{\mathrm{tor}}(\mathcal{S}) = \int_{S_{\mathrm{pol}}(\mathcal{S})} \mathbf{B} \cdot d\mathbf{A}
$$

where $\Phi_{\mathrm{tor}}(\mathcal{S})$ is the toroidal magnetic flux associated with the nested magnetic flux surface $\mathcal{S}$, $S_{\mathrm{pol}}(\mathcal{S})$ is the poloidal cross-section bounded by that surface at fixed toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, $Z$ is vertical height, $\mathbf{B}$ is the magnetic-field vector, and $d\mathbf{A}$ is the oriented area element whose positive normal is $+\hat{\phi}$.

The scope is the total toroidal projection of magnetic flux through the entire enclosed poloidal cross-section for each nested magnetic surface. It is not a local magnetic-field value, not a flux-surface average, and not a source-separated contribution; [toroidal magnetic flux at the plasma boundary](name:toroidal_magnetic_flux_at_plasma_boundary) is the boundary-specific value of the same quantity.

At the magnetic axis the enclosed poloidal cross-section shrinks to zero area, so $\Phi_{\mathrm{tor}}=0$ there. Together with [poloidal magnetic flux](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux) $\psi$, it provides a radial flux-surface label; the [safety factor](name:safety_factor) $q$ is related to the two fluxes by the differential relation $q = d\Phi_{\mathrm{tor}}/d\psi$ for consistent flux definitions.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the net magnetic flux through the poloidal cross-section is directed along increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: toroidal_magnetic_flux_due_to_diamagnetic_drift
NAMES.short: Signed toroidal magnetic-flux contribution calculated for a plasma equilibrium from the pressure-gradient-driven diamagnetic response relative to its reference field.
NAMES.long:
Toroidal diamagnetic flux is the signed magnetic flux associated with the toroidal component of the magnetic-field change caused by the plasma's pressure-gradient-driven diamagnetic response. For a specified equilibrium, it denotes the equilibrium-derived value of this contribution.

The defining toroidal flux contribution is

$$
\Phi_{\mathrm{dia},\phi} = \int_{S_p} \left(\mathbf{B} - \mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{ref}}\right) \cdot \hat{\boldsymbol{\phi}}\,\mathrm{d}S
$$

where $\Phi_{\mathrm{dia},\phi}$ is the toroidal diamagnetic flux, $\mathbf{B}$ is the plasma magnetic-field vector, $\mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{ref}}$ is the corresponding magnetic field without the pressure-gradient-driven diamagnetic response, $S_p$ is the poloidal surface enclosing the plasma cross-section, $\mathrm{d}S$ is an oriented surface element, and $\hat{\boldsymbol{\phi}}$ is the toroidal unit vector; $\phi$ is the toroidal angle.

This quantity applies to the global plasma region and aggregates the diamagnetic magnetic-field change over the enclosing poloidal surface after selecting its toroidal component. It excludes magnetic flux already present in the reference field and contributions not attributable to the diamagnetic response; it is not the total toroidal magnetic flux.

The toroidal component is a directional specialization of the [magnetic-flux contribution due to diamagnetic drift](name:magnetic_flux_due_to_diamagnetic_drift), whose vector quantity retains the corresponding directional components. It is also distinct from [external magnetic flux](name:external_magnetic_flux), which is produced by sources outside the plasma current distribution rather than by the plasma's diamagnetic response.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the diamagnetic magnetic-field change points in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ through a poloidal surface oriented along $\hat{\boldsymbol{\phi}}$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: toroidal_vacuum_magnetic_field
NAMES.short: Signed toroidal component of the current-free vacuum magnetic field at a reference major radius, defining the nominal externally generated field strength.
NAMES.long:
The vacuum toroidal magnetic field $B_0$ is the signed toroidal component of the equilibrium magnetic-field vector in the current-free region surrounding the plasma, evaluated at a reference major radius.

The reference value is defined by

$$
B_0 = B_{\\phi,\mathrm{vac}}(R_0)
$$

where $B_0$ is the vacuum toroidal field at the reference major radius, $B_{\phi,\mathrm{vac}}$ is the toroidal component of the vacuum magnetic field, and $R_0$ is the major-radius coordinate of the reference location in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

This quantity applies to the equilibrium vacuum field generated by external sources, with contributions from plasma currents omitted. It is a single signed reference value rather than a spatial average, surface integral, local total field, or Fourier perturbation coefficient. The vector quantity it specializes is the [vacuum magnetic field](name:vacuum_magnetic_field); it is distinct from the [toroidal perturbed vacuum magnetic field real part](name:toroidal_perturbed_vacuum_magnetic_field_real_part), which describes a first-order perturbation. The normalization product $R_0 B_0$ represents the conserved major-radius-weighted toroidal field of an axisymmetric vacuum field, for which $R B_{\phi,\mathrm{vac}}(R) = R_0 B_0$, where $R$ is the major-radius coordinate.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the associated vacuum magnetic-field vector has a toroidal component in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: triangularity_of_plasma_boundary
NAMES.short: Dimensionless shape parameter for the plasma-boundary poloidal cross-section, expressing the aggregate inward radial displacement of its upper and lower extrema relative to the geometric center.
NAMES.long:
Plasma-boundary triangularity is a dimensionless shaping parameter describing the asymmetry of the boundary’s poloidal cross-section through the inward displacement of its upper and lower radial extrema relative to the geometric center. It characterizes the complete boundary rather than either half-plane extremum alone.

For the upper and lower boundary extrema, the aggregate triangularity is defined as

$$
\delta = \frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{R_0-R_u}{a}+\frac{R_0-R_l}{a}\right)
$$

where $\delta$ is the plasma-boundary triangularity, $R_0$ is the major-radius coordinate of the geometric center, $R_u$ and $R_l$ are the major-radius coordinates of the upper and lower boundary extrema, and $a$ is the boundary minor radius. The coordinates refer to the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

This quantity applies to the entire plasma boundary and aggregates the upper and lower extremal displacements into one shape parameter. It excludes the separately resolved [upper triangularity of the plasma boundary](name:upper_triangularity_of_plasma_boundary) and [lower triangularity of the plasma boundary](name:lower_triangularity_of_plasma_boundary), which retain only one extremum. It also differs from [triangularity of a flux surface](name:triangularity_of_flux_surface), which describes an individual nested magnetic flux surface rather than the outer plasma boundary.

sources.leaf_definition: Triangularity of the plasma boundary
sources.parent_definition: Description of the plasma boundary. The boundary can be either the real separatrix (provided by a free boundary equilibrium solver) or the 0.99x psi_norm flux surface provided by a fixed boundary equilibrium

NAMES.name: lower_triangularity_of_plasma_boundary
NAMES.short: Dimensionless shaping parameter equal to the normalized inward radial displacement of the lower plasma-boundary extremum from the geometric center.
NAMES.long:
Lower triangularity of the plasma boundary is a signed dimensionless measure of the horizontal displacement of its lower poloidal extremum relative to the geometric center. This component selects the lower extremum rather than averaging the upper and lower contributions.

$$
\delta_l = \frac{R_0-R_l}{a}
$$

Here, $\delta_l$ is the lower triangularity; $R_0$ is the major-radius coordinate of the geometric center; $R_l$ is the major-radius coordinate of the lower vertical extremum; and $a$ is the minor radius of the plasma boundary. These coordinates are defined in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

This quantity applies only to the lower extremum of the plasma boundary and represents one term in the boundary-shaping description. It is not the upper contribution or an average over both extrema; the corresponding upper contribution is [upper triangularity](name:upper_triangularity_of_plasma_boundary).

The parent [triangularity of the plasma boundary](name:triangularity_of_plasma_boundary) is the arithmetic mean of the upper and lower contributions: $\delta=(\delta_u+\delta_l)/2$, where $\delta$ is the parent triangularity and $\delta_u$ is the upper triangularity.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the lower extremum is displaced inward, toward decreasing major radius $R$, relative to the geometric center.

NAMES.name: upper_triangularity_of_flux_surface
NAMES.short: Dimensionless upper triangularity shape parameter for a nested magnetic flux surface, given by the normalized inward radial displacement of its upper vertical extremum.
NAMES.long:
Upper triangularity of a flux surface is the dimensionless triangularity shape parameter defined at the upper vertical extremum of a nested magnetic flux surface. It is the normalized inward radial displacement of that upper extremum in a poloidal cross-section.

For the upper vertical extremum, the defining relation is:

$$
\delta_u = \frac{R_{\mathrm{axis}} - R_u}{a}
$$

where $\delta_u$ is upper triangularity, $R_{\mathrm{axis}}$ is the major-radius coordinate of the magnetic axis, $R_u$ is the major-radius coordinate of the upper vertical extremum, and $a$ is the minor radius of the flux surface. These coordinates are defined in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

This quantity applies separately to each nested magnetic flux surface identified by its poloidal magnetic-flux label. It represents only the upper extremum and is not an aggregate over the upper and lower extrema or over multiple flux surfaces.

It is distinct from [lower triangularity of a flux surface](name:lower_triangularity_of_flux_surface), which uses the lower vertical extremum. It also differs from [upper triangularity of the plasma boundary](name:upper_triangularity_of_plasma_boundary), which applies only to the outer plasma boundary rather than to an arbitrary nested flux surface.

Upper triangularity is the upper-extremum branch of [triangularity of a flux surface](name:triangularity_of_flux_surface), whose definition permits the relevant upper or lower vertical extremum. The upper and lower quantities together describe the asymmetric triangular shaping of a flux-surface cross-section.

NAMES.name: upper_triangularity_of_plasma_boundary
NAMES.short: Dimensionless shape parameter for the plasma-boundary poloidal cross-section, expressing the inward radial displacement of its upper extremum relative to the geometric center.
NAMES.long:
Upper triangularity of the plasma boundary is a dimensionless shaping parameter describing the inward radial displacement of the upper extremum of the boundary’s poloidal cross-section relative to its geometric center. It selects the upper extremum rather than combining the two vertical halves.

For the upper boundary extremum, it is defined as

$$
\delta_u = \frac{R_0-R_u}{a}
$$

where $\delta_u$ is the upper triangularity, $R_0$ is the major-radius coordinate of the geometric center, $R_u$ is the major-radius coordinate of the upper boundary extremum, and $a$ is the boundary minor radius. These coordinates refer to the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

This quantity applies to the outer plasma boundary and uses only its upper poloidal extremum; it is not averaged over the upper and lower extrema. It is a boundary-shape parameter rather than a local field value or the triangularity of an individual nested magnetic flux surface.

The [triangularity of the plasma boundary](name:triangularity_of_plasma_boundary) aggregates the upper and lower components, with $\delta = (\delta_u+\delta_l)/2$, where $\delta$ is the aggregate boundary triangularity and $\delta_l$ is the [lower triangularity of the plasma boundary](name:lower_triangularity_of_plasma_boundary). It differs from [triangularity of a flux surface](name:triangularity_of_flux_surface), which describes a nested magnetic flux surface rather than the outer plasma boundary.

NAMES.name: vertical_coordinate_of_geometric_axis
NAMES.short: Signed vertical position of the plasma boundary’s geometric axis, defined as the midpoint of its maximum and minimum Z extents in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The geometric-axis vertical coordinate is the midpoint of the plasma boundary’s maximum and minimum vertical positions in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame. Here $R$ is the major-radius coordinate, $\phi$ is the toroidal angle, and $Z$ is the vertical coordinate. It characterizes the boundary’s vertical placement rather than the location of a magnetic-flux extremum.

For the specified plasma boundary, the defining relation is

$$
Z_{\mathrm{axis}} = \frac{Z_{\max}+Z_{\min}}{2}
$$

where $Z_{\mathrm{axis}}$ is the vertical coordinate of the geometric axis, $Z_{\max}$ is the boundary’s maximum vertical coordinate, and $Z_{\min}$ is its minimum vertical coordinate.

The quantity applies to the complete plasma boundary and uses the global extrema with equal weighting; it is not a local boundary coordinate, an arc-length average, or a flux-surface average. It is distinct from the [vertical coordinate of the magnetic axis](name:vertical_coordinate_of_magnetic_axis), which identifies the vertical position of the interior poloidal-flux extremum rather than the midpoint of the boundary extent.

NAMES.name: vertical_coordinate_of_magnetic_axis
NAMES.short: Signed vertical Z coordinate of the magnetic axis in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame, marking the interior extremum organizing nested magnetic flux surfaces.
NAMES.long:
The quantity is the signed vertical coordinate $Z_\mathrm{axis}$ of the magnetic-axis point in a poloidal cross-section. The magnetic axis is the interior extremum of the poloidal magnetic-flux function around which nested magnetic flux surfaces are organized.

For an equilibrium with poloidal flux function $\psi(R,Z)$, the magnetic-axis point satisfies the stationary-point condition

$$
\left.\frac{\partial \psi}{\partial R}\right|_{\mathrm{axis}}
=
\left.\frac{\partial \psi}{\partial Z}\right|_{\mathrm{axis}}
=0
$$

where $\psi$ is the poloidal magnetic-flux function, $R$ is the major-radius coordinate, $Z$ is the vertical coordinate, and the subscript $\mathrm{axis}$ denotes evaluation at the magnetic-axis point. The derivatives are taken in the poloidal cross-section, and $0$ denotes a vanishing derivative.

The coordinate is defined in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $\phi$ is the toroidal angle. It applies to the single interior magnetic-axis point, has no species or particle-population scope, and is neither averaged nor integrated over a surface, region, or volume. It records only the vertical coordinate; the corresponding radial coordinate is required to locate the point fully.

This quantity is distinct from the [vertical coordinate of the geometric axis](name:vertical_coordinate_of_geometric_axis), which describes a boundary-derived geometric center, and from the [vertical coordinate of the X-point](name:vertical_coordinate_of_x_point), which identifies a magnetic null where separatrix branches meet.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the magnetic axis lies in the direction of increasing vertical coordinate $Z$ from the origin of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: vertical_coordinate_of_measurement_position
NAMES.short: Signed vertical coordinate of a generic measurement location, measured from the machine midplane along the Z direction of the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The vertical coordinate of a measurement position is its signed height relative to the machine midplane in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame. Here $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

The coordinate is defined by

$$
Z_{\mathrm{meas}} = \mathbf{r}_{\mathrm{meas}} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{Z}}
$$

where $Z_{\mathrm{meas}}$ is the vertical coordinate, $\mathbf{r}_{\mathrm{meas}}$ is the position vector of the measurement location relative to the machine-midplane origin, and $\hat{\mathbf{Z}}$ is the vertical unit vector.

This quantity applies to the geometric measurement position independently of the diagnostic type or physical quantity measured there. It represents one coordinate of one position, with no averaging over positions, populations, or physical regions, and it is not the value of a plasma field evaluated at that location.

The generic position coordinate has the same geometric meaning as the object-specific [vertical coordinate of a camera](name:vertical_coordinate_of_camera) and [vertical coordinate of a diagnostic aperture](name:vertical_coordinate_of_diagnostic_aperture); those quantities differ only in the object whose position is identified.

NAMES.name: vertical_coordinate_of_primary_x_point
NAMES.short: Signed vertical position of the primary magnetic X-point, the poloidal-field null where separatrix branches meet, in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The primary X-point is the main poloidal magnetic-field null on the plasma boundary, where separatrix branches meet. This quantity gives that point’s vertical coordinate in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

$$
Z_{\mathrm{X,primary}} = \mathbf{r}_{\mathrm{X,primary}} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{Z}}
$$

Here, $Z_{\mathrm{X,primary}}$ is the vertical coordinate of the primary X-point, $\mathbf{r}_{\mathrm{X,primary}}$ is its position vector relative to the coordinate origin, and $\hat{\mathbf{Z}}$ is the vertical unit vector of the cylindrical frame.

The locus is specifically the primary, or main, boundary X-point rather than an unspecified or secondary X-point. This is a pointwise geometric coordinate with no spatial averaging, surface integration, population aggregation, or species dependence; it excludes the radial coordinate of the same point.

The generic [vertical coordinate of an X-point](name:vertical_coordinate_of_x_point) represents the same signed Z coordinate without restricting the locus to the primary X-point, while the [radial coordinate of an X-point](name:radial_coordinate_of_x_point) supplies the corresponding major-radius coordinate.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the primary X-point lies in the direction of increasing vertical coordinate $Z$.

NAMES.name: vertical_coordinate_of_strike_point
NAMES.short: Signed vertical (Z) coordinate of the inner divertor strike point, where the inner separatrix leg intersects the divertor target in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The vertical coordinate of the inner divertor strike point is the signed Z location where the inner leg of the plasma separatrix intersects the divertor target. It identifies a boundary contact point in the poloidal geometry, rather than the magnetic null.

This quantity applies specifically to the inner strike point and represents one geometric coordinate value; it is not an average over strike points, a target-surface extent, or a toroidal aggregation. It is distinct from the corresponding outer strike-point location, which describes the outer separatrix leg.

Together with the [major-radius coordinate of a magnetic strike point](name:radial_coordinate_of_strike_point), this coordinate locates the same strike point in the poloidal cross-section of the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame. It must not be interpreted as the [vertical coordinate of an X-point](name:vertical_coordinate_of_x_point), because an X-point is a magnetic null rather than a separatrix–target intersection.

NAMES.name: vertical_magnetic_field
NAMES.short: Vertical magnetic-field component of the local total magnetic induction, resolved along increasing vertical height in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The vertical magnetic field $B_Z$ is the signed component of the local total [magnetic induction](name:magnetic_field) resolved along the vertical direction. It represents directional field strength rather than the full magnetic-induction vector or its magnitude.

The vertical component is defined by

$$
B_Z = \mathbf{B} \cdot \hat{Z}
$$

where $\mathbf{B}$ is the local total magnetic induction, $\hat{Z}$ is the unit vector in the direction of increasing vertical height, and $B_Z$ is the resulting vertical component.

This quantity is defined locally in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. It does not select a plasma, vacuum, perturbed, or other source contribution, and it has no restriction to a particular region or species. At a point it is the local projection, not a sum or integral over a region, source, or population; when a finite sensing volume defines the value, the projected component is averaged over that volume.

It is distinct from the [radial magnetic field](name:radial_magnetic_field) and [toroidal magnetic field](name:toroidal_magnetic_field), which are projections onto the other cylindrical directions, and from the [poloidal magnetic field](name:poloidal_magnetic_field), which is the magnitude in the poloidal plane. Together, these component quantities resolve the local [magnetic induction](name:magnetic_field) in the cylindrical frame.
NAMES.sign: Positive when $B_Z$ points in the direction of increasing vertical height $Z$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: volume_of_flux_surface
NAMES.short: Geometric volume contained within a nested magnetic flux surface, cumulative from the magnetic axis toward the outermost closed surface.
NAMES.long:
The quantity is the three-dimensional volume enclosed inside a nested magnetic flux surface. It characterizes the geometry of the region interior to that magnetic surface.

The enclosed volume is defined by

$$
V(\chi) = \int_{\Omega_\chi} d^3x
$$

where $V(\chi)$ is the volume associated with flux-surface label $\chi$, $\Omega_\chi$ is the region inside the corresponding magnetic surface $S_\chi$, and $d^3x$ is the three-dimensional volume element.

The quantity applies to each nested magnetic surface across the modeled plasma region, including confined-plasma and scrape-off-layer surfaces where such surfaces are defined. It is a cumulative volume over the complete interior of the surface, increasing outward from the magnetic axis; it is not the volume of an infinitesimal shell.

It is distinct from [surface area of a flux surface](name:surface_area_of_flux_surface) and from [poloidal-plane cross-sectional area of a flux surface](name:poloidal_plane_cross_sectional_area_of_flux_surface). The [volume of the plasma boundary](name:volume_of_plasma_boundary) is the boundary value of this enclosed-volume function, while [the derivative with respect to poloidal magnetic flux coordinate of volume of flux surface](name:derivative_with_respect_to_poloidal_magnetic_flux_coordinate_of_volume_of_flux_surface) and [the derivative with respect to toroidal flux coordinate of volume of flux surface](name:derivative_with_respect_to_toroidal_flux_coordinate_of_volume_of_flux_surface) describe its local change with different flux labels.

NAMES.name: derivative_with_respect_to_poloidal_magnetic_flux_coordinate_of_volume_of_flux_surface
NAMES.short: Derivative of the enclosed volume of a nested magnetic flux surface with respect to its signed poloidal magnetic-flux label.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the local geometric rate at which the volume enclosed by a nested magnetic flux surface changes as the signed poloidal magnetic-flux label changes. It describes the differential volume associated with an increment of that label, rather than the enclosed volume itself.

The defining derivative is

$$
\frac{dV}{d\psi}(\psi) = \lim_{\Delta\psi \to 0} \frac{V(\psi + \Delta\psi) - V(\psi)}{\Delta\psi}
$$

where $V(\psi)$ is the volume enclosed by the nested magnetic flux surface labeled by the signed poloidal magnetic flux $\psi$, and $\Delta\psi$ is an increment of that flux label.

The quantity applies to nested closed magnetic flux surfaces and uses the cumulative volume interior to each surface, ordered from the magnetic axis toward the outermost closed surface. It is a scalar geometric metric based on dimensional poloidal magnetic flux; it excludes volume outside the selected surface and is not an integral over a finite range of flux labels.

It is the differential counterpart of the [volume of a flux surface](name:volume_of_flux_surface), obtained by differentiating that enclosed-volume quantity with respect to $\psi$. As a flux-coordinate Jacobian factor, it contributes to flux-surface averages, pressure-balance relations, and one-dimensional transport formulations. It must be distinguished from a derivative with respect to the [normalized poloidal flux coordinate](name:normalized_poloidal_flux_coordinate), which includes the coordinate normalization in its chain rule.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the enclosed volume increases toward increasing signed poloidal magnetic flux $\psi$; with positive plasma current in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height, $\psi$ decreases outward and the outward increase of volume therefore gives a negative derivative.

NAMES.name: derivative_with_respect_to_toroidal_flux_coordinate_of_volume_of_flux_surface
NAMES.short: Radial rate of change of the volume enclosed by a nested magnetic flux surface as its dimensionful toroidal flux coordinate increases.
NAMES.long:
The quantity is the local derivative of the cumulative three-dimensional volume enclosed by a nested magnetic flux surface with respect to its dimensionful toroidal flux coordinate. It is a geometric metric coefficient used in flux-surface-averaged equilibrium and transport relations.

The defining relation is

$$
\frac{dV}{d\rho_{\mathrm{tor}}}
=
\frac{d}{d\rho_{\mathrm{tor}}}
\left(\int_{\Omega(\rho_{\mathrm{tor}})} d^3x\right)
$$

where $V$ is the volume enclosed by the flux surface, $\rho_{\mathrm{tor}}$ is the dimensionful toroidal flux coordinate labeling that surface, $\Omega(\rho_{\mathrm{tor}})$ is the region inside it, and $\mathbf{x}$ is the spatial position whose volume element is $d^3x$.

This quantity applies to each nested magnetic flux surface, with the enclosed volume accumulated from the magnetic axis outward and differentiated locally with respect to the toroidal-flux-coordinate label. It is a purely geometric scalar with no species, field-component, or process aggregation; it is neither the enclosed volume itself nor a flux-surface average.

It is the derivative of the [volume enclosed by a flux surface](name:volume_of_flux_surface). It differs from the [derivative with respect to toroidal flux coordinate of flux-surface area](name:derivative_with_respect_to_toroidal_flux_coordinate_of_area_of_flux_surface), which differentiates enclosed cross-sectional area, and from the [toroidal flux coordinate gradient magnitude](name:toroidal_flux_coordinate_gradient_magnitude), which describes spatial variation of the coordinate rather than volume accumulation.

NAMES.name: volume_of_plasma_boundary
NAMES.short: Volume enclosed by the plasma boundary, representing the total confined-plasma region inside the last closed magnetic flux surface.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the geometric volume of the confined plasma enclosed by the plasma boundary, identified with the last closed magnetic flux surface. It represents the full enclosed region rather than a local flux-surface shell or material volume.

The volume is defined by

$$
V = \int_{\Omega_{\mathrm{plasma}}} d^3\mathbf{x}
$$

where $V$ is the enclosed plasma volume, $\Omega_{\mathrm{plasma}}$ is the spatial domain inside the plasma boundary, and $d^3\mathbf{x}$ is the differential volume element at position $\mathbf{x}$.

The integration domain is the entire confined-plasma region bounded by the last closed magnetic flux surface, and the result is the total volume aggregated over that domain. It excludes regions outside the plasma boundary and volumes belonging to material structures or other non-confined regions.

This quantity is the terminal enclosed value of [volume of a flux surface](name:volume_of_flux_surface) when the flux surface coincides with the plasma boundary. It provides the integration domain for volume-averaged quantities such as [volume-averaged ion temperature](name:volume_averaged_ion_temperature).

NAMES.name: flux_surface_averaged_magnetic_field_magnitude
NAMES.short: Flux-surface average of the local magnetic-field strength, retaining the pointwise modulus before averaging over each magnetic surface.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the flux-surface average of the magnitude of the total equilibrium magnetic-field vector. It represents the mean field strength on a magnetic surface, rather than a component or a vector average.

The flux-surface average is defined by

$$
\left\langle \lvert\mathbf{B}\rvert \right\rangle_{\psi} = \frac{\oint_{\psi} \lvert\mathbf{B}\rvert\,\mathrm{d}S/\lvert\nabla\psi\rvert}{\oint_{\psi} \mathrm{d}S/\lvert\nabla\psi\rvert}
$$

where $\mathbf{B}$ is the total equilibrium magnetic-field vector, $\psi$ is the scalar label of the magnetic flux surface, $\mathrm{d}S$ is the surface-area element, and $\nabla\psi$ is the spatial gradient of that surface label. The aggregation is the normalized surface integral with weighting $\mathrm{d}S/\lvert\nabla\psi\rvert$.

The quantity applies to all components of the equilibrium field on the selected magnetic flux surface and is non-negative. It excludes any signed field component, any species or source decomposition, and the magnitude of a vector obtained by averaging $\mathbf{B}$ before taking its modulus.

It is the flux-surface-averaged transformation of [magnetic-field magnitude]. It differs from [flux-surface-averaged square of magnetic-field magnitude](name:flux_surface_averaged_square_of_magnetic_field_magnitude), which averages the squared field strength rather than the field strength itself.

NAMES.name: minimum_over_flux_surface_magnetic_field_magnitude
NAMES.short: Smallest total magnetic-field strength attained along a specified nested magnetic flux surface, using the field magnitude rather than a signed component.
NAMES.long:
The minimum magnetic-field magnitude is the smallest total field strength attained anywhere on a specified nested magnetic flux surface. It is sign-invariant because it uses the modulus of the magnetic-field vector rather than a signed component.

For a surface labeled by the magnetic-flux coordinate $\psi$, the quantity is defined by

$$
B_{\min}(\psi) = \min_{\mathbf{x} \in S(\psi)} \left|\mathbf{B}(\mathbf{x})\right|
$$

where $B_{\min}(\psi)$ is the minimum magnetic-field magnitude, $\mathbf{x}$ is a position on the surface, $S(\psi)$ is the set of positions belonging to the flux surface labeled by $\psi$, and $\mathbf{B}(\mathbf{x})$ is the total magnetic-field vector at that position.

The minimum is taken over all positions on each nested magnetic flux surface and includes the complete equilibrium field, including its poloidal and toroidal contributions. It is not a signed component minimum, a flux-surface average, or a minimum taken across multiple flux surfaces.

Unlike the [flux-surface-averaged inverse square of magnetic-field magnitude](name:flux_surface_averaged_inverse_of_square_of_magnetic_field_magnitude), this quantity reduces the field magnitude itself by a pointwise minimum rather than averaging its reciprocal square.

NAMES.name: minimum_safety_factor
NAMES.short: Signed safety-factor value on the closed magnetic flux surface where the magnitude of field-line winding is smallest, distinct from that surface’s location.
NAMES.long:
The minimum safety factor is the signed field-line winding number evaluated on the nested closed magnetic flux surface where the magnitude of the safety factor is smallest. It represents the extremal value of the safety-factor function within the confined closed-surface domain.

The minimizing value is defined by

$$
q_{\min} = q(\rho_\ast), \qquad \rho_\ast \in \operatorname*{arg\,min}_{0 \leq \rho \leq 1} |q(\rho)|
$$

where $q(\rho)$ is the signed [safety factor](name:safety_factor) on the flux surface labeled by $\rho$, $\rho_\ast$ is the label of a surface at which the magnitude $|q(\rho)|$ is minimized, and $q_{\min}$ is the signed value evaluated there. The label $\rho$ is a monotonic flux-surface coordinate whose endpoints denote the magnetic axis and the last closed flux surface. In flux coordinates $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$, $\theta$ is the poloidal angle and $\phi$ is the toroidal angle of the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius and $Z$ is vertical height.

The extremum is taken over all nested closed magnetic flux surfaces and is neither a flux-surface average nor a sum. The location-defining quantity is separate: [poloidal magnetic flux at minimum safety factor](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_minimum_safety_factor) identifies the corresponding surface, while this quantity reports only the signed safety factor. It is also distinct from a safety factor evaluated at a prescribed locus, such as the magnetic axis.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the toroidal angle advance of a magnetic field line is in the direction of increasing $\phi$ as the poloidal angle $\theta$ increases.

NAMES.name: normalized_poloidal_flux_coordinate_of_plasma_boundary
NAMES.short: Radial flux-surface location of the selected plasma boundary, expressed by the normalized poloidal flux coordinate. It is the linear normalized poloidal flux value, increasing from zero at the magnetic axis to one at the separatrix, of the closed flux surface taken as the plasma boundary; fixed-boundary equilibrium calculations commonly set it slightly below one to select a surface just inside the separatrix.
NAMES.long:
The normalized poloidal flux coordinate of the plasma boundary is the value of the [normalized poloidal flux coordinate](name:normalized_poloidal_flux_coordinate) on the closed flux surface selected as the plasma boundary. It is the linear normalized poloidal flux, labeling the boundary's radial position between the magnetic axis and the last closed flux surface.

Its value is the poloidal flux difference from the magnetic axis normalized to the axis-to-separatrix flux difference:

$$
\psi_{\mathrm{N}}^{\mathrm{boundary}} = \frac{\psi_{\mathrm{boundary}} - \psi_{\mathrm{axis}}}{\psi_{\mathrm{sep}} - \psi_{\mathrm{axis}}}
$$

where $\psi_{\mathrm{boundary}}$ is the [poloidal magnetic flux](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux) on the selected plasma-boundary surface, $\psi_{\mathrm{axis}}$ is the [poloidal magnetic flux at the magnetic axis](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_magnetic_axis), and $\psi_{\mathrm{sep}}$ is the poloidal magnetic flux at the separatrix (last closed flux surface).

The label equals zero at the magnetic axis and equals one when the selected plasma boundary coincides with the separatrix; a value below one selects an internal closed flux surface. Its defining role is to specify, for fixed-boundary equilibrium representations, which closed flux surface is taken as the plasma boundary, commonly a surface just inside the separatrix so that the boundary remains strictly closed.

This is the linear normalized poloidal flux value itself, not its square root, and it is a flux-surface label rather than a signed poloidal-flux value or a geometric minor-radius measure. It is distinct from the toroidal-flux-based boundary label [normalized toroidal flux coordinate at the plasma boundary](name:normalized_toroidal_flux_coordinate_at_plasma_boundary), and it belongs to the same locus-valued family as the [normalized poloidal flux coordinate at minimum safety factor](name:normalized_poloidal_flux_coordinate_at_minimum_safety_factor) and the [normalized poloidal flux coordinate of the pedestal](name:normalized_poloidal_flux_coordinate_of_pedestal).

NAMES.name: safety_factor_at_magnetic_axis
NAMES.short: Limiting signed field-line winding number on the innermost closed flux surface, giving toroidal turns per poloidal circuit at the magnetic axis.
NAMES.long:
The safety factor at the magnetic axis is the limiting signed field-line winding number as nested closed magnetic flux surfaces contract toward the magnetic axis. It gives the toroidal transits per complete poloidal circuit in that limit.

The axis value is defined by

$$
q_{\rm axis} = \lim_{\psi \to \psi_{\rm axis}} q(\psi)
$$

where $q_{\rm axis}$ is the safety factor at the magnetic axis, $q(\psi)$ is the safety factor on the flux surface labeled by $\psi$, and $\psi_{\rm axis}$ is the value of that flux-surface label at the magnetic axis.

This quantity applies only to the magnetic-axis limit of nested closed flux surfaces in an equilibrium. It is a single equilibrium winding value with no species, population, or charge-state aggregation, and it is distinct from safety factor values on finite-radius surfaces such as the [safety factor at the plasma boundary](name:safety_factor_at_plasma_boundary).

It is the magnetic-axis specialization of the [safety factor](name:safety_factor): the parent quantity describes field-line winding as a function of flux-surface label, while this quantity selects its limiting value at $\psi_{\rm axis}$. The parent relation is the signed flux-increment ratio $q = d\Phi_{\rm tor}/(d\Phi_{\rm pol}/2\pi)$, where $\Phi_{\rm tor}$ is toroidal magnetic flux and $\Phi_{\rm pol}$ is poloidal magnetic flux.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the toroidal magnetic-flux increment $d\Phi_{\rm tor}$ and poloidal magnetic-flux increment $d\Phi_{\rm pol}$ have the same sign for the positively oriented field-line circuit, with $\phi$ increasing in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

NAMES.name: safety_factor_at_normalized_poloidal_magnetic_flux_equal_to_0_95
NAMES.short: Signed field-line winding number on the closed magnetic flux surface labeled by normalized poloidal magnetic flux 0.95, near but inside the plasma boundary.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the signed field-line winding number on the closed magnetic flux surface labeled by normalized poloidal magnetic flux 0.95. It gives the toroidal transits per complete poloidal circuit on that specific surface.

The locus-specific evaluation is

$$
q_{95}=q(\psi_N=0.95)
$$

where $q_{95}$ is the safety factor at the specified locus, $q$ is the [safety factor](name:safety_factor), and $\psi_N$ is the normalized poloidal magnetic-flux coordinate. The value 0.95 selects the surface at 95% of the normalized poloidal-flux interval, with the magnetic axis and plasma boundary serving as the inner and outer reference surfaces.

The quantity applies only to that single closed flux surface. It is a scalar flux-surface value, with no summation, integration, or averaging over neighboring surfaces. It is distinct from the [safety factor at the magnetic axis](name:safety_factor_at_magnetic_axis) and the [safety factor at the plasma boundary](name:safety_factor_at_plasma_boundary), which use different evaluation loci.

Thus, this quantity is the normalized-poloidal-flux-locus specialization of the parent [safety factor](name:safety_factor); the field-line winding definition is unchanged, and only the evaluation surface differs. The right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame has $R$ as major radius, $\phi$ as toroidal angle, and $Z$ as vertical height.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the signed toroidal and poloidal magnetic-flux increments defining the field-line winding ratio have the same sign in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: safety_factor_at_plasma_boundary
NAMES.short: Signed field-line winding ratio evaluated on the outermost closed magnetic flux surface, counting toroidal turns per poloidal circuit at the plasma boundary.
NAMES.long:
The boundary safety factor is the signed helical winding of magnetic field lines on the outermost closed magnetic flux surface, counting toroidal turns per poloidal circuit at the plasma boundary.

It is defined by the differential ratio of toroidal to poloidal magnetic flux:

$$
q_{\mathrm{b}} = \left.\frac{d\Phi_{\mathrm{tor}}}{d\Phi_{\mathrm{pol}}}\right|_{\mathrm{b}}
$$

where $q_{\mathrm{b}}$ is the safety factor at the boundary, $\Phi_{\mathrm{tor}}$ is toroidal magnetic flux, $\Phi_{\mathrm{pol}}$ is poloidal magnetic flux, and the subscript $\mathrm{b}$ denotes evaluation on the plasma-boundary flux surface.

The quantity applies to the single outermost closed flux surface defining the plasma boundary. It is a flux-surface value, not a volume average, region integral, or value at an interior normalized-flux surface; in particular, it is distinct from the safety factor at normalized poloidal magnetic flux 0.95, commonly represented by [safety factor at normalized poloidal magnetic flux equal to 0.95](name:safety_factor_at_normalized_poloidal_magnetic_flux_equal_to_0_95).

This quantity is the boundary-specific instance of the general [safety factor](name:safety_factor), obtained by evaluating the same flux-increment relation on the plasma-boundary surface.

NAMES.name: energy_confinement_enhancement_factor
NAMES.short: Dimensionless ratio comparing the plasma energy confinement time with the IPB98(y,2) reference scaling prediction.
NAMES.long:
The energy confinement enhancement factor is the multiplicative departure of a plasma’s global energy confinement time from the IPB98(y,2) reference scaling prediction. It indicates whether energy is retained longer or shorter than the reference predicts for the corresponding scaling inputs.

The factor is defined by:

$$
h_{98} = \frac{\tau_E}{\tau_{E,\mathrm{IPB98(y,2)}}}
$$

where $h_{98}$ is the energy confinement enhancement factor, $\tau_E$ is the plasma energy confinement time, and $\tau_{E,\mathrm{IPB98(y,2)}}$ is the energy confinement time predicted by the IPB98(y,2) reference scaling.

This is a global plasma quantity: the numerator represents the confinement of the total stored plasma energy relative to the corresponding net energy-loss power, aggregated over the plasma rather than assigned to a local region or individual transport channel. It is not itself an energy confinement time, stored energy, power, or local transport coefficient.

A value of one denotes agreement with the reference scaling; a value greater than one denotes longer confinement, and a value less than one denotes shorter confinement than the reference prediction.

NAMES.name: ipb98y2_confinement_time
NAMES.short: IPB98(y,2) empirical-scaling reference for global energy confinement time, providing the denominator for the H98 confinement enhancement factor.
NAMES.long:
The IPB98(y,2) energy confinement time is the global energy-confinement timescale predicted by the IPB98(y,2) empirical scaling law. It is an energy-channel performance benchmark rather than a species-resolved or local transport time.

The underlying global energy confinement time is defined by

$$
\tau_E = \frac{W}{P_{\mathrm{loss}}}
$$

where $\tau_E$ is the global energy confinement time, $W$ is the total thermal energy stored in the plasma, and $P_{\mathrm{loss}}$ is the net power leaving the plasma. The quantity documented here is the IPB98(y,2) scaling prediction of this timescale, not the directly evaluated confinement time for a particular plasma state.

The value applies to the complete plasma energy content and its global loss balance; it is not a local profile quantity, a particle confinement time, or a confinement time assigned to an individual species. It is a single empirical reference value for the energy channel.

The [energy confinement enhancement factor](name:energy_confinement_enhancement_factor) compares the actual global energy confinement time with this reference through $H_{98} = \tau_E / \tau_{E,98}$, where $H_{98}$ is the dimensionless confinement enhancement factor and $\tau_{E,98}$ is this IPB98(y,2) scaling prediction.

NAMES.name: krypton_density_at_plasma_boundary
NAMES.subject: krypton
NAMES.short: Number density of krypton ions at the plasma boundary, evaluated as the local, intensive particle count per physical volume on the last closed magnetic flux surface.
NAMES.long:
Number density of krypton ions at the plasma boundary is the local, intensive particle count per physical volume for the krypton-ion population evaluated on the last closed magnetic flux surface. The plasma boundary is the limiting closed magnetic flux surface separating confined plasma from the open-field-line scrape-off-layer region.

The local krypton ion number density is the sum of the zeroth velocity moments over all krypton ionization states at a boundary point:

$$
n_{\mathrm{Kr}}(\mathbf{x}_b,t) = \sum_{q \in \mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{Kr}}} \int f_{\mathrm{Kr}^{q+}}(\mathbf{x}_b,\mathbf{v},t)\,d^3v
$$

where $n_{\mathrm{Kr}}$ is the krypton ion number density, $\mathbf{x}_b$ is a point on the last closed magnetic flux surface, $t$ is time, $q$ is the krypton ionization-state index, $\mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{Kr}}$ is the set of all positively charged krypton ionization states, $f_{\mathrm{Kr}^{q+}}$ is the phase-space distribution function for state $q$, $\mathbf{v}$ is particle velocity, and $d^3v$ is the velocity-space volume element.

This quantity applies specifically to krypton ions and is summed over all included ionization states. It excludes neutral krypton and all other ion species, and it is a local boundary value with no averaging over the boundary surface or over a volume.

It is the krypton-specific instance of [density at the plasma boundary](name:density_at_plasma_boundary). The related [krypton density](name:krypton_density) represents the same charge-state-summed ion population at a general plasma location, whereas [flux-surface-averaged krypton density at the plasma boundary](name:flux_surface_averaged_krypton_density_at_plasma_boundary) averages the krypton density over the complete last closed magnetic flux surface rather than evaluating it locally.
