NAMES.name: accumulated_deposited_energy_of_plasma_facing_component
NAMES.short: Pulse-integrated heat deposited in a plasma-facing component, including heat recovered during post-discharge cooling as the component returns toward thermal equilibrium.
NAMES.long:
Accumulated deposited energy is the total heat energy transferred to a plasma-facing component during a complete plasma discharge and its post-discharge return toward thermal equilibrium. It represents a component-level thermal load rather than the plasma's stored thermal energy.

The accumulated quantity is defined by integrating the deposition-associated power over the full interval:

$$
E_{\mathrm{dep}} = \int_{t_{\mathrm{start}}}^{t_{\mathrm{end}}} P_{\mathrm{dep}}(t)\,\mathrm{d}t
$$

where $E_{\mathrm{dep}}$ is the accumulated deposited energy, $P_{\mathrm{dep}}(t)$ is the power associated with heat deposited in the component at time $t$, and $t_{\mathrm{start}}$ and $t_{\mathrm{end}}$ define an interval covering the discharge and subsequent thermal return.

The quantity applies to the complete plasma-facing component and aggregates all deposited contributions into one total; it is not resolved by particle species or population. The accumulation includes heat recovered after the plasma pulse and excludes instantaneous power, local energy flux density, and plasma stored energy.

A mechanism-specific rate such as [power due to convection](name:power_due_to_convection) may contribute to the integral, but it is not itself the accumulated component-level energy.

NAMES.name: coolant_transit_time_of_plant_component_port
NAMES.short: Elapsed time for coolant to traverse the associated plant component from inlet to outlet, defining the thermal delay between the two coolant states.
NAMES.long:
Coolant transit time is the elapsed travel time for the coolant stream to pass through the plant component associated with the specified port, from its inlet to its outlet. It represents the transport delay between the inlet and outlet thermal states.

The transit time is defined as

$$
\tau_{\mathrm{c}} = t_{\mathrm{out}} - t_{\mathrm{in}}
$$

where $\tau_{\mathrm{c}}$ is the coolant transit time, $t_{\mathrm{in}}$ is the instant when the coolant crosses the component inlet, and $t_{\mathrm{out}}$ is the instant when the same coolant stream crosses the component outlet.

The quantity applies to the coolant path through one associated plant component and uses the inlet-to-outlet interval as its aggregation convention. It is not a plant-wide sum over components or ports, and it excludes transport outside the component, instrumentation or network latency, and a thermal time constant of the component material.

The transit time establishes the temporal correspondence between inlet conditions and the delayed outlet state represented by the [coolant temperature at outlet](name:coolant_temperature_at_outlet). It is distinct from the [coolant mass flow rate](name:ratio_of_coolant_mass_to_time), which describes transported mass per time rather than travel duration, and it provides the thermal-delay correction relevant to [total thermal coolant absorbed power at wall](name:total_thermal_coolant_absorbed_power_at_wall).

sources.leaf_definition: Transit time for the coolant to go from the input to the output of the component
sources.parent_definition: Set of components on which calorimetry measurements are carried out

NAMES.name: ratio_of_coolant_mass_to_time
NAMES.short: Net coolant mass throughput per unit time across a flow boundary, applicable to cooling loops and plant-component fluid ports.
NAMES.long:
Coolant mass flow rate is the net rate at which coolant crosses a defined flow boundary. It represents fluid throughput rather than a thermodynamic state or an energy-transfer quantity.

The instantaneous rate is defined by

$$
\dot{m}_c(t) = \frac{dM_c(t)}{dt}
$$

where $\dot{m}_c(t)$ is the coolant mass flow rate, $M_c(t)$ is the cumulative net coolant mass that has crossed the boundary, $t$ is time, and the subscript $c$ denotes coolant.

The quantity applies to the coolant stream as a whole, with its mass contributions aggregated into one net rate. It is generic with respect to the flow boundary: no particular inlet, outlet, cooling loop, or plant component is implied. It excludes coolant temperature, enthalpy change, transit time, and deposited thermal power.

This quantity is the time-rate derivative of [coolant mass](name:coolant_mass), so it describes transport of mass rather than the amount of coolant present. When inlet and outlet states are specified, [coolant_temperature_at_inlet](name:coolant_temperature_at_inlet) and [coolant_temperature_at_outlet](name:coolant_temperature_at_outlet) provide the corresponding thermal states for an enthalpy balance; the mass flow rate itself is not that balance or its resulting power.
NAMES.sign: Positive when net coolant transport is in the adopted positive flow direction across the defined boundary.

NAMES.name: ion_current_of_mass_spectrometer_channel
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Collected conventional electrical current carried by the ion population assigned to one mass-resolved channel.
NAMES.long:
The collected ion current is the conventional electrical current delivered to a detector by ions assigned to one selected atomic-mass or mass-to-charge channel. It represents the channel-specific ion population rather than the complete detector signal across all mass channels.

The defining charge-collection relation is

$$
I_{\mathrm{ion}} = \frac{dQ_{\mathrm{ion}}}{dt} = \sum_{k \in \mathcal{C}} q_k\frac{dN_k}{dt}
$$

where $I_{\mathrm{ion}}$ is the collected ion current, $Q_{\mathrm{ion}}$ is the charge delivered by collected ions, $t$ is time, $\mathcal{C}$ is the set of ion populations assigned to the selected channel, $q_k$ is the charge carried by an ion in population $k$, and $N_k$ is the cumulative number of ions from population $k$ collected by the detector.

The aggregation is over all ion arrivals assigned to the selected channel and species, including any charge states represented by that channel; it is not an aggregate over the full mass spectrum or over unrelated channels. The quantity excludes neutral-gas pressure and the detector-bias potential represented by the [voltage of a mass-spectrometer channel](name:voltage_of_mass_spectrometer_channel).

Unlike [ion current density](name:ion_current_density), which is a local vector charge flux per area, this quantity is the total collected current associated with one channel. Its channel-specific value can therefore contribute to determining the corresponding species abundance, while remaining distinct from a current density.
NAMES.sign: Positive when positive ion charge is collected by the detector channel.

NAMES.name: toroidal_coordinate_of_aperture
NAMES.short: Azimuthal angle locating the geometric center of an aperture about the machine symmetry axis in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The toroidal coordinate of an aperture is the azimuthal angle locating the aperture’s geometric center around the machine symmetry axis. It identifies the center’s toroidal position in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

This quantity applies specifically to the geometric center of the aperture as a diagnostic component. It is a point coordinate, not the toroidal coordinate of the aperture boundary, an angular extent, or an average over the aperture or any plasma region.

Together with the [vertical coordinate of the aperture](name:vertical_coordinate_of_aperture), it locates the aperture center in the cylindrical frame. It is the aperture-specific member of the geometric-center coordinate family represented by the [toroidal coordinate of an optical element](name:toroidal_coordinate_of_optical_element).

NAMES.name: voltage_of_mass_spectrometer_channel
NAMES.short: Signed bias potential applied between the photomultiplier detector electrode and its electronics reference for one mass-resolved channel, setting ion-signal gain.
NAMES.long:
The mass-spectrometer channel voltage is the detector-bias potential difference associated with one channel assigned to a selected atomic mass. It is an instrumental operating parameter of the photomultiplier detector that controls the gain applied to the collected ion signal, rather than a plasma thermodynamic or field quantity.

The defining potential difference is

$$
V_{\mathrm{ch}} = \phi_{\mathrm{det}} - \phi_{\mathrm{ref}}
$$

where $V_{\mathrm{ch}}$ is the channel detector-bias voltage, $\phi_{\mathrm{det}}$ is the electric potential of the photomultiplier detector electrode, and $\phi_{\mathrm{ref}}$ is the electronics reference potential.

This quantity applies to one mass-resolved channel and its associated detector circuit. It is not summed or averaged across channels, mass assignments, detector electrodes, or ion populations, and it does not represent a local plasma voltage.

The channel-level quantity specializes the device-level [mass-spectrometer detector bias voltage](name:voltage_of_mass_spectrometer) to one channel. It is distinct from the [ion current of a mass-spectrometer channel](name:ion_current_of_mass_spectrometer_channel), which is the collected electrical signal, and from the [voltage of a spectrometer channel](name:voltage_of_spectrometer_channel), which denotes an electrical output signal rather than the detector-bias potential.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the detector electrode potential exceeds the electronics reference potential.

sources.leaf_definition: Voltage applied to the photomultiplier
sources.parent_definition: Set of mass channels, each corresponding to a given atomic mass measured continuously by the spectrometer

NAMES.name: line_averaged_effective_charge
NAMES.short: Dimensionless line-averaged effective ionic charge of a plasma mixture, obtained by averaging local effective charge along a prescribed plasma line of sight.
NAMES.long:
Line-averaged effective ionic charge characterizes the charge composition of a plasma mixture through the average of its local effective charge along a prescribed line of sight.

The line average is defined by

$$
\overline{Z}_{\mathrm{eff}} = \frac{1}{L} \int_{0}^{L} Z_{\mathrm{eff}}(\ell)\,d\ell
$$

where $\overline{Z}_{\mathrm{eff}}$ is the line-averaged effective ionic charge, $L$ is the total path length through the plasma, $\ell$ is distance along the line of sight, and $Z_{\mathrm{eff}}(\ell)$ is the local effective charge at position $\ell$.

This quantity applies to the complete included ion mixture along the line of sight. At each position, the ionic contribution is summed over all represented ion species and charge states, while the line aggregation is a uniform average over physical path length.

The local integrand is the [effective charge](name:effective_charge), defined from the second ionic charge moment divided by free-electron density. This quantity is distinct from a local effective charge at a single position and from the [volume-averaged effective charge](name:volume_averaged_effective_charge), which uses volume weighting rather than line-of-sight path-length weighting; it also differs from the [flux-surface-averaged effective charge at the plasma boundary](name:flux_surface_averaged_effective_charge_at_plasma_boundary), which averages over a boundary surface.

sources.leaf_definition: Average effective charge along the line of sight
sources.parent_definition: Set of channels (detector or pixel of a camera)

NAMES.name: line_averaged_electron_temperature
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Thermal energy of the bulk electron population expressed as an energy-equivalent temperature, averaged along a plasma chord.
NAMES.long:
Line-averaged electron temperature is the energy-equivalent measure of the mean random kinetic energy of the bulk electron population, averaged along a plasma chord.

The defining path-length average is:

$$
T_{e,\mathrm{line}} = \frac{1}{L}\int_0^L T_e(l)\,dl
$$

where $T_{e,\mathrm{line}}$ is the line-averaged electron temperature, $T_e(l)$ is the local [electron temperature](name:electron_temperature) at path coordinate $l$, and $L$ is the total chord length. The coordinate $l$ measures distance along the specified plasma chord, and the averaging is uniform with respect to path length.

This is an intensive quantity for the bulk electron population, aggregated along the chord rather than summed over electron energies or particle populations. It excludes ion temperatures and differs from the local electron temperature because it combines values along the entire chord.

The line average is a chord-integrated representation of the parent [electron_temperature](name:electron_temperature), whereas [volume_averaged_electron_temperature](name:volume_averaged_electron_temperature) applies a volume average over the confined plasma and is therefore a distinct spatial aggregation.

sources.leaf_definition: Value
sources.parent_definition: Electron temperature

NAMES.name: line_averaged_hydrogen_density
NAMES.subject: hydrogen
NAMES.short: Line-averaged number density of hydrogen (protium) ions in the plasma, giving the path-length-normalized H+ concentration along a specified chord.
NAMES.long:
The line-averaged hydrogen density quantifies the mean concentration of protium ions along a specified chord through the plasma. It represents the path-integrated hydrogen ion content normalized by the chord length.

The line average is defined as

$$
\overline{n}_H = \frac{1}{L}\int_{\mathcal{C}} n_H(\mathbf{r}(l))\,dl
$$

where $\overline{n}_H$ is the line-averaged hydrogen density, $n_H(\mathbf{r}(l))$ is the local protium-ion number density at position $\mathbf{r}(l)$ along the chord, $l$ is the path-length coordinate, $\mathcal{C}$ is the specified chord, and $L$ is its total length.

The quantity applies to charged protium ions, with any included protium ion charge states summed before the line average; neutral atomic hydrogen and heavier hydrogenic isotopes are excluded. It is a chord average rather than the local [hydrogen density](name:hydrogen_density) at a point or the volume average represented by [volume_averaged_hydrogen_density](name:volume_averaged_hydrogen_density).

Unlike [line_averaged_total_ion_density](name:line_averaged_total_ion_density), it does not include other ion species or hydrogen isotopes. The path-length normalization preserves the same density meaning as the parent local quantity while replacing its pointwise value with an average along the chord.

sources.leaf_definition: Value
sources.parent_definition: Hydrogen (H)

NAMES.name: radial_coordinate_of_thomson_scattering_laser
NAMES.short: Major-radius location of the Thomson-scattering laser endpoint, measured as perpendicular distance from the toroidal symmetry axis in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The radial coordinate of a Thomson-scattering laser is the major-radius position of its laser-beam endpoint, measured from the toroidal symmetry axis in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

$$
R_{\mathrm{end}} = \sqrt{x_{\mathrm{end}}^2+y_{\mathrm{end}}^2}
$$

where $R_{\mathrm{end}}$ is the endpoint major-radius coordinate, and $x_{\mathrm{end}}$ and $y_{\mathrm{end}}$ are the endpoint coordinates along the two horizontal axes of the right-handed Cartesian basis $(\hat{x},\hat{y},\hat{z})$, with $\hat{z}$ aligned with the vertical direction $\hat{Z}$.

This quantity applies to one laser endpoint and is a geometric point coordinate, not a path average, scattering-volume coordinate, beam attribute, or plasma-population quantity. It is neither summed nor averaged over lasers, endpoints, or plasma regions.

It is the Thomson-scattering-laser-specific realization of [radial coordinate](name:radial_coordinate), providing the $R$ coordinate of the endpoint. It is distinct from the [toroidal coordinate of the Thomson-scattering laser](name:toroidal_coordinate_of_thomson_scattering_laser), which specifies the endpoint's toroidal angle $\phi$.

sources.leaf_definition: Major radius
sources.parent_definition: Position of the laser end point

NAMES.name: ratio_of_ion_density_to_electron_density
NAMES.short: Local ion concentration relative to the electron population, defined as the number-density ratio for a specified impurity or fuel ion species.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the local abundance of a specified impurity or fuel ion species relative to the free-electron population. It compares particle populations rather than electric charge density or mass density.

The local ion-to-electron concentration ratio is defined by

$$
\mathcal{R}_{i/e} = \frac{n_i}{n_e}
$$

where $\mathcal{R}_{i/e}$ is the ion-to-electron concentration ratio, $n_i$ is the local number density of the specified ion species, $n_e$ is the local free-electron number density, $i$ identifies the selected ion species, and $e$ identifies the electron population.

Both densities are evaluated at the same local plasma point. For a species-level numerator without an explicitly selected charge state, $n_i$ is summed over all ionization states of that species; a charge-state-resolved numerator applies only to the selected state. No spatial average or line integration is implied.

The numerator is supplied by the corresponding [ion density](name:ion_density), while [ion charge state density](name:ion_charge_state_density) represents the density when one charge state is isolated. A named-species example of the same construction is the [ratio of iron density to electron density](name:ratio_of_iron_density_to_electron_density). This quantity is distinct from an ion charge-state fraction, electric charge-density ratio, or mass-density ratio.

sources.leaf_definition: Ion concentration (ratio of the ion density over the electron density) at the channel measurement point
sources.parent_definition: Physical quantities related to ion species and charge stage (H+, D+, T+, He+2, Li+3, Be+4, C+6, N+7, O+8, Ne+10, Si+14, Ar+16 or Ar+18) derived from the measured charge exchange emission of each species, at the position of the measurement

NAMES.name: accumulated_total_particle_count_due_to_gas_injection
NAMES.short: Cumulative equivalent-electron inventory of all gas particles delivered since plasma breakdown, summed over every injected species and injection location.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the cumulative inventory of gas delivered after plasma breakdown, expressed as equivalent electrons. Each injected atom or molecule contributes according to its total nuclear charge, so the quantity represents delivered gas inventory rather than the free-electron population currently present in the plasma.

$$
N_{\mathrm{eq}} = \sum_s Z_s N_s
$$

where $N_{\mathrm{eq}}$ is the cumulative equivalent-electron inventory, $s$ indexes the injected gas species, $Z_s$ is the total nuclear charge per particle of species $s$, and $N_s$ is the cumulative number of particles of species $s$ delivered after breakdown.

The aggregation includes all injected gas species and all injection locations, producing one total inventory rather than a per-species or per-inlet value. It excludes gas introduced during prefill before plasma breakdown and does not represent the number of free electrons remaining in the plasma or the ionization-state-resolved plasma content.

Species-specific accumulated inventories, such as [accumulated_neon_count](name:accumulated_neon_count), contribute to this total under the same equivalent-electron convention. The post-breakdown quantity is distinct from [accumulated_total_prefill_gas_count](name:accumulated_total_prefill_gas_count), which accounts for gas introduced before plasma breakdown.

sources.leaf_definition: Value
sources.parent_definition: Total accumulated injected gas (sum over species)

NAMES.name: coolant_temperature_at_inlet
NAMES.short: Absolute thermodynamic temperature of coolant entering a cooling loop or plant component, establishing the upstream state for enthalpy-based heat-transfer balances.
NAMES.long:
The coolant inlet temperature is the absolute thermodynamic temperature of the coolant or working fluid at the entrance to a cooling loop, plant component, or cooling module. It specifies the upstream thermal state of the fluid before heat transfer through the associated cooled volume.

The quantity is a local boundary value at the relevant inlet and is not an average or aggregate over multiple components, loops, or inlet streams. It applies to the coolant population crossing that inlet, rather than to the cooled solid or the plasma.

It is distinct from the downstream [coolant temperature at outlet](name:coolant_temperature_at_outlet) and does not represent the temperature change across the cooled component or loop.

In an enthalpy balance, the inlet temperature supplies the upstream thermal state and is used with the outlet temperature and [coolant mass flow rate](name:ratio_of_coolant_mass_to_time) to determine thermal power transferred to the coolant. The quantity itself is a temperature, not a power or a coolant-flow measurement.

NAMES.name: coolant_temperature_at_outlet
NAMES.short: Absolute thermodynamic temperature of coolant leaving a cooling component or loop, specifying the fluid’s outlet thermal state for enthalpy-based heat balance.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the absolute thermodynamic temperature of the coolant fluid at the outlet of a cooling component, cooling loop, or comparable coolant circuit. It describes the bulk fluid state at the exit boundary.

The scope is limited to coolant at an outlet and does not represent the inlet temperature, a wall temperature, or an aggregate temperature over the entire cooling system. It is an outlet state value for the selected cooling path, not a mass-flow rate or a deposited-power quantity.

Together with the [coolant temperature at the inlet](name:coolant_temperature_at_inlet) and the [coolant mass flow rate](name:ratio_of_coolant_mass_to_time), this temperature determines the coolant enthalpy change used to assess heat transferred into the fluid. The enthalpy balance distinguishes thermal power deposited in the coolant from the outlet temperature itself.

NAMES.name: gas_flow
NAMES.short: Pressure-volume throughput of a gas stream, expressed as the product of gas pressure and volumetric flow rate at a flow boundary.
NAMES.long:
Gas flow is the pressure-volume throughput of a gas stream crossing a defined flow boundary. It represents the aggregate gas stream rather than a particular molecular species, charge state, mass flow, or particle-number rate.

The defining pressure-volume throughput is

$$
Q_g = p_g \frac{dV_g}{dt}
$$

where $Q_g$ is gas pressure-volume throughput, $p_g$ is the gas pressure at the flow boundary, $V_g$ is the volume of gas crossing that boundary, and $t$ is time.

This quantity applies to the gas stream delivered through an injection system and is not itself restricted to an upper or lower operating limit. The [maximum gas flow](name:maximum_gas_flow) is the largest reliably deliverable value of this throughput, while the [minimum gas flow](name:minimum_gas_flow) is the smallest reliably deliverable value; both are limiting instances of the general quantity.

NAMES.name: maximum_gas_flow
NAMES.short: Maximum gas flow is the largest pressure-volume throughput that a gas injection valve can reliably deliver, defining the upper bound of its controllable range.
NAMES.long:
Maximum gas flow is the upper reliable operating limit of the pressure-volume throughput delivered by a gas injection valve. It represents the aggregate gas stream rather than a particular molecular species, charge state, mass flow, or particle-number rate.

The defining pressure-volume throughput at the upper delivery limit is

$$
Q_g^{\max} = p_g \frac{dV_g}{dt}
$$

where $Q_g^{\max}$ is the maximum gas pressure-volume throughput, $p_g$ is the gas pressure at the flow boundary, $V_g$ is the volume of gas crossing that boundary, and $t$ is time.

This quantity applies to gas delivered through a gas injection valve for fueling, impurity seeding, or disruption mitigation. The maximum qualifier denotes a reliable upper delivery limit for the aggregate gas stream, not a species-resolved flow, mass-flow rate, or particle-number rate.

The quantity is the upper-bound member of the [gas flow](name:gas_flow) family: gas flow denotes the same pressure-volume throughput without an upper-limit restriction, while [minimum gas flow](name:minimum_gas_flow) denotes its lower reliable operating limit.

sources.leaf_definition: Maximum flow rate of the valve
sources.parent_definition: Set of valves connecting a gas bottle to pipes

NAMES.name: minimum_gas_flow
NAMES.short: Minimum gas flow is the smallest pressure-volume gas throughput that a gas injection valve can reliably deliver, defining the lower bound of its controllable range.
NAMES.long:
Minimum gas flow is the lower reliable operating limit of the pressure-volume throughput delivered by a gas injection valve. It identifies the smallest controllable value of the aggregate gas stream throughput, rather than a molecular-species flow or particle-number rate.

The pressure-volume throughput represented by this quantity is defined as

$$
Q_g = p_g \frac{dV_g}{dt}
$$

where $Q_g$ is gas pressure-volume throughput, $p_g$ is gas pressure at the flow boundary, $V_g$ is the volume of gas crossing that boundary, and $t$ is time.

This quantity applies to the aggregate gas stream delivered through an injection system across a defined flow boundary. The stream is not restricted to a particular molecular species or charge state, and this quantity is distinct from mass flow and particle-number rate. Its defining distinction is the lower reliable operating bound, rather than an unrestricted instantaneous throughput.

The [gas flow](name:gas_flow) quantity defines the same pressure-volume throughput without imposing a lower-limit condition; minimum gas flow is its lower reliable operating bound. Conversely, [maximum gas flow](name:maximum_gas_flow) is the upper reliable operating bound, so the two quantities delimit the controllable range rather than represent different throughput definitions.

NAMES.name: total_neutral_source_rate_due_to_gas_injection
NAMES.subject: neutral
NAMES.short: Instantaneous equivalent-electron source rate of neutral gas introduced into the vessel by gas injection, summed over all injected species.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the instantaneous neutral-gas throughput supplied to the vessel by gas injection, expressed as an equivalent-electron rate. It combines all injected neutral species rather than representing one gas species.

For the set of injected species, the equivalent-electron rate is defined by:

$$
\dot{N}_{\mathrm{eq}} = \sum_{s \in \mathcal{S}} Z_s\,\dot{N}_s
$$

where $\dot{N}_{\mathrm{eq}}$ is the total equivalent-electron source rate, $\mathcal{S}$ is the set of injected neutral gas species, $\dot{N}_s$ is the particle injection rate of species $s$, and $Z_s$ is the equivalent-electron weighting per injected particle. For an atomic species, $Z_s$ is its atomic number; for a molecule, it is the sum of the atomic numbers of its constituent atoms.

The quantity applies to the vessel-level gas input and is aggregated by summing over all injected neutral species. It is an instantaneous rate, not a time-integrated inventory, and excludes ionization and subsequent plasma particle sources. Species-resolved rates such as the [hydrogen source rate due to gas injection](name:hydrogen_source_rate_due_to_gas_injection) provide individual contributions to this total. Unlike the [total lower gas source rate of the vacuum vessel due to gas injection](name:total_lower_gas_source_rate_of_vacuum_vessel_due_to_gas_injection), it is not restricted to the lower vessel region.

The corresponding accumulated quantity, such as the [accumulated hydrogen count due to gas injection](name:accumulated_hydrogen_count_due_to_gas_injection), is obtained by time integration and represents delivered inventory rather than instantaneous throughput.

sources.leaf_definition: Value
sources.parent_definition: Total gas injection rate (sum over species)

NAMES.name: normalized_toroidal_flux_coordinate_at_pellet_path
NAMES.short: Normalized toroidal magnetic-flux surface label assigned to each pellet location, identifying the nested magnetic surface reached along the pellet’s in-plasma ablation trajectory.
NAMES.long:
This quantity identifies the nested magnetic surface containing the pellet at a specified location along its in-plasma ablation trajectory. It is a magnetic-surface coordinate, not a cylindrical distance or a local vector component.

At pellet position $\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm p}$, the normalized toroidal flux coordinate is defined by

$$
\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}(\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm p}) = \left[\frac{\Phi_{\mathrm{tor}}(\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm p}) - \Phi_{\mathrm{tor,axis}}}{\Phi_{\mathrm{tor,boundary}} - \Phi_{\mathrm{tor,axis}}}\right]^{1/2}
$$

where $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}$ is the normalized toroidal flux coordinate, $\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm p}$ is the pellet position, $\Phi_{\mathrm{tor}}(\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm p})$ is the toroidal magnetic flux labeling the magnetic surface through that position, $\Phi_{\mathrm{tor,axis}}$ is its value at the magnetic axis, and $\Phi_{\mathrm{tor,boundary}}$ is its value at the equilibrium boundary. The position is interpreted in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

The scope is the pellet’s in-plasma ablation trajectory, with the coordinate evaluated pointwise at each pellet location. It does not represent distance traveled along the path, a path integral, an average over the trajectory, or an aggregate over multiple pellets.

This is the locus-specific realization of the [normalized toroidal flux coordinate](name:normalized_toroidal_flux_coordinate). The axis and boundary references set the coordinate endpoints, so the value increases outward across nested magnetic surfaces while remaining distinct from a cylindrical radial coordinate.

sources.leaf_definition: Normalized toroidal coordinate along the pellet path
sources.parent_definition: 1-D profiles of plasma and pellet along the pellet path

NAMES.name: radial_coordinate_of_shatter_cone
NAMES.short: Major-radius coordinate of the shatter-cone origin, locating its reference point by perpendicular distance from the toroidal symmetry axis.
NAMES.long:
The radial coordinate of a shatter-cone origin is the major-radius location of that geometric reference point relative to the toroidal symmetry axis. It is the $R$ coordinate in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, with basis vectors $(\hat{R}, \hat{\phi}, \hat{Z})$ satisfying $\hat{R} \times \hat{\phi} = \hat{Z}$.

This quantity applies specifically to the origin of the elliptic shatter cone. It denotes one geometric coordinate of that reference point, with no averaging, integration, or aggregation over the cone surface, its axis, or injected fragments; it is distinct from radial coordinates assigned to other injector features or positions.

It is a locus-specific specialization of [radial coordinate](name:radial_coordinate): the parent defines the major-radius coordinate generally, while this quantity evaluates it at the shatter-cone origin.

sources.leaf_definition: Major radius
sources.parent_definition: Coordinates of the origin of the shatter cone

NAMES.name: radial_outline_of_limiter_tile
NAMES.short: Major-radius coordinate R locating each point on the boundary outline of a plasma-facing limiter tile in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The radial outline coordinate is the major-radius value $R$ of each point on the geometric boundary outline of a plasma-facing limiter tile. It describes tile geometry rather than a plasma field or a flux-surface coordinate.

In a right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, the major-radius coordinate is defined from Cartesian coordinates by

$$
R = \sqrt{x^2+y^2}
$$

where $R$ is the perpendicular distance from the toroidal symmetry axis, and $x$ and $y$ are Cartesian coordinate values along the $\hat{x}$ and $\hat{y}$ axes of the right-handed $(\hat{x},\hat{y},\hat{z})$ basis.

The quantity is evaluated pointwise for every contour point of the limiter-tile outline. It is not an average, maximum, area, or integrated boundary measure; for a closed contour, the first point is not repeated at the end.

Together with the [vertical outline of the limiter tile](name:vertical_outline_of_limiter_tile), it supplies the complementary radial and vertical coordinates that locate the outline in a poloidal cross-section. The related [radial coordinate](name:radial_coordinate) expresses the same geometric coordinate concept without specifying the limiter-tile outline locus.

sources.leaf_definition: Major radius
sources.parent_definition: Irregular outline of the limiting surface. Repeat the first point in case of a closed contour

NAMES.name: ratio_of_iron_density_to_electron_density
NAMES.short: Dimensionless abundance ratio of charge-state-summed iron-ion number density to local free-electron number density.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the local iron-to-electron abundance ratio in a plasma, comparing the population of iron ions with unbound free electrons.

$$
R_{\mathrm{Fe}/e} = \frac{n_{\mathrm{Fe}}}{n_e}
$$

where $R_{\mathrm{Fe}/e}$ is the iron-to-electron abundance ratio, $n_{\mathrm{Fe}}$ is the total [iron-ion number density](name:iron_density), and $n_e$ is the local [free-electron number density](name:electron_density).

The numerator is summed over all positive iron ionization states, while the denominator counts free electrons and excludes electrons bound in atoms, molecules, or ions. This is a local ratio with no volume averaging, maximum operation, or specified spatial locus.

The ratio is the iron-specific counterpart of the general [ion-density-to-electron-density ratio](name:ratio_of_ion_density_to_electron_density); its numerator is the charge-state-summed iron density and its denominator is the electron-density parent quantity.

sources.leaf_definition: Value
sources.parent_definition: Iron (Fe)

NAMES.name: ratio_of_volume_averaged_beryllium_density_to_volume_averaged_electron_density
NAMES.short: Dimensionless beryllium abundance formed by dividing the volume-averaged beryllium density by the volume-averaged electron density.
NAMES.long:
Dimensionless beryllium abundance formed by dividing the volume-averaged beryllium density by the volume-averaged electron density. It represents the abundance of ionized beryllium relative to free electrons in the confined plasma volume.

The abundance is defined by the ratio of the two volume averages:

$$
a_{\mathrm{Be}} =
\frac{\langle n_{\mathrm{Be}} \rangle_V}{\langle n_e \rangle_V}
=
\frac{\left\langle \sum_{q=1}^{4} n_{\mathrm{Be}^{q+}} \right\rangle_V}{\langle n_e \rangle_V}
$$

where $a_{\mathrm{Be}}$ is the beryllium abundance ratio, $\langle \cdot \rangle_V$ denotes averaging over the confined plasma volume, $n_{\mathrm{Be}}$ is the charge-state-summed beryllium ion number density, $n_{\mathrm{Be}^{q+}}$ is the number density of beryllium ions in charge state $q$, and $n_e$ is the [electron density](name:electron_density).

The numerator is the [volume-averaged beryllium density](name:volume_averaged_beryllium_density), summed over all ionized beryllium charge states and excluding neutral beryllium atoms. The denominator is the [volume-averaged electron density](name:volume_averaged_electron_density) over the same confined plasma volume.

This quantity is a ratio of two global volume averages, not a pointwise impurity fraction and not the volume average of $n_{\mathrm{Be}}/n_e$. It is not charge-weighted; a charge-weighted beryllium contribution to quasineutrality would use terms proportional to $q n_{\mathrm{Be}^{q+}}$ rather than the unweighted ion sum. The local pre-averaged counterpart of the numerator is [beryllium density](name:beryllium_density).

sources.parent_definition: Beryllium (Be)

NAMES.name: ratio_of_volume_averaged_boron_density_to_volume_averaged_electron_density
NAMES.short: Dimensionless global boron abundance ratio using separately volume-averaged boron and electron number densities, with neutral boron and every ionic charge state included.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the global abundance of elemental boron relative to the electron population. It characterizes plasma composition over the full plasma volume rather than at a local point or along a line of sight.

The defining ratio is

$$
f_B = \frac{\overline{n}_B}{\overline{n}_e}
$$

where $f_B$ is the boron-to-electron abundance ratio, $\overline{n}_B$ is the volume-averaged elemental boron number density, and $\overline{n}_e$ is the volume-averaged electron number density. The overbar denotes averaging over the plasma volume.

The numerator includes neutral boron and every ionic boron charge state, while the denominator represents the complete electron population. For the associated plasma-composition convention, the ratio is evaluated at the time of peak electron density.

This quantity is distinct from local [boron density](name:boron_density) and from [line-averaged boron density](name:line_averaged_boron_density): it is a quotient of two separately volume-averaged densities, not a volume average of a pointwise ratio or a line average. Its numerator is the [volume-averaged boron density](name:volume_averaged_boron_density), making this ratio the corresponding normalized composition measure.

NAMES.name: ratio_of_volume_averaged_carbon_density_to_volume_averaged_electron_density
NAMES.short: Dimensionless plasma-wide carbon abundance defined as the ratio of volume-averaged carbon number density to volume-averaged electron number density. The carbon density is summed over all carbon charge states.
NAMES.long:
Dimensionless plasma-wide carbon abundance is the ratio of volume-averaged carbon number density to volume-averaged electron number density. It represents the elemental carbon abundance relative to electrons over the same plasma volume.

The defining ratio is

$$
f_{C,V} = \frac{\langle n_C \rangle_V}{\langle n_e \rangle_V} = \frac{\left\langle \sum_{q=0}^{6} n_{\mathrm{C},q} \right\rangle_V}{\langle n_e \rangle_V}
$$

where $f_{C,V}$ is the ratio of volume-averaged carbon density to volume-averaged electron density, $\langle n_C \rangle_V$ is the [volume-averaged carbon density](name:volume_averaged_carbon_density), $\langle n_e \rangle_V$ is the [volume-averaged electron density](name:volume_averaged_electron_density), $n_C$ is the [carbon density](name:carbon_density), $n_{\mathrm{C},q}$ is the local number density of carbon nuclei in charge state $q$, $q$ is the carbon charge-state index with $q=0$ for neutral carbon and $q=6$ for fully stripped carbon, and $\langle\cdot\rangle_V$ denotes averaging over the same plasma volume for numerator and denominator.

The population is elemental carbon in the plasma volume, with the numerator summed over neutral carbon and all ionic charge states. The aggregation convention is a ratio of two volume averages using the same volume weighting; it is not the volume average of the local ratio $n_C/n_e$.

This quantity is not an ion-only carbon abundance, not a fraction of total particle density, and not a charge-weighted impurity measure. It is the carbon member of the same volume-averaged impurity-abundance family as the [boron abundance ratio](name:ratio_of_volume_averaged_boron_density_to_volume_averaged_electron_density), and it differs from the [ratio of total ion density to electron density](name:ratio_of_total_ion_density_to_electron_density), which aggregates over all ion species rather than isolating elemental carbon.

NAMES.name: ratio_of_volume_averaged_oxygen_density_to_volume_averaged_electron_density
NAMES.short: Volume-averaged oxygen ion density relative to volume-averaged electron density for the plasma, with oxygen summed over ionized charge states and neutral oxygen excluded.
NAMES.long:
Volume-averaged oxygen ion density relative to volume-averaged electron density is a scalar oxygen impurity fraction for the plasma. It compares the charge-state-summed volume average of ionized oxygen number density with the corresponding volume average of electron number density over the same averaging volume.

The ratio is defined by

$$
f_O = \frac{\left\langle \sum_{q=1}^{8} n_{O^{q+}} \right\rangle_V}{\langle n_e \rangle_V}
$$

where $f_O$ is this oxygen-to-electron density ratio, $\langle\cdot\rangle_V$ denotes a volume average over the averaging volume $V$, $q$ is the oxygen charge-state index, $n_{O^{q+}}$ is the local number density of oxygen ions in charge state $q+$, and $n_e$ is the local electron number density. The denominator $\langle n_e\rangle_V$ is the [volume-averaged electron density](name:volume_averaged_electron_density).

The numerator is summed over ionized oxygen charge states $O^{1+}$ through $O^{8+}$ and excludes neutral oxygen. This quantity is a single scalar composition fraction formed from volume-averaged populations; it is distinct from a local [oxygen density](name:oxygen_density), from a [line-averaged oxygen density](name:line_averaged_oxygen_density), and from a neutral-inclusive [volume-averaged oxygen density](name:volume_averaged_oxygen_density) when that quantity includes neutral oxygen.

The essential relationship is normalization: the charge-state-summed volume-averaged oxygen ion density is divided by the [volume-averaged electron density](name:volume_averaged_electron_density), so the result represents oxygen ion abundance relative to the electron population rather than an absolute density.

NAMES.name: ratio_of_volume_averaged_tungsten_density_to_volume_averaged_electron_density
NAMES.short: Dimensionless tungsten abundance ratio equal to the plasma-volume-averaged elemental tungsten density divided by the plasma-volume-averaged electron density.
NAMES.long:
Dimensionless tungsten abundance ratio equal to the plasma-volume-averaged elemental tungsten density divided by the plasma-volume-averaged electron density. It compares the charge-state-summed tungsten-ion population with the free-electron population in the same plasma volume.

The ratio is defined from the two volume averages over the plasma volume $V$ as

$$
a_{\mathrm{W},V}
=
\frac{\langle n_{\mathrm{W}}\rangle_V}{\langle n_e\rangle_V}
=
\frac{V^{-1}\int_V \sum_{z=1}^{74} n_{\mathrm{W}^{z+}}(\mathbf{x})\, dV}{V^{-1}\int_V n_e(\mathbf{x})\, dV}
$$

where $a_{\mathrm{W},V}$ denotes this tungsten abundance ratio, $V$ denotes the plasma volume enclosed by the last closed flux surface over which both averages are formed, $\langle n_{\mathrm{W}}\rangle_V$ is the [volume-averaged tungsten density](name:volume_averaged_tungsten_density), $\langle n_e\rangle_V$ is the [volume-averaged electron density](name:volume_averaged_electron_density), $n_{\mathrm{W}^{z+}}(\mathbf{x})$ is the local number density of tungsten ions in charge state $z$ at position $\mathbf{x}$, $n_e(\mathbf{x})$ is the local free-electron number density, $z=1,\ldots,74$ indexes the positive tungsten ionization states, and $dV$ is the volume element.

The scope is the confined plasma volume: both numerator and denominator use the same volume and the same volume-averaging operation. The tungsten population is elemental tungsten in positive ionization states, summed over charge state; neutral tungsten is excluded. The aggregation is the ratio of the two volume averages, not the volume average of the local ratio $n_{\mathrm{W}}/n_e$, and the quantity is defined only when $\langle n_e\rangle_V$ is nonzero.

This ratio is an unweighted tungsten-nucleus abundance relative to free electrons; it is not a charge-weighted tungsten contribution to electron density and is not an effective-charge measure. It is the tungsten member of the same volume-averaged composition-ratio family as the [deuterium-tritium abundance ratio](name:ratio_of_volume_averaged_deuterium_tritium_density_to_volume_averaged_electron_density) and the [carbon abundance ratio](name:ratio_of_volume_averaged_carbon_density_to_volume_averaged_electron_density), which replace the tungsten numerator with the corresponding species volume average while retaining the same electron-density denominator.

NAMES.name: area_of_diagnostic_aperture
NAMES.short: Geometric area of the designated diagnostic aperture surface that admits or collects radiation or particles.
NAMES.long:
Diagnostic aperture area is the geometric extent of the designated limiting surface through which radiation or particles are admitted or collected. It may describe a clear aperture opening or a collecting face when that face defines the aperture.

The area is defined by the surface integral

$$
A = \int_S dS
$$

where $A$ is the diagnostic aperture area, $S$ is the designated aperture surface, and $dS$ is the differential area element on that surface.

This quantity applies to the specified aperture surface of the diagnostic and is not an automatically aggregated area for unrelated apertures. It is a geometric area, excluding surrounding housing, supports, and other structures unless they form the designated aperture surface; it is not an effective area weighted by transmission, sensitivity, or angular response.

The area is distinct from the [radius of a diagnostic aperture](name:radius_of_diagnostic_aperture) and the [width of a diagnostic aperture], which describe linear dimensions. For a circular aperture of radius $r$, where $r$ is the geometric distance from the aperture center to its boundary, the area satisfies $A = \pi r^2$, with $\pi$ denoting the circle constant.

NAMES.name: cold_neutral_fraction
NAMES.subject: neutral
NAMES.short: Dimensionless fraction of the cold recycled component of a hydrogen-isotope neutral population relative to the total neutral atom population.
NAMES.long:
The cold neutral fraction is a dimensionless ratio bounded in $[0, 1]$ expressing the relative abundance of the cold, low-energy recycled component of a hydrogen-isotope neutral population. It is a component of the broader [neutral fraction](name:ratio_of_neutral_state_density_to_total_hydrogenic_density), distinct from the hot charge-exchange-born component.

The fraction is defined as:

$$
f_{\mathrm{cold}} = \frac{n_{\mathrm{cold}}}{n_{\mathrm{cold}} + n_{\mathrm{hot}}}
$$

where $f_{\mathrm{cold}}$ is the cold neutral fraction, $n_{\mathrm{cold}}$ is the number density of cold recycled neutral atoms, and $n_{\mathrm{hot}}$ is the number density of hot charge-exchange-born neutral atoms.

The quantity applies to a specified hydrogen isotope and uses the two-component neutral-population model. Its denominator is the total neutral population formed by the cold and hot components for that isotope; it is not summed across different isotopes and does not represent the hot component itself.

Within this model, the cold and hot fractions are complementary and sum to unity. The [hot neutral fraction](name:hot_neutral_fraction) gives the corresponding charge-exchange-born component, with the energy threshold separating the two components defined by the applicable population model.

sources.leaf_definition: Fraction of cold neutrals for this isotope (n_cold_neutrals/(n_cold_neutrals+n_hot_neutrals))
sources.parent_definition: Set of isotopes

NAMES.name: etendue_of_hard_xray_detector
NAMES.short: Geometric optical throughput of a hard X-ray detector’s optical system, determined by its effective collecting area and accepted solid angle.
NAMES.long:
Étendue is the geometric throughput of the optical system associated with a hard X-ray detector. It characterizes the angular and spatial acceptance that determines how incident radiation is coupled into the detector.

The defining relation is

$$
G = A\Omega
$$

where $G$ is the detector étendue, $A$ is the effective collecting area, and $\Omega$ is the accepted solid angle.

This quantity applies to the detector-level optical system and uses effective area and angular acceptance for the associated detector; it does not specify whether those properties arise from one or multiple optical elements. It is distinct from the detector’s linear dimensions, such as its [height](name:height_of_hard_xray_detector) and width, which do not determine optical throughput alone.

Étendue provides the geometric factor relating incident [hard X-ray brightness](name:hard_xray_brightness) to radiation coupled into the detector and is the same physical optical-throughput concept represented by [etendue_of_spectrometer](name:etendue_of_spectrometer), with the owning optical system changed from a spectrometer to a hard X-ray detector.

sources.leaf_definition: Etendue (geometric extent) of the channel's optical system
sources.parent_definition: Set of channels (detector or pixel of a camera)

NAMES.name: etendue_of_spectrometer_channel
NAMES.short: Optical phase-space acceptance of a radiation-collection system, determined by effective collecting area and accepted ray directions and optionally weighted by spectral response.
NAMES.long:
Optical étendue is the geometric phase-space acceptance of a radiation-collection system. It describes how the collecting area and range of accepted ray directions jointly determine the system's throughput for radiation from an observed source.

For an effective area and accepted solid angle, the étendue $G$ is defined by:

$$
G = A_{\mathrm{eff}}\Omega_{\mathrm{eff}}
$$

where $G$ is the optical étendue, $A_{\mathrm{eff}}$ is the effective collecting area, and $\Omega_{\mathrm{eff}}$ is the accepted solid angle.

The quantity applies to radiation entering an optical collection system from a plasma or other observed source and aggregates acceptance over the collecting area and accepted ray directions. It is non-negative and does not itself represent radiance, collected power, detector signal, or spectral intensity. The [spectral étendue of a spectrometer channel](name:spectral_etendue_of_spectrometer_channel) is a narrower response-weighted form in which the optical acceptance is weighted by the channel's wavelength response, while [étendue of a spectrometer](name:etendue_of_spectrometer) represents the corresponding unweighted spectrometer-level acceptance.

sources.leaf_definition: Etendue (geometric extent) of the channel's optical system
sources.parent_definition: Set of channels (detector or pixel of a camera)

NAMES.name: hard_xray_brightness
NAMES.subject: hard_xray
NAMES.short: Band-integrated hard X-ray photon radiance received by a channel, normalized by projected collecting area and accepted solid angle.
NAMES.long:
Hard X-ray brightness is the photon radiance received from a viewing direction by a channel. It represents photon arrival rate with the photon-energy dependence integrated over the selected hard X-ray band.

The band-integrated photon radiance is defined by

$$
B_{\mathrm{HX}} = \frac{dN_\gamma}{dt\,dA_{\mathrm{proj}}\,d\Omega}
$$

where $B_{\mathrm{HX}}$ is the hard X-ray brightness, $N_\gamma$ is the number of received photons in the selected energy band, $t$ is time, $A_{\mathrm{proj}}$ is projected collecting area, and $\Omega$ is accepted solid angle.

This quantity applies to hard X-ray photons received by a channel and is evaluated separately for each selected energy band. Its aggregation convention is integration over photon energy within that band while retaining normalization by projected area and solid angle. It is a received radiometric quantity, not a local volumetric source term, and it counts photons rather than their deposited or carried energy.

The local production counterpart is [hard X-ray emissivity](name:hard_xray_emissivity), which describes photon generation per unit volume and solid angle before propagation to the channel. Integrating this brightness over the collecting geometry represented by the [etendue of a hard X-ray detector](name:etendue_of_hard_xray_detector) gives the received photon rate under the corresponding angular and area acceptance. Unlike [incident soft X-ray radiance](name:incident_soft_xray_radiance), which is energy-weighted, this quantity is photon-count radiance; photon registration probability is a separate detector property described by [spectral efficiency of a hard X-ray detector](name:spectral_efficiency_of_hard_xray_detector).

sources.leaf_definition: Photons received by the detector per unit time, per unit solid angle and per unit area (i.e. photon flux divided by the etendue), in multiple energy bands if available from the detector
sources.parent_definition: Set of channels (detector or pixel of a camera)

NAMES.name: hard_xray_emissivity
NAMES.subject: hard_xray
NAMES.short: Local production rate of hard-X-ray bremsstrahlung photons per plasma volume and emission solid angle, integrated over a specified photon-energy band.
NAMES.long:
Hard-X-ray emissivity is the local bremsstrahlung photon production rate per plasma volume and emission solid angle, integrated over the selected hard-X-ray photon-energy band. It represents emission from suprathermal electrons at a physical location and in a specified emission direction.

The band-integrated emissivity is defined by

$$
\varepsilon_{\mathrm{HXR}}(\mathbf{r},\Omega;E_1,E_2)=\int_{E_1}^{E_2}\varepsilon_{\mathrm{HXR}}^{(E)}(\mathbf{r},\Omega,E)\,\mathrm{d}E
$$

where $\varepsilon_{\mathrm{HXR}}$ is the band-integrated hard-X-ray photon emissivity, $\varepsilon_{\mathrm{HXR}}^{(E)}$ is the differential photon emissivity with respect to photon energy, $\mathbf{r}$ is the emission location, $\Omega$ is the emission direction labeled by solid angle, $E$ is photon energy, and $E_1$ and $E_2$ are the lower and upper limits of the selected energy band.

This quantity is local and directional: it is not integrated along a line of sight, over a plasma volume, or over emission directions. It applies to hard-X-ray photons produced by suprathermal-electron bremsstrahlung and excludes the total bremsstrahlung electromagnetic power and detector-received radiation.

In an optically thin plasma, [hard X-ray brightness](name:hard_xray_brightness) is obtained from the corresponding local emissivity by propagation and integration along a viewing path; brightness is therefore a received radiance, whereas this quantity is the local photon source density.

sources.parent_definition: Emissivity profile per energy band (assumed common to all channels used in the profile reconstruction)

NAMES.name: hot_neutral_fraction
NAMES.subject: neutral
NAMES.short: Dimensionless fraction of the hot charge-exchange-born component of a hydrogen-isotope neutral population relative to the total neutral atom population.
NAMES.long:
The hot neutral fraction is a dimensionless ratio bounded in $[0, 1]$ expressing the relative abundance of the hot, charge-exchange-born component of a hydrogen-isotope neutral population. It is a component of the broader [neutral fraction](name:ratio_of_neutral_state_density_to_total_hydrogenic_density), distinct from the cold recycled component.

The fraction is defined as:

$$
f_{\mathrm{hot}} = \frac{n_{\mathrm{hot}}}{n_{\mathrm{cold}} + n_{\mathrm{hot}}}
$$

where $f_{\mathrm{hot}}$ is the hot neutral fraction, $n_{\mathrm{hot}}$ is the number density of hot charge-exchange-born neutral atoms, and $n_{\mathrm{cold}}$ is the number density of cold recycled neutral atoms.

The quantity applies to a specified hydrogen isotope and uses the two-component neutral-population model. Its denominator is the total neutral population formed by the cold and hot components for that isotope; it is not summed across different isotopes and does not represent the cold component itself.

Within this model, the hot and cold fractions are complementary and sum to unity. The [cold neutral fraction](name:cold_neutral_fraction) gives the corresponding recycled component, with the energy threshold separating the two components defined by the applicable population model.

sources.leaf_definition: Fraction of hot neutrals for this isotope (n_hot_neutrals/(n_cold_neutrals+n_hot_neutrals))
sources.parent_definition: Set of isotopes

NAMES.name: incident_soft_xray_radiance
NAMES.short: Incident soft X-ray power radiance gives received electromagnetic power per projected detector area and solid angle, integrated over the selected energy band.
NAMES.long:
Incident soft-X-ray power radiance is the energy-integrated radiant power arriving at a receiving surface from the viewing direction, expressed per projected area and per solid angle.

$$
L_{\rm inc} = \int_{\mathcal{E}} L_E^{\rm inc}\,dE = \frac{dP_{\rm inc}}{dA_\perp\,d\Omega}
$$

where $L_{\rm inc}$ is the incident power radiance, $L_E^{\rm inc}$ is the incident spectral power radiance at photon energy $E$, $\mathcal{E}$ is the selected photon-energy band or collection of bands, $P_{\rm inc}$ is incident radiant power, $A_\perp$ is projected receiving area, and $\Omega$ is accepted solid angle.

The quantity applies to soft X-ray radiation incident on a detector channel, with spectral dependence integrated over the selected energy band or bands. It is an incoming radiometric quantity per area and solid angle, not a total power integrated over the detector aperture or viewing directions, and it is distinct from detector-registration efficiency.

Integrating this radiance over the relevant projected area and solid angle gives the band-integrated received power represented by [power of soft X-ray detector](name:power_of_soft_xray_detector). Unlike [hard X-ray brightness](name:hard_xray_brightness), which is photon-number radiance, this quantity is power radiance; [spectral efficiency of soft X-ray detector](name:spectral_efficiency_of_soft_xray_detector) instead describes the probability that incident photons are registered.

sources.leaf_definition: Power flux received by the detector, per unit solid angle and per unit area (i.e. power divided by the etendue), in multiple energy bands if available from the detector
sources.parent_definition: Set of channels (detector or pixel of a camera)

NAMES.name: intensity_at_spectral_line
NAMES.short: Uncalibrated photoelectron detection rate obtained by integrating the measured emission signal across an identified spectral line.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the uncalibrated photoelectron count rate associated with one identified emission line. It represents the detector signal integrated across the wavelength interval assigned to that line, rather than an absolutely calibrated photon radiance.

The line-integrated count rate is defined by

$$
I_{\rm line} = \int_{\lambda_1}^{\lambda_2} i(\lambda)\,d\lambda
$$

where $I_{\rm line}$ is the integrated photoelectron count rate, $i(\lambda)$ is the spectral photoelectron count-rate density, $\lambda$ is wavelength, and $\lambda_1$ and $\lambda_2$ delimit the interval assigned to the identified emission line.

The quantity applies to a single identified spectral line and uses line integration as its aggregation convention. It is non-calibrated and is not background-subtracted; no aggregation over multiple spectral lines or conversion to absolute photon radiance is included.

It is the uncalibrated line-integrated counterpart of [photon-count radiance at a spectral line](name:photon_radiance_at_spectral_line), which additionally represents an absolutely calibrated radiance and includes background subtraction. Unlike [spectral flux of a spectrometer channel](name:spectral_flux_of_spectrometer_channel), this quantity is resolved at one identified line rather than describing the channel-level spectral signal.

sources.leaf_definition: Non-calibrated intensity (integrated over the spectrum for this line)
sources.parent_definition: Set of processed spectral lines

NAMES.name: lower_bound_photon_energy
NAMES.short: Lower boundary of an X-ray photon-energy band, specifying the minimum photon energy included in the defined detection or emission band.
NAMES.long:
Lower boundary of an X-ray photon-energy band is the minimum photon energy included in the specified detection or emission band. It defines the low-energy cutoff of that band.

The photon-energy band defined by this lower boundary and its complementary upper boundary satisfies:

$$
E_\mathrm{low} \le E \le E_\mathrm{up}
$$

where $E_\mathrm{low}$ is the lower-bound photon energy, $E$ is the photon energy being classified, and $E_\mathrm{up}$ is the [upper photon energy](name:upper_photon_energy).

The scope is an X-ray spectral band for photon detection, photon counting, or energy-resolved emissivity. This quantity is a band boundary, not an observed photon energy, photon-energy width, photon flux, count rate, emissivity, or detector-response amplitude; it is a single boundary for one specified band and implies no averaging or summation over photons.

Together with the [upper photon energy](name:upper_photon_energy), it specifies the spectral interval of the band. The lower boundary must not exceed the upper boundary, and any derived band width is their difference.

NAMES.name: photon_radiance_at_spectral_line
NAMES.short: Photon-count radiance from an identified emission transition, integrated over its spectral line interval and resolved by projected area and viewing solid angle.
NAMES.long:
Photon-count line radiance is the photon emission rate from one identified transition accumulated along the emitting line of sight, resolved by projected collecting area and viewing solid angle.

The defining photon-count radiance is

$$
L_{\gamma,\ell} = \frac{d^3 N_{\gamma,\ell}}{dt\,dA_{\perp}\,d\Omega}
$$

where $L_{\gamma,\ell}$ is the line radiance, $N_{\gamma,\ell}$ is the number of photons from transition $\ell$, $\ell$ identifies the emission transition, $t$ is time, $A_{\perp}$ is collecting area projected normal to the viewing direction, and $\Omega$ is viewing solid angle.

The quantity applies to one identified emission transition without imposing a particular emitting species, charge state, or line-splitting mechanism. Photon counts are integrated across the selected spectral-line interval and accumulated along the viewing path; the result is not resolved per wavelength.

Integrating [photon-number spectral radiance](name:spectral_radiance) over wavelength across the selected line interval gives this line radiance under matching projected-area and solid-angle conventions. The qualified [motional-Stark photon radiance at a spectral line](name:motional_stark_photon_radiance_at_spectral_line) is a specialized instance restricted to an identified motional-Stark-split component. Unlike energy radiance, this quantity counts photons without weighting them by photon energy; conversion to energy radiance requires applying that energy weighting before integration.

NAMES.name: power_of_soft_xray_detector
NAMES.short: Band-integrated radiant power received by a soft X-ray detector channel over its selected photon-energy band or bands.
NAMES.long:
Soft X-ray detector power is the radiant power carried by incident soft X-ray photons and received by one detector channel after spectral selection. It represents radiation power rather than the detector’s electrical output.

For a selected photon-energy band, the received power is defined by:

$$
P_{\mathcal{B}} = \int_{\mathcal{B}} E\,\Phi_E(E)\,dE
$$

where $P_{\mathcal{B}}$ is the received power for band $\mathcal{B}$, $E$ is photon energy, $\Phi_E(E)$ is the photon arrival-rate density as a function of photon energy, $\mathcal{B}$ is the selected energy interval, and $dE$ is an infinitesimal photon-energy interval.

The quantity applies to soft X-ray radiation received by a particular detector channel and is integrated over photon energy within its selected bandpass. It is not summed over detector channels, viewing directions, or distinct energy bands; when multiple bands are resolved, each band has its own band-integrated received-power value. It excludes plasma-emitted power before arrival at the detector and electrical power generated by detector electronics.

The quantity is distinct from [spectral_efficiency_of_soft_xray_detector](name:spectral_efficiency_of_soft_xray_detector), which describes the probability of registering an incident photon rather than the received radiant power. It is also distinct from [hard_xray_brightness](name:hard_xray_brightness), which describes photon radiance rather than the power collected by a channel over its energy band and collection geometry.

NAMES.name: radiated_power_over_core_region
NAMES.short: Total electromagnetic power radiated by plasma inside the last closed flux surface, representing the core-region contribution to global radiative energy loss.
NAMES.long:
Radiated power over the core region is the total electromagnetic energy-loss rate carried away by radiation emitted within the plasma volume inside the last closed flux surface (LCFS). It is a regional integral rather than a local radiated-power density.

The defining volume integral is

$$
P_{\rm core} = \int_{V_{\rm core}} p_{\rm rad}(\mathbf{r})\,dV
$$

where $P_{\rm core}$ is the core-region radiated power, $p_{\rm rad}(\mathbf{r})$ is the local volumetric radiated-power density at position $\mathbf{r}$, $V_{\rm core}$ is the plasma volume inside the LCFS, and $dV$ is the differential volume element.

The quantity includes the aggregate electromagnetic radiation from all emission channels within the LCFS. It excludes radiation emitted in the scrape-off layer, divertor, and other plasma regions outside the LCFS; it is therefore distinct from [total plasma radiated power](name:total_plasma_radiated_power), which integrates radiation over the full plasma volume.

The integrand is the local [power density due to radiation](name:power_density_due_to_radiation), and integration over the core region gives its corresponding regional total.

NAMES.name: ratio_of_neutral_density_of_isotope_to_difference_of_total_neutral_density_and_neutral_density_of_isotope
NAMES.short: Odds ratio of the neutral density of a selected hydrogen isotope to the summed neutral density of all other hydrogen isotopes, distinguishing composition odds from total isotope fraction.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the neutral-population odds ratio for one selected hydrogen isotope relative to all other hydrogen isotopes. It characterizes isotope composition using neutral atoms only, with the comparison population aggregated across every other isotope.

$$
R_i = \frac{n_i}{\sum_{j \ne i} n_j}
$$

Here, $R_i$ is the isotope density ratio, $i$ identifies the selected hydrogen isotope, $n_i$ is its neutral number density, and $n_j$ is the neutral number density of another hydrogen isotope. The summation includes all hydrogen isotopes other than the selected isotope.

The denominator is a total over the other neutral isotope populations, while the numerator contains only the selected isotope. This quantity excludes ionized populations and differs from [total_hydrogenic_density](name:total_hydrogenic_density), which includes the hydrogenic population across its applicable charge states and isotopes. It is an odds ratio rather than the selected isotope's fraction of the total neutral population; if $f_i$ denotes that corresponding neutral isotope fraction, then $f_i = R_i/(1+R_i)$.

NAMES.name: spectral_bremsstrahlung_radiance
NAMES.short: Photon-number radiance of free-free plasma emission resolved per unit wavelength and viewing direction.
NAMES.long:
Bremsstrahlung spectral radiance is the directional photon-number radiance of the free-free continuum emitted when plasma electrons accelerate in Coulomb fields of charged particles. It represents the continuum contribution to radiation resolved spectrally rather than a discrete emission transition.

For wavelength-resolved photon radiance, the defining relation is:

$$
L^{\mathrm{ff}}_{\lambda} = \frac{dN_{\gamma}}{dA_{\perp}\,dt\,d\Omega\,d\lambda}
$$

where $L^{\mathrm{ff}}_{\lambda}$ is the bremsstrahlung spectral radiance, $N_{\gamma}$ is the photon count, $A_{\perp}$ is area projected normal to the viewing direction, $t$ is time, $\Omega$ is solid angle, and $\lambda$ is wavelength. The superscript $\mathrm{ff}$ denotes free-free bremsstrahlung.

This quantity applies to plasma bremsstrahlung accumulated along a viewing direction, with photon emission resolved by wavelength and solid angle. It is a continuum radiance and is not integrated over wavelength, summed over viewing directions, or restricted to a specified emitting species when no such restriction is stated.

It is the mechanism-specific component of the broader [spectral radiance](name:spectral_radiance), which includes plasma emission resolved by wavelength and viewing direction without restricting the emission mechanism. Unlike [photon radiance at a spectral line](name:photon_radiance_at_spectral_line), it describes continuum emission rather than radiation integrated over a discrete spectral transition.

NAMES.name: spectral_flux_of_spectrometer_channel
NAMES.short: Uncalibrated rate of detected photoelectrons representing spectrometer spectral intensity after electronic gain compensation and relative channel calibration, before absolute radiometric calibration.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the detected photoelectron event rate representing emission intensity from a spectrometer channel. It is a detector-response quantity rather than an absolute photon radiance.

The rate is defined by

$$
I = \frac{dN_{\rm pe}}{dt}
$$

where $I$ is the detected photoelectron rate, $N_{\rm pe}$ is the accumulated number of detected photoelectrons, and $t$ is elapsed time.

For wavelength-resolved emission, the quantity applies to a selected wavelength pixel. For an identified spectral line, it is integrated over the line profile. Electronic gain compensation and relative channel calibration are included, but absolute radiometric calibration is not; no background subtraction is implied where the underlying signal remains unprocessed.

This rate must not be interpreted as incident photon flux or calibrated radiance. The distinct [photon radiance at a spectral line](name:photon_radiance_at_spectral_line) represents the absolutely calibrated photon emission rate per projected collecting area and solid angle, whereas this quantity remains detector-response dependent.

NAMES.name: spectral_radiance
NAMES.short: Calibrated photon-number spectral radiance of plasma emission, resolved by wavelength and viewing direction per projected area, solid angle, and wavelength interval.
NAMES.long:
Spectral radiance is the calibrated photon-emission rate from plasma radiation resolved by wavelength and viewing direction. It represents the radiance density associated with an infinitesimal projected collecting area, solid angle, wavelength interval, and time interval.

The photon-number spectral radiance is defined by

$$
L_\lambda = \frac{\mathrm{d}^3 N_\gamma}{\mathrm{d}A_{\mathrm{proj}}\,\mathrm{d}t\,\mathrm{d}\Omega\,\mathrm{d}\lambda}
$$

where $L_\lambda$ is spectral radiance, $N_\gamma$ is the number of emitted photons, $A_{\mathrm{proj}}$ is projected collecting area normal to the viewing direction, $t$ is time, $\Omega$ is solid angle, and $\lambda$ is wavelength.

This quantity applies to plasma emission over the resolved wavelength and viewing-direction domains and is calibrated to an absolute photon-number radiance scale. It is a spectral density, not radiance integrated over a wavelength band or an identified emission line.

Integrating $L_\lambda$ over the wavelength interval of an identified transition gives the corresponding [photon radiance at a spectral line](name:photon_radiance_at_spectral_line). The quantity remains generic with respect to the emission mechanism, whereas [spectral bremsstrahlung radiance](name:spectral_bremsstrahlung_radiance) is restricted to free-free emission.

NAMES.name: spectral_signal_to_noise_ratio_of_spectrometer_channel
NAMES.short: Spectral signal-to-noise ratio of a spectrometer channel is the channel-level logarithmic comparison between integrated spectral power in a selected signal band and integrated spectral power in a selected line-free reference band. It characterizes spectral signal quality independent of the particular spectroscopic application motivating the band selection.
NAMES.long:
Spectral signal-to-noise ratio of a spectrometer channel is the channel-level logarithmic comparison between the integrated spectral power in a selected signal band containing spectral features of interest and the integrated spectral power in a selected line-free reference band. It characterizes the spectral signal quality of the channel as a whole, independent of the particular spectroscopic application motivating the band selection.

The quantity is a base-ten logarithmically scaled power ratio:

$$
\mathrm{SNR} = 10 \log_{10}\!\left( \frac{P_{\mathrm{sig}}}{P_{\mathrm{ref}}} \right)
$$

where $P_{\mathrm{sig}}$ is the spectral power integrated over the selected signal band and $P_{\mathrm{ref}}$ is the spectral power integrated over the selected line-free reference band of the same channel.

The quantity applies to a single spectrometer channel and to one selected pair of spectral bands. The signal and reference bands are a selection convention of the spectroscopic analysis and are not fixed by this name: any band pair chosen to compare feature-bearing spectral content against feature-free spectral content of the same channel yields an instance of this quantity. The value is positive when the signal-band integrated power exceeds the reference-band integrated power and negative when it is smaller.

It is a band-integrated power ratio expressed on a logarithmic scale. It is not an amplitude ratio, which would carry a factor of twenty rather than ten before the base-ten logarithm; it is not a pointwise spectral-intensity ratio at a single wavelength; and it is not a noise variance, noise standard deviation, or detector time-domain signal-to-noise ratio.

The [logarithm of spectral signal-to-noise ratio of a spectrometer channel](name:logarithm_of_spectral_signal_to_noise_ratio_of_spectrometer_channel) is the member of this family whose name makes the base-ten logarithmic transform explicit; it shares the defining relation above and is attested for band pairs selected for isotope-ratio analysis, where the signal band contains the isotope lines of interest. This parent subsumes that member together with any analogous logarithmically scaled band-pair comparison arising in other spectroscopic applications of the channel.

NAMES.name: spectral_wavelength_of_optical_element
NAMES.short: Photon vacuum wavelength values defining the spectral coordinate for a soft X-ray filter window’s wavelength-dependent optical response.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the vacuum wavelength of photons at which the optical response of a soft X-ray filter window is specified. It identifies the spectral position of each response value.

The wavelength–frequency relation is

$$
\lambda = \frac{c}{\nu}
$$

where $\lambda$ is the photon vacuum wavelength, $c$ is the speed of light in vacuum, and $\nu$ is the photon frequency.

The quantity applies to the spectral response of the filter window and uses one wavelength coordinate at a time; it is not a band-integrated response or a nominal filter-center value. It is distinct from the geometric [thickness of the filter](name:thickness_of_filter) and from the nominal [wavelength of the filter](name:wavelength_of_filter).

Wavelength-dependent response quantities, including [spectral absorptivity of the filter](name:spectral_absorptivity_of_filter) and [spectral efficiency of the filter](name:spectral_efficiency_of_filter), are functions evaluated at this wavelength coordinate.

NAMES.name: temperature_of_soft_xray_detector
NAMES.short: Thermodynamic temperature of the soft X-ray detector assembly, describing its physical thermal state for calibration and monitoring rather than a plasma temperature inferred from radiation.
NAMES.long:
The quantity is the thermodynamic temperature of the physical soft X-ray detector assembly and describes the thermal state of its hardware.

It applies to the detector object as a whole, with no implied plasma population, spatial subcomponent, or charge-state aggregation. It is distinct from the plasma electron temperature inferred from detected soft X-ray radiation and does not represent a photon-energy or spectral-response quantity.

The temperature is the thermal operating state relevant to calibration and hardware-condition monitoring. It is conceptually analogous to [temperature of neutron detector](name:temperature_of_neutron_detector), while [spectral efficiency of soft X-ray detector](name:spectral_efficiency_of_soft_xray_detector) describes photon-registration probability rather than detector hardware temperature.

NAMES.name: thickness_of_filter
NAMES.short: Geometric thickness of one diagnostic filter window, determining the amount of material available for photon attenuation and spectral selection.
NAMES.long:
Filter thickness is the geometric separation of the two opposing surfaces of one filter window, measured locally along the material normal. It represents the material thickness itself rather than a photon path length through the window.

For corresponding points on the opposing surfaces, the local thickness is defined by

$$
d = \left| (\mathbf{r}_2 - \mathbf{r}_1) \cdot \hat{\mathbf{n}} \right|
$$

where $d$ is the filter thickness, $\mathbf{r}_1$ and $\mathbf{r}_2$ are the position vectors of the corresponding surface points, and $\hat{\mathbf{n}}$ is the local unit normal to the filter surface.

This quantity applies to the material of a single filter window used for X-ray spectral selection, including soft-X-ray, hard-X-ray, and crystal-spectrometer filter windows. It is not a sum over multiple windows, diagnostic channels, or detector elements, and it is distinct from the longer oblique photon path through the material.

For homogeneous material at normal incidence, thickness enters the attenuation relation $T(E) = \exp[-\mu(E)d]$, where $T(E)$ is photon transmission at energy $E$, $E$ is photon energy, and $\mu(E)$ is the material attenuation coefficient. Thus, thickness is a geometric input to [spectral absorptivity of the filter](name:spectral_absorptivity_of_filter), whereas [filter width] describes the wavelength span of the transmitted passband rather than the material dimension.
