NAMES.name: toroidal_coordinate_at_detector_pixel
NAMES.short: Azimuthal angle locating the geometric center of a detector pixel in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame, where R is major radius, φ is toroidal angle, and Z is vertical height.
NAMES.long:
Azimuthal angle locating the geometric center of a detector pixel is the value of the toroidal angle $\phi$ assigned to the pixel center in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. In this frame $R$ is major radius from the machine symmetry axis, $\phi$ is toroidal angle about that axis, and $Z$ is vertical height; $\hat{Z}$ denotes the unit direction of increasing $Z$.

The scope is the detector-pixel geometric center only. It does not describe the angular extent of the pixel, a pixel boundary, an aperture, a line of sight, or any average over the pixel sensitive area; there is no aggregation over multiple pixels.

Together with the [radial coordinate at detector pixel](name:radial_coordinate_of_detector_pixel) and [vertical coordinate at detector pixel](name:vertical_coordinate_of_detector_pixel), it identifies the position of the same pixel center in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. It is distinct from the [toroidal coordinate of aperture](name:toroidal_coordinate_of_aperture), which locates an aperture rather than a detector pixel.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the angular displacement from the $\phi=0$ reference is in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ (counter-clockwise when viewed from above $+\hat{Z}$).

sources.leaf_definition: Toroidal angle (oriented counter-clockwise when viewing from above)
sources.parent_definition: Position of the centre of each pixel. First dimension : line index (x1 axis). Second dimension: column index (x2 axis).

NAMES.name: toroidal_coordinate_of_camera
NAMES.short: Toroidal coordinate of a camera's geometric center in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame, where φ is the toroidal angle about the machine symmetry axis.
NAMES.long:
Toroidal coordinate of a camera is the angular coordinate $\phi_c$ of the camera's geometric center in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. It specifies the position of that center around the machine symmetry axis.

The camera center has cylindrical coordinates $(R_c, \phi_c, Z_c)$:

$$
\mathbf{r}_c \leftrightarrow (R_c, \phi_c, Z_c)
$$

where $\mathbf{r}_c$ is the position vector of the camera's geometric center, $R_c$ is the [radial coordinate of the camera](name:radial_coordinate_of_camera), and $Z_c$ is the [vertical coordinate of the camera](name:vertical_coordinate_of_camera).

This quantity locates the camera center only; it is not an orientation angle, viewing direction, or field-of-view angle of the camera.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the camera center is displaced in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$, counter-clockwise when viewed from above $+\hat{Z}$.

NAMES.name: toroidal_coordinate_of_line_of_sight
NAMES.short: Toroidal angular coordinate of the first reference point on a diagnostic line of sight, locating that point around the machine symmetry axis.
NAMES.long:
The toroidal coordinate of a line of sight is the azimuthal angle of its first reference point about the machine symmetry axis. It specifies the point's circumferential location in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

For a point expressed in the right-handed Cartesian $(\hat{x}, \hat{y}, \hat{z})$ basis, the toroidal angle is defined by

$$
\phi = \operatorname{atan2}(y,x)
$$

where $x$ and $y$ are the horizontal Cartesian coordinates of the first reference point, and $\phi=0$ is the facility-defined toroidal reference direction.

This quantity applies specifically to the first reference point of a diagnostic line of sight. It is a point coordinate, not an angle describing the line-of-sight direction, and it is not an aggregate over the line or over multiple reference points. Unlike [toroidal_coordinate_of_optical_element](name:toroidal_coordinate_of_optical_element), which locates an optical-element center, it locates the designated first line-of-sight point.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the angular displacement from the $\phi=0$ reference direction is counter-clockwise when viewed from above the $+\hat{Z}$ axis.

NAMES.name: total_plasma_radiated_power
NAMES.short: Total plasma radiated power is the electromagnetic power emitted by the full plasma, summed over all photon-emission mechanisms and integrated over the plasma volume.
NAMES.long:
Total plasma radiated power is the total rate at which electromagnetic radiation carries energy away from the plasma. It is the full-plasma radiation loss quantity formed from all photon-emission mechanisms, including line radiation, bremsstrahlung, recombination, synchrotron, and any other radiative emission present.

The defining relation is the volume integral of the local radiation power density over the plasma volume:

$$
P_{\mathrm{rad}} = \int_{V_{\mathrm{plasma}}} p_{\mathrm{rad}}(\mathbf{r})\, dV
$$

where $P_{\mathrm{rad}}$ is total plasma radiated power, $V_{\mathrm{plasma}}$ is the full plasma volume, $p_{\mathrm{rad}}(\mathbf{r})$ is the [power density due to radiation](name:power_density_due_to_radiation) at position $\mathbf{r}$, and $dV$ is the volume element.

The scope is the plasma as a whole; the aggregation convention is integration over the full plasma volume together with summation over all electromagnetic emission mechanisms and spectral contributions. It is not a region-restricted quantity such as [radiated power over core region](name:radiated_power_over_core_region), and it is not a diagnostic-channel signal or line-of-sight quantity.

[Bremsstrahlung power](name:bremsstrahlung_power) is one radiative contribution when defined for the same plasma population, whereas total plasma radiated power includes all radiative contributions. [Total neutron power] is distinct because it is kinetic energy carried by neutrons rather than electromagnetic radiation. In an energy balance, total plasma radiated power is a non-negative emitted power that enters as a loss according to the balance convention; it is not itself a signed source term.

NAMES.name: upper_photon_energy
NAMES.short: High-energy boundary of an X-ray photon-acceptance band, defining the maximum photon energy included in a selected spectral window.
NAMES.long:
Upper photon energy is the high-energy edge of an X-ray spectral band used to select photons or define an energy-resolved emissivity interval. It identifies a band boundary, not a representative photon energy for the band.

For a band bounded by lower and upper photon energies, the accepted interval is defined by

$$
E_{\rm lower} \leq E_\gamma \leq E_{\rm upper}
$$

where $E_\gamma$ is the photon energy, $E_{\rm lower}$ is the lower photon-energy boundary, and $E_{\rm upper}$ is this quantity.

The quantity applies to one selected X-ray spectral band used for channel counting or for an emissivity quantity. It is one upper boundary for that band; no summation or averaging over channels, bands, or photon energies is implied.

Together with the corresponding lower boundary, it fixes the spectral window. It is distinct from [energy of detector pixel](name:energy_of_detector_pixel), which denotes a central or representative energy, while [upper bound energy of detector pixel](name:upper_bound_energy_of_detector_pixel) applies the same upper-edge concept specifically to an individual detector pixel.

NAMES.name: vertical_coordinate_of_camera
NAMES.short: Signed vertical position of a camera’s geometric center along Z in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the signed vertical coordinate of a camera’s geometric center in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame. It specifies the camera’s position rather than its viewing direction or detector orientation.

The coordinate is the projection of the camera-center position vector onto the vertical basis direction:

$$
Z_{\mathrm{cam}} = \mathbf{r}_{\mathrm{cam}} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{Z}}
$$

where $Z_{\mathrm{cam}}$ is the camera-center vertical coordinate, $\mathbf{r}_{\mathrm{cam}}$ is the position vector of the camera’s geometric center, and $\hat{\mathbf{Z}}$ is the vertical unit vector. The frame is right-handed with basis $(\hat{R},\hat{\phi},\hat{Z})$, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

The scope is restricted to the geometric center of the camera as a whole and represents one positional coordinate, with no averaging over pixels, channels, viewing rays, or detector surfaces. It is distinct from [vertical coordinate of an aperture](name:vertical_coordinate_of_aperture), which refers to a different diagnostic object.

Together with the [radial coordinate of the camera](name:radial_coordinate_of_camera), this quantity gives the camera center’s radial and vertical positional components in the cylindrical frame; it does not describe camera orientation or angular imaging coverage.

NAMES.name: vertical_coordinate_of_detector_pixel
NAMES.short: Vertical coordinate locating the geometric center of an individual detector pixel in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the vertical position of the geometric center of one detector pixel. It locates that center along the cylindrical $Z$ direction rather than describing a pixel dimension, boundary, or radiation signal.

The coordinate is defined in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. It applies separately to each detector pixel and is neither summed nor averaged over pixels, channels, detectors, or cameras.

The quantity describes the center point of the pixel and excludes pixel span, edge coordinates, detector response, and any detector-local coordinate components. Together with the [radial coordinate of a detector pixel](name:radial_coordinate_of_detector_pixel), it locates the same pixel center in the cylindrical $R$-$Z$ plane. Its generic detector-pixel scope distinguishes it from the corresponding coordinate defined for a specifically identified [soft X-ray detector](name:vertical_coordinate_of_soft_xray_detector).

NAMES.name: cold_neutral_temperature
NAMES.subject: neutral
NAMES.short: Translational kinetic temperature, expressed as energy per particle, of the cold neutral population, based on random translational motion after removal of its bulk flow.
NAMES.long:
Translational kinetic temperature, expressed as energy per particle, of the cold neutral population, based on random translational motion after removal of its bulk flow. It characterizes the low-energy neutral component associated with a selected hydrogen isotope.

For the cold neutral population, the translational temperature is defined by

$$
T_c = \frac{2}{3 n_c}\int \frac{1}{2}m_c \lvert\mathbf{v}-\mathbf{u}_c\rvert^2 f_c(\mathbf{v})\,d^3v
$$

Here $T_c$ is the cold-neutral translational temperature, $n_c$ is the cold-neutral number density, $m_c$ is the mass of a cold neutral atom, $\mathbf{v}$ is particle velocity, $\mathbf{u}_c$ is the bulk velocity of the cold neutral population, $f_c(\mathbf{v})$ is its velocity distribution, and $d^3v$ is differential volume in velocity space. The distribution is normalized by $n_c=\int f_c(\mathbf{v})\,d^3v$.

The quantity applies to the low-energy neutral-atom population in the plasma edge or scrape-off layer and is specific to the selected hydrogen isotope. It is averaged over particles in that cold population, not summed with the energetic neutral population or with other isotopes. It excludes bulk flow energy and does not represent a temperature associated with an internal quantum or excitation state.

This quantity is the cold-population specialization of [neutral temperature](name:neutral_temperature), while [hot neutral temperature](name:hot_neutral_temperature) applies the same translational definition to the energetic neutral population. Unlike [volume-averaged neutral temperature](name:volume_averaged_neutral_temperature), it is not defined by averaging the temperature over a plasma volume.

NAMES.name: normalized_toroidal_flux_coordinate_of_line_of_sight
NAMES.short: Signed normalized toroidal-flux label at the line-of-sight point closest to the magnetic axis, positive above and negative below the axis.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the normalized toroidal flux label assigned to the point on a line of sight that approaches the magnetic axis most closely. Its sign records whether that closest point lies above or below the magnetic axis.

The signed closest-approach value is defined by

$$
\rho_{\mathrm{LOS}} = \operatorname{sgn}(Z_* - Z_{\mathrm{axis}})\,\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}(\mathbf{x}_*),
\qquad
\mathbf{x}_* = \underset{\mathbf{x}\in\mathrm{LOS}}{\operatorname{arg\,min}}\,\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}(\mathbf{x})
$$

where $\rho_{\mathrm{LOS}}$ is this signed line-of-sight value, $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}$ is the [normalized toroidal flux coordinate](name:normalized_toroidal_flux_coordinate), $\mathbf{x}$ is a point on the line of sight, $\mathbf{x}_*$ is the closest-approach point, and $\mathrm{LOS}$ denotes the line of sight. The function $\operatorname{sgn}$ supplies the sign of its argument; $Z_*$ is the vertical coordinate of the closest-approach point and $Z_{\mathrm{axis}}$ is the vertical coordinate of the magnetic axis. Here $R$, $\phi$, and $Z$ are the major-radius, toroidal-angle, and vertical coordinates in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

The quantity applies to one line of sight and uses only the selected closest-approach point; it is not a line average, line integral, flux-surface average, or volume aggregate. Unlike [normalized toroidal flux coordinate of measurement position](name:normalized_toroidal_flux_coordinate_of_measurement_position), it does not describe the coordinate at an arbitrary single measurement point.

It is obtained from the parent [normalized toroidal flux coordinate](name:normalized_toroidal_flux_coordinate) by evaluating that magnetic-surface label at the closest-approach point and appending the above/below-axis sign. The underlying unsigned label increases outward from the magnetic axis toward the equilibrium boundary.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the closest point on the line of sight lies above the magnetic axis, meaning $Z_* > Z_{\mathrm{axis}}$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: radial_coordinate_of_camera
NAMES.short: Major-radius location of a camera’s geometric center, measured from the toroidal symmetry axis in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The radial coordinate of a camera is the major-radius position of its geometric center, measured perpendicular to the toroidal symmetry axis. It identifies the camera center rather than any individual detector pixel, aperture, or line-of-sight point.

The coordinate is defined from the Cartesian coordinates of the camera center:

$$
R_{\mathrm{cam}} = \sqrt{x_{\mathrm{cam}}^2 + y_{\mathrm{cam}}^2}
$$

where $R_{\mathrm{cam}}$ is the camera-center radial coordinate, and $x_{\mathrm{cam}}$ and $y_{\mathrm{cam}}$ are the camera-center coordinates in the right-handed Cartesian $(\hat{x},\hat{y},\hat{z})$ basis. The corresponding cylindrical frame is the right-handed $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

This quantity applies to the geometric center of the camera as a whole and is not an average over pixels, viewing directions, or detector elements. It is the camera-specific specialization of the parent [radial coordinate](name:radial_coordinate). Together with the [vertical coordinate of the camera](name:vertical_coordinate_of_camera) and [toroidal coordinate of the camera](name:toroidal_coordinate_of_camera), it specifies the camera-center position.

NAMES.name: radial_coordinate_of_detector_pixel
NAMES.short: Major-radius coordinate of a detector pixel’s geometric center, locating the pixel relative to the machine symmetry axis in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the major-radius coordinate of the geometric center of an individual detector pixel. It identifies the pixel center’s perpendicular distance from the toroidal symmetry axis in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

Using the corresponding right-handed Cartesian basis $(x, y, z)$, with the symmetry axis at $x=y=0$, the coordinate is defined by

$$
R_{\mathrm{pix}} = \sqrt{x_{\mathrm{pix}}^2+y_{\mathrm{pix}}^2}
$$

where $R_{\mathrm{pix}}$ is the pixel-center major-radius coordinate, and $x_{\mathrm{pix}}$ and $y_{\mathrm{pix}}$ are the Cartesian coordinates of that center perpendicular to the symmetry axis.

The quantity applies to each detector-pixel center individually; it is not an average over pixels, a radiation-weighted position, or the radial coordinate of the camera as a whole. It is the detector-pixel specialization of the [radial coordinate](name:radial_coordinate), while the corresponding vertical location is given by the [vertical coordinate of detector pixel](name:vertical_coordinate_of_detector_pixel).

NAMES.name: radial_coordinate_of_diagnostic_aperture
NAMES.short: Major-radius coordinate of the geometric center of a diagnostic aperture, locating it from the toroidal symmetry axis in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The quantity is the major-radius coordinate of the geometric center of a diagnostic aperture, locating that center relative to the toroidal symmetry axis.

In the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, its defining relation is:

$$
R_{\rm ap} = \sqrt{x_{\rm ap}^{\,2}+y_{\rm ap}^{\,2}}
$$

where $R_{\rm ap}$ is the aperture-center major radius, and $x_{\rm ap}$ and $y_{\rm ap}$ are the horizontal Cartesian coordinates of that center in the right-handed Cartesian $(x,y,z)$ frame, with $z$ aligned with the vertical coordinate $Z$.

This quantity applies specifically to the geometric center of the diagnostic aperture. For a circular aperture, the center is the circle center; for a planar aperture, it is the origin of the local aperture coordinates within the aperture area. It is not an area average, radial extent, or coordinate of the radiation path.

This is the aperture-specific realization of the [radial coordinate](name:radial_coordinate). Together with the [vertical coordinate of the diagnostic aperture](name:vertical_coordinate_of_diagnostic_aperture), it locates the aperture center in the poloidal plane of the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame; the toroidal coordinate is not represented by this quantity.

NAMES.name: radial_coordinate_of_filter_window
NAMES.short: Major-radius coordinate of a filter window’s geometric center in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The radial coordinate of a filter window is the major-radius coordinate $R$ locating the geometric center of the filter-window surface relative to the toroidal symmetry axis.

For Cartesian coordinates of the geometric center, the major radius is defined by

$$
R = \sqrt{x^2+y^2}
$$

where $R$ is the major-radius coordinate, and $x$ and $y$ are the Cartesian coordinates in the right-handed Cartesian basis $(\hat{x},\hat{y},\hat{z})$. In the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, $\phi$ is the toroidal angle and $Z$ is the vertical coordinate.

This quantity applies to each filter-window center individually and is not an average, integral, or radial size of the window. It identifies the center position of the filter window, including circular or rectangular window geometries, and excludes the [radius of the filter window](name:radius_of_filter_window), which describes the window’s spatial extent.

This is the filter-window-specific realization of the general [radial coordinate](name:radial_coordinate). The complete center position is described jointly with the [toroidal coordinate of the filter window](name:toroidal_coordinate_of_filter_window) and the [vertical coordinate of the filter window](name:vertical_coordinate_of_filter_window).

NAMES.name: radial_coordinate_of_line_of_sight
NAMES.short: Major-radius coordinate of a specified geometric point associated with a line of sight, measured from the toroidal symmetry axis in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the major-radius coordinate of a specified geometric point associated with a line of sight. It locates that point by its perpendicular distance from the toroidal symmetry axis in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

$$
R_{\mathrm{los}} = \sqrt{x_{\mathrm{los}}^2+y_{\mathrm{los}}^2}
$$

where $R_{\mathrm{los}}$ is the radial coordinate of the specified line-of-sight point, and $x_{\mathrm{los}}$ and $y_{\mathrm{los}}$ are the horizontal Cartesian coordinate values of that point in the right-handed Cartesian $(\hat{x},\hat{y},\hat{z})$ basis, whose origin lies on the toroidal symmetry axis.

The quantity is geometric and pointwise: it applies to a designated point associated with a line of sight and has no plasma-population or regional aggregation. A line of sight can contain multiple such points, so this name alone does not select a first point, second point, third point, endpoint, line-integrated radius, or averaged radius.

It is a locus-specific instance of the general [radial coordinate](name:radial_coordinate) quantity, with the line of sight identifying the associated geometric locus rather than defining a new radial-coordinate concept.

NAMES.name: radial_coordinate_of_spectrometer_channel
NAMES.short: Major-radius coordinate of an interpolated geometry point associated with a spectrometer channel, measured from the toroidal symmetry axis in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The quantity is the major-radius coordinate of an interpolated geometry point associated with a spectrometer channel. It locates that point by its perpendicular distance from the toroidal symmetry axis in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

At each interpolated geometry point, the coordinate is defined from its transverse Cartesian coordinates:

$$
R = \sqrt{x^2+y^2}
$$

where $R$ is the major-radius coordinate, and $x$ and $y$ are the Cartesian coordinates along the $\hat{x}$ and $\hat{y}$ directions. The right-handed Cartesian basis is $(\hat{x},\hat{y},\hat{z})$, with $\hat{z}$ equal to the vertical unit direction $\hat{Z}$; in the cylindrical frame, $\phi$ is toroidal angle and $Z$ is vertical height.

The quantity applies pointwise to each interpolated geometry knot associated with one spectrometer channel and is not summed, averaged, or integrated over knots, channels, viewing paths, or plasma regions. It identifies a geometry-point locus rather than a single radial location for the channel body or a channel-wide average.

This is the spectrometer-channel-specific instance of the [radial coordinate](name:radial_coordinate). It retains the parent quantity's major-radius definition while restricting its locus to an interpolated point in the channel geometry.

NAMES.name: ratio_of_volume_averaged_krypton_density_to_volume_averaged_electron_density
NAMES.short: Volume-averaged krypton density divided by volume-averaged electron density is the plasma-volume krypton abundance ratio relative to electrons, with krypton number density summed over all charge states.
NAMES.long:
Volume-averaged krypton density divided by volume-averaged electron density is the plasma-volume krypton abundance ratio formed from the same averaging volume for krypton and electrons. The krypton density is the species-level krypton number density summed over all charge states, including neutral through fully stripped krypton.

The ratio is defined by the quotient of the two volume averages:

$$
f_{\mathrm{Kr},V} = \frac{\langle n_{\mathrm{Kr}} \rangle_V}{\langle n_e \rangle_V} = \frac{V_p^{-1}\int_{V_p}\sum_{q=0}^{Z_{\mathrm{Kr}}} n_{\mathrm{Kr},q}(\mathbf{x})\,dV}{V_p^{-1}\int_{V_p} n_e(\mathbf{x})\,dV}
$$

where $f_{\mathrm{Kr},V}$ is this krypton abundance ratio, $\langle n_{\mathrm{Kr}} \rangle_V$ is the [volume-averaged krypton density](name:volume_averaged_krypton_density), $\langle n_e \rangle_V$ is the [volume-averaged electron density](name:volume_averaged_electron_density), $V_p$ is the averaging plasma volume, $n_{\mathrm{Kr},q}$ is the krypton number density in charge state $q$, $q=0$ denotes neutral krypton, $q=Z_{\mathrm{Kr}}$ denotes fully stripped krypton, $Z_{\mathrm{Kr}}$ is the nuclear charge of krypton, $n_e$ is the electron number density, $\mathbf{x}$ is spatial position, and $dV$ is an infinitesimal volume element.

This quantity applies to the krypton and electron populations inside the same plasma volume $V_p$. Its aggregation convention is volumetric averaging for both numerator and denominator; because krypton density is an extensive per-volume species amount, the species-level krypton density is charge-state-summed before the volume average is taken.

It is not normalized by the maximum local electron density and is not a krypton-to-electron density ratio at a single position. It is also distinct from [line-averaged krypton density](name:line_averaged_krypton_density), which averages krypton density along a path rather than over the plasma volume.

The numerator is exactly [volume-averaged krypton density](name:volume_averaged_krypton_density), and the denominator is exactly [volume-averaged electron density](name:volume_averaged_electron_density). Replacing the denominator by a maximum electron density gives the related but different [ratio of volume-averaged krypton density to maximum electron density](name:ratio_of_volume_averaged_krypton_density_to_volume_averaged_electron_density).

NAMES.name: ratio_of_volume_averaged_neon_density_to_volume_averaged_electron_density
NAMES.short: Dimensionless elemental abundance ratio of charge-state-summed neon nuclei to free electrons, formed from their respective mean number densities inside the last closed flux surface.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the abundance of neon nuclei relative to free electrons, with both species represented by number densities averaged over the plasma volume enclosed by the last closed flux surface. Neon is summed over all charge states, so the quantity is an elemental composition ratio rather than a charge-state-specific abundance or a local density ratio.

The ratio of volume-averaged densities is defined by

$$
\frac{\overline{n}_{\mathrm{Ne}}}{\overline{n}_e} = \frac{\displaystyle \frac{1}{V_p}\int_{V_p} n_{\mathrm{Ne}}(\mathbf{x})\,dV}{\displaystyle \frac{1}{V_p}\int_{V_p} n_e(\mathbf{x})\,dV}
$$

where $\overline{n}_{\mathrm{Ne}}$ is the [volume-averaged neon density](name:volume_averaged_neon_density), $\overline{n}_e$ is the [volume-averaged electron density](name:volume_averaged_electron_density), $n_{\mathrm{Ne}}(\mathbf{x})$ is the local neon nuclear number density summed over charge states, $n_e(\mathbf{x})$ is the local free-electron number density, $V_p$ is the plasma volume enclosed by the last closed flux surface, $\mathbf{x}$ is position, and $dV$ is the volume element.

Both operands use the same plasma volume and the same volume-averaging convention. This quantity is the ratio of the two global means, not the volume average of the local ratio $n_{\mathrm{Ne}}(\mathbf{x})/n_e(\mathbf{x})$; its denominator is specifically the parent [volume-averaged electron density](name:volume_averaged_electron_density), while its numerator is the corresponding [volume-averaged neon density](name:volume_averaged_neon_density).

NAMES.name: ratio_of_volume_averaged_nitrogen_density_to_volume_averaged_electron_density
NAMES.short: Dimensionless abundance ratio of charge-state-summed nitrogen nuclei to electrons, with both number densities averaged over the plasma volume bounded by the last closed flux surface.
NAMES.long:
Dimensionless abundance ratio of charge-state-summed nitrogen nuclei to electrons, with both number densities averaged over the plasma volume bounded by the last closed flux surface. It represents the species-level nitrogen abundance relative to the free-electron population in the confined plasma.

The defining ratio is:

$$
f_{\mathrm{N/e}} = \frac{\left\langle \sum_{q=0}^{7} n_{\mathrm{N}^{q+}} \right\rangle_V}{\left\langle n_e \right\rangle_V}
$$

where $f_{\mathrm{N/e}}$ is the nitrogen-to-electron abundance ratio, $n_{\mathrm{N}^{q+}}$ is the nitrogen number density in charge state $q$, $q=0$ denotes neutral nitrogen, $q=7$ denotes fully stripped nitrogen, $n_e$ is the [electron density](name:electron_density), and $\langle\cdot\rangle_V$ denotes averaging over the plasma volume bounded by the last closed flux surface.

The numerator is the charge-state-summed [nitrogen density](name:nitrogen_density) after volume averaging, equivalently the [volume-averaged nitrogen density](name:volume_averaged_nitrogen_density). The denominator is the [volume-averaged electron density](name:volume_averaged_electron_density) evaluated with the same volume-averaging convention.

This quantity is a ratio of separate volume averages, not the volume average of a local nitrogen-to-electron density ratio. It is species-level and charge-state-summed, so it differs from any charge-state-resolved nitrogen abundance that retains a single ionization state in the numerator. It follows the same abundance-ratio convention as [ratio of volume-averaged neon density to volume-averaged electron density](name:ratio_of_volume_averaged_neon_density_to_volume_averaged_electron_density) and [ratio of volume-averaged iron density to volume-averaged electron density](name:ratio_of_iron_density_to_electron_density).

NAMES.name: wavelength_of_filter
NAMES.short: Wavelength of a filter is the vacuum-wavelength spectral coordinate identifying the nominal center of the filter transmission band. It characterizes the central filter response, not the lower or upper bandpass edge.
NAMES.long:
Wavelength of a filter is the vacuum-wavelength spectral coordinate identifying the nominal center of the filter transmission band. It is a property of the filter transmission response and denotes the central or nominal wavelength of the passband selected for spectral transmission.

For a filter characteristic associated with temporal frequency $\nu_f$, the vacuum wavelength $\lambda_f$ is defined by:

$$
\lambda_f = \frac{c}{\nu_f}
$$

where $\lambda_f$ is the wavelength of the filter, $c$ is the speed of light in vacuum, and $\nu_f$ is the corresponding temporal frequency.

This quantity applies to the filter passband response, not to radiation after propagation in a material medium and not to the rest-frame wavelength of an emitted or absorbed spectral feature such as the [wavelength of a spectral line](name:wavelength_of_spectral_line). It is distinct from the [lower wavelength of a filter](name:lower_wavelength_of_filter) and [upper wavelength of a filter](name:upper_wavelength_of_filter), which identify the short-wavelength and long-wavelength bandpass edges.

The wavelength of a filter is also distinct from the [width of a filter]: that related quantity denotes a geometric extent of the filter window, not a spectral passband interval. The lower and upper wavelength quantities bound the transmitted spectral band, while the wavelength of a filter identifies its nominal central spectral coordinate.

NAMES.name: lower_wavelength_of_filter
NAMES.short: Lower wavelength of a filter is the spectral coordinate, expressed as vacuum wavelength, that identifies the short-wavelength boundary of a diagnostic filter's transmitted spectral band.
NAMES.long:
Lower wavelength of a filter is the vacuum-wavelength spectral coordinate that identifies the short-wavelength boundary of a diagnostic filter's transmitted spectral band. It marks the high-photon-energy edge of the interval selected by the filter transmission response.

For a lower-bound characteristic associated with temporal frequency $\nu_\mathrm{lower}$, the vacuum wavelength is defined by:

$$
\lambda_\mathrm{lower} = \frac{c}{\nu_\mathrm{lower}}
$$

where $\lambda_\mathrm{lower}$ is the lower filter-boundary vacuum wavelength, $c$ is the speed of light in vacuum, and $\nu_\mathrm{lower}$ is the temporal frequency corresponding to that boundary.

This quantity applies to the transmitted spectral band of the filter and is a single lower-edge value, not a wavelength average, an integrated spectral quantity, or the complete transmission function. It is distinct from a spectral-line rest wavelength and from a wavelength defined inside a material medium.

As the lower-bound member of [wavelength of a filter](name:wavelength_of_filter), it identifies one characteristic point of the filter response. Together with the [upper wavelength of a filter](name:upper_wavelength_of_filter), it defines the passband span represented by the [width of a filter].

NAMES.name: upper_wavelength_of_filter
NAMES.short: Upper wavelength of a filter is the vacuum-wavelength coordinate marking the long-wavelength, low-frequency edge of its transmitted spectral band.
NAMES.long:
Upper wavelength of a filter is the spectral coordinate, expressed as vacuum wavelength, that identifies the long-wavelength boundary of a filter's transmitted spectral band. It is a property of the filter transmission response, rather than the rest-frame wavelength of a spectral line or the wavelength inside a material medium.

For the upper boundary associated with the lower temporal frequency, the vacuum wavelength is defined by:

$$
\lambda_{\mathrm{upper}} = \frac{c}{\nu_{\mathrm{low}}}
$$

where $\lambda_{\mathrm{upper}}$ is the upper boundary vacuum wavelength, $c$ is the speed of light in vacuum, and $\nu_{\mathrm{low}}$ is the lower temporal frequency corresponding to that boundary.

This quantity applies specifically to the long-wavelength boundary of the transmitted passband and is not a band-average or a full transmission function. It complements the [lower wavelength of a filter](name:lower_wavelength_of_filter), which marks the short-wavelength boundary; together, the two boundaries determine the [width of a filter]. The parent [wavelength of a filter](name:wavelength_of_filter) also includes nominal characteristic wavelengths such as a reference wavelength.

NAMES.name: wavelength_of_spectral_line
NAMES.short: Characteristic vacuum wavelength assigned to an atomic, ionic, molecular, or nuclear spectral transition, identifying its central line position.
NAMES.long:
The wavelength of a spectral line is the characteristic vacuum spectral coordinate of an emission or absorption transition. It identifies the central line position associated with the transition or processed spectral feature.

For an unshifted transition, the vacuum wavelength is related to the transition energy by:

$$
\lambda_0 = \frac{hc}{\Delta E}
$$

where $\lambda_0$ is the unshifted vacuum wavelength, $h$ is Planck's constant, $c$ is the speed of light in vacuum, and $\Delta E$ is the energy difference between the transition's quantum states.

The quantity applies to one identified atomic, ionic, molecular, or nuclear spectral line and is a central wavelength, not a wavelength interval, spectral width, or aggregate over multiple lines. Depending on the spectral-line definition, it may denote the unshifted transition reference or a central wavelength that includes a physical shift of the observed feature; it is not inherently a wavelength displacement.

This quantity specializes the broader wavelength concept by locating a spectral transition. A displacement from a specified reference wavelength is represented separately by [difference_of_fast_neutral_beam_motional_stark_wavelength_and_fast_neutral_beam_reference_wavelength_of_spectral_line](name:difference_of_fast_neutral_beam_motional_stark_wavelength_and_fast_neutral_beam_reference_wavelength_of_spectral_line).

NAMES.name: toroidal_angular_width_of_limiter_tile
NAMES.short: Full toroidal angular span of one limiter tile between its minimum and maximum φ coordinates in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The toroidal angular width of an individual limiter tile is the full angular span occupied by that tile around the machine symmetry axis. It is a non-negative geometric extent in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

The width is defined from the extrema of the tile's toroidal-angle extent:

$$
\Delta\phi_{\mathrm{tile}} = \phi_{\max} - \phi_{\min}
$$

where $\Delta\phi_{\mathrm{tile}}$ is the tile's toroidal angular width, and $\phi_{\max}$ and $\phi_{\min}$ are the maximum and minimum toroidal-angle coordinates of the tile, evaluated on a continuous angular branch when the extent crosses the angular periodic boundary.

This quantity applies to one individual limiter tile and represents its complete toroidal span; it is not summed over tiles, limiter units, or periodic repetitions. It is distinct from a toroidal-angle coordinate, a tile-center angle, and the angular width of an entire limiter assembly.

The toroidal extent complements the boundary geometry described by the [vertical outline of the limiter tile](name:vertical_outline_of_limiter_tile), while the analogous camera field-of-view quantity [toroidal angular width of a camera](name:toroidal_angular_width_of_camera) applies to an optical viewing extent rather than a structural tile.

sources.leaf_definition: Simplified description of toroidal angle extensions of the unit, by a list of zones defined by their centre and full width (in toroidal angle).  In each of these zones, the unit outline remains the same. Leave this node empty for an axisymmetric unit. The first dimension gives the centre and full width toroidal angle values for the unit. The second dimension represents the toroidal occurrences of the unit countour (i.e. the number of toroidal zones).
sources.parent_definition: Set of limiter units. Whenever relevant, multiple units should be ordered so that they define contiguous sections, clockwise in the poloidal direction.

NAMES.name: vertical_outline_of_limiter_tile
NAMES.short: Signed vertical (Z) coordinate of each point on a limiter-tile boundary contour in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The vertical outline of a limiter tile gives the signed vertical coordinate of each point on the tile’s geometric boundary contour. It describes the contour geometry rather than a material property, thickness, or surface-load quantity.

For contour point $i$, the vertical coordinate is defined by

$$
Z_i = \mathbf{r}_i \cdot \hat{\mathbf{Z}}
$$

where $Z_i$ is the vertical coordinate of point $i$, $\mathbf{r}_i$ is its position vector, and $\hat{\mathbf{Z}}$ is the vertical unit vector in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame. Here, $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

The quantity applies pointwise to the irregular outline of one limiter tile in its poloidal cross section. The contour is closed by connecting its final point to its initial point, without duplicating the initial point; no averaging, summation, or other aggregation over contour points is implied. Unlike the [radial outline of a limiter tile](name:radial_outline_of_limiter_tile), this quantity gives the vertical coordinate rather than the major-radius coordinate of the boundary.

The same geometric carrier and coordinate meaning apply to the [vertical outline of a divertor tile](name:vertical_outline_of_divertor_tile), but that related quantity belongs to a divertor tile rather than a limiter tile.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the contour point lies toward increasing $Z$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

sources.leaf_definition: Height
sources.parent_definition: Irregular outline of the limiting surface. Repeat the first point in case of a closed contour

NAMES.name: vertical_outline_of_plasma_facing_component
NAMES.short: The vertical coordinate of each point on a plasma-facing component boundary outline is the signed height in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The vertical outline coordinate is the signed height $Z$ of each boundary-contour point belonging to a plasma-facing component. It describes the component boundary in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

For outline point $i$, the coordinate is defined by

$$
Z_i = \mathbf{r}_i \cdot \hat{\mathbf{Z}}
$$

where $Z_i$ is the vertical coordinate of point $i$, $\mathbf{r}_i$ is that point's position vector relative to the cylindrical coordinate origin, and $\hat{\mathbf{Z}}$ is the unit vector in the vertical direction. The quantity applies pointwise to one component boundary outline and is not an average, extremum, centroid coordinate, or integrated geometric measure. A closed outline does not repeat its first point as a closing point.

This coordinate has the same geometric meaning as the corresponding outline coordinate for a limiter tile or divertor tile, such as [vertical outline of limiter tile](name:vertical_outline_of_limiter_tile) and [vertical outline of divertor tile](name:vertical_outline_of_divertor_tile), but its locus is the plasma-facing component boundary in general.
NAMES.sign: Positive when $Z_i$ increases in the $+\hat{\mathbf{Z}}$ direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: argon_density_at_magnetic_axis
NAMES.subject: argon
NAMES.short: Particle number density of argon ions evaluated at the magnetic axis is the local argon-ion count per physical volume at that location, summed over all argon ionic charge states.
NAMES.long:
Particle number density of argon ions evaluated at the magnetic axis is the local argon-ion count per physical volume at that location, summed over all argon ionic charge states. It represents argon ions specifically, rather than electrons, neutrals, or another plasma population.

The defining relation is

$$
n_{\mathrm{Ar},\mathrm{axis}} = \left.\frac{dN_{\mathrm{Ar}}}{dV}\right|_{\mathrm{axis}}
$$

where $n_{\mathrm{Ar},\mathrm{axis}}$ is the argon-ion number density at the magnetic axis, $N_{\mathrm{Ar}}$ is the number of argon ions summed over all ionic charge states, and $V$ is physical volume.

The quantity is local to the magnetic axis, the innermost location of nested closed poloidal magnetic-flux surfaces where the gradient of the poloidal magnetic flux vanishes. It applies to the complete ionic argon population at that location and is charge-state summed; neutral argon is excluded. It is neither a flux-surface or volume integral nor a density for another species.

This is the argon-specific realization of [density at the magnetic axis](name:density_at_magnetic_axis), with the population fixed to argon ions and the aggregation fixed to a sum over ionic charge states. The corresponding species specialization for oxygen is [oxygen density at the magnetic axis](name:oxygen_density_at_magnetic_axis), which uses the same magnetic-axis locus but a different ion population.

NAMES.name: atomic_count
NAMES.short: Stoichiometric multiplicity of a selected element within the chemical formula of an atomic or molecular species.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the number of atoms belonging to a selected element in one atomic or molecular species, as specified by its composition. It is a composition property rather than a particle population or field quantity.

For an atomic species, the count is one for its constituent element; for a molecular species, it is the element's stoichiometric coefficient in the molecular formula. The count applies to the selected species composition and is not a number density, abundance, or present/absent flag. It is not summed over particles or charge states, and changing the ionization state does not change the elemental atom count.

The selected element is identified independently by its [atomic number](name:atomic_number), while this quantity gives the number of atoms of that element in the species. The same composition count can therefore be used for neutral or ionized forms of a species and for elemental constituents of reaction participants.

NAMES.name: atomic_mass
NAMES.short: Mass parameter assigned to a specified ion or neutral particle species, encoding its isotope or constituent composition for inertial and transport calculations.
NAMES.long:
Atomic mass is the intrinsic mass parameter assigned to one specified ion or neutral particle species. It identifies an isotope for an atomic species or the constituent composition for a molecular or compound neutral, and provides the inertial scale used in collisional and transport physics.

The mass is represented relative to the atomic mass unit by

$$
m_s = A_s m_u
$$

where $m_s$ is the atomic mass of the specified species, $A_s$ is its relative atomic mass, and $m_u$ is the atomic mass unit.

The scope is one species definition at a time: either an ion species or a neutral particle species. No aggregation over separate species, charge states, or plasma populations is implied; for a molecular or compound neutral, combining constituent masses is part of that species definition. The ion-specific form [ion atomic mass](name:ion_atomic_mass) and neutral-specific form [neutral species atomic mass](name:neutral_species_atomic_mass) are corresponding instances of this quantity.

Atomic masses provide the species-dependent weighting used when forming aggregate quantities such as [total plasma mass density](name:total_plasma_mass_density); they are not themselves densities, particle counts, or aggregate plasma masses.

NAMES.name: atomic_number
NAMES.short: Nuclear charge number identifying an element by the number of protons in its nucleus, independent of isotope and ionization state.
NAMES.long:
Atomic number is the intrinsic nuclear-charge identifier of an element constituent in an atomic or molecular species. It specifies the element regardless of whether the atom is neutral, ionized, or part of an isotope.

$$
Z = N_p
$$

where $Z$ is the atomic number and $N_p$ is the number of protons in the nucleus.

This quantity applies to the specified element and is neither summed nor averaged over isotopes, ionization states, or molecular constituents. It is distinct from ionic charge, which describes the net charge state, and from [atomic mass](name:atomic_mass), which distinguishes isotope or constituent mass.

The same nuclear charge identifies every isotope and ionization state of an element; a role-specific instance such as [fast-ion atomic number](name:fast_ion_atomic_number) represents this same property for a restricted fast-ion population. When a formula contains multiple atoms of the element, [atomic count](name:atomic_count) gives the stoichiometric multiplicity separately.

NAMES.name: beryllium_density_at_magnetic_axis
NAMES.subject: beryllium
NAMES.short: Particle number density of the beryllium ion population evaluated at the magnetic axis is the local beryllium-ion count per physical volume there, summed over all beryllium ionization states.
NAMES.long:
Particle number density of the beryllium ion population evaluated at the magnetic axis is the local beryllium-ion count per physical volume at that location, summed over all beryllium ionization states. It represents beryllium ions specifically, rather than neutral beryllium, electrons, or other ion species.

The defining relation is

$$
n_{\mathrm{Be},\mathrm{axis}} = \sum_Z n_{\mathrm{Be}^{Z+},\mathrm{axis}} = \left.\frac{dN_{\mathrm{Be}}}{dV}\right|_{\mathrm{axis}}
$$

where $n_{\mathrm{Be},\mathrm{axis}}$ is the total beryllium-ion number density at the magnetic axis, $n_{\mathrm{Be}^{Z+},\mathrm{axis}}$ is the number density of beryllium ions in charge state $Z$, $Z$ is the ionic charge-state number, $N_{\mathrm{Be}}$ is the number of beryllium ions included in the sum, and $V$ is physical volume.

The quantity is local to the magnetic axis, the innermost location of nested closed poloidal magnetic-flux surfaces where the poloidal-flux gradient vanishes. It applies to the complete beryllium-ion population at that location and is summed over all beryllium ionic charge states. It excludes neutral beryllium and is neither a flux-surface or volume integral nor the density of another species.

This is the beryllium-specific realization of the population-independent [density at the magnetic axis](name:density_at_magnetic_axis). Like [boron density at the magnetic axis](name:boron_density_at_magnetic_axis), it is species-resolved while retaining charge-state aggregation; it differs from [beryllium density at the plasma boundary](name:beryllium_density_at_plasma_boundary) only in its evaluation locus.

NAMES.name: boron_density_at_magnetic_axis
NAMES.subject: boron
NAMES.short: Particle number density of the boron ion population evaluated at the magnetic axis is the local boron-ion count per physical volume, summed over all boron ionic charge states.
NAMES.long:
Particle number density of the boron ion population evaluated at the magnetic axis is the local boron-ion count per physical volume at that location. It represents boron ions specifically, rather than electrons, neutrals, or another plasma population, and is summed over all boron ionic charge states.

The defining relation is

$$
n_{\mathrm{B,axis}} = \left.\frac{dN_{\mathrm{B}}}{dV}\right|_{\mathrm{axis}}
$$

where $n_{\mathrm{B,axis}}$ is the boron ion number density at the magnetic axis, $N_{\mathrm{B}}$ is the number of boron ions summed over all ionic charge states, and $V$ is physical volume.

The quantity is local to the magnetic axis, the innermost location of nested closed poloidal magnetic-flux surfaces where the poloidal-flux gradient vanishes. It applies to the complete ionized boron population at that location and excludes neutral boron; it is neither a flux-surface or volume integral nor a density for another species.

This is the boron-specific realization of the population-independent [density at the magnetic axis](name:density_at_magnetic_axis). It has the same locus and aggregation convention as [beryllium density at the magnetic axis](name:beryllium_density_at_magnetic_axis), but represents boron ions rather than beryllium ions. It differs from [boron density at the internal transport barrier](name:boron_density_at_internal_transport_barrier), which is evaluated at a different plasma location.

NAMES.name: carbon_density_at_magnetic_axis
NAMES.subject: carbon
NAMES.short: Particle number density of the carbon-ion population evaluated at the magnetic axis is the local carbon-ion count per physical volume, summed over all carbon ion charge states.
NAMES.long:
Particle number density of the carbon-ion population evaluated at the magnetic axis is the local carbon-ion count per physical volume at that location, summed over all carbon ion charge states. It represents carbon ions specifically, rather than electrons, other ion species, or neutral carbon.

The defining relation is

$$
n_{\mathrm{C,axis}} = \left.\frac{dN_{\mathrm{C}}}{dV}\right|_{\mathrm{axis}}
$$

where $n_{\mathrm{C,axis}}$ is the carbon-ion number density at the magnetic axis, the subscript $\mathrm{C}$ denotes the carbon-ion population, $N_{\mathrm{C}}$ is the number of carbon ions, $V$ is physical volume, and the subscript axis denotes evaluation at the magnetic axis.

The quantity is local to the magnetic axis, the innermost location of nested closed poloidal magnetic-flux surfaces where the poloidal-flux gradient vanishes. It applies to the complete carbon-ion population at that location and is summed over all carbon ion charge states; it is neither a flux-surface or volume integral nor a neutral-carbon density.

This is the carbon-specific realization of the population-independent [density at the magnetic axis](name:density_at_magnetic_axis). It differs from [oxygen density at the magnetic axis](name:oxygen_density_at_magnetic_axis) only in the counted ion species, and from [carbon density at the internal transport barrier](name:carbon_density_at_internal_transport_barrier) in the evaluation locus.

NAMES.name: deuterium_density_at_magnetic_axis
NAMES.subject: deuterium
NAMES.short: Particle number density of the deuterium ion population evaluated at the magnetic axis is the local deuterium-ion count per physical volume there, summed over all deuterium ionic charge states.
NAMES.long:
Particle number density of the deuterium ion population evaluated at the magnetic axis is the local deuterium-ion count per physical volume at that location, summed over all deuterium ionic charge states. It represents deuterium ions specifically, rather than neutral deuterium, electrons, or another ion species.

The defining relation is

$$
n_{D,\mathrm{axis}} = \left.\frac{dN_D}{dV}\right|_{\mathrm{axis}}
$$

where $n_{D,\mathrm{axis}}$ is the deuterium ion number density at the magnetic axis, $N_D$ is the number of deuterium ions summed over all ionic charge states, and $V$ is physical volume.

The quantity is local to the magnetic axis, the innermost location of nested closed poloidal magnetic-flux surfaces where the poloidal-flux gradient vanishes. It applies to the complete deuterium ion population at that location and is charge-state-summed; it is neither a flux-surface or volume integral nor a neutral, electron, or other-ion density.

This is the deuterium-specific realization of the population-independent [density at the magnetic axis](name:density_at_magnetic_axis). It must be distinguished from [hydrogen density at the magnetic axis](name:hydrogen_density_at_magnetic_axis), which counts hydrogen ions rather than deuterium ions.

NAMES.name: deuterium_tritium_density_at_magnetic_axis
NAMES.subject: deuterium_tritium
NAMES.short: Particle number density of the deuterium-tritium fuel-ion pseudo-species evaluated at the magnetic axis is the local effective fuel-ion count per physical volume at that location.
NAMES.long:
Particle number density of the deuterium-tritium fuel-ion pseudo-species evaluated at the magnetic axis is the local effective fuel-ion count per physical volume at that location. It represents the deuterium–tritium mixture as one effective ion population rather than as separate deuterium and tritium species.

The defining relation is

$$
n_{\mathrm{DT,axis}} = \left.\frac{dN_{\mathrm{DT}}}{dV}\right|_{\mathrm{axis}}
$$

where $n_{\mathrm{DT,axis}}$ is the deuterium-tritium pseudo-species number density at the magnetic axis, $N_{\mathrm{DT}}$ is the number of effective deuterium-tritium pseudo-ions, and $V$ is physical volume.

The quantity is local to the magnetic axis, the innermost location of nested closed poloidal magnetic-flux surfaces where the poloidal-flux gradient vanishes. The aggregation convention treats the deuterium-tritium mixture as one effective ion population; this quantity is not separately resolved by isotope and is neither a flux-surface, line, nor volume average or integral.

This is the deuterium-tritium specialization of the population-independent [density at the magnetic axis](name:density_at_magnetic_axis). It differs from [deuterium-tritium density](name:deuterium_tritium_density) by explicitly fixing the evaluation locus at the magnetic axis rather than leaving the locus unspecified.

NAMES.name: electron_density_at_magnetic_axis
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Particle number density of the electron population evaluated at the magnetic axis is the local electron count per physical volume at that location.
NAMES.long:
Particle number density of the electron population evaluated at the magnetic axis is the local electron count per physical volume at that location. It represents electrons specifically, rather than ions, neutrals, or another plasma population.

The defining relation is

$$
n_{e,\mathrm{axis}} = \left.\frac{dN_e}{dV}\right|_{\mathrm{axis}}
$$

where $n_{e,\mathrm{axis}}$ is the electron number density at the magnetic axis, $N_e$ is the number of electrons, and $V$ is physical volume.

The quantity is local to the magnetic axis, the innermost location of nested closed poloidal magnetic-flux surfaces where the poloidal-flux gradient vanishes. It applies to the complete electron population at that location and is neither a flux-surface or volume integral nor an ion or neutral density.

This is the electron-specific realization of the population-independent [density at the magnetic axis](name:density_at_magnetic_axis). It must be distinguished from [total ion density at the magnetic axis](name:total_ion_density_at_magnetic_axis), which counts ions, and from [electron temperature at the magnetic axis](name:electron_temperature_at_magnetic_axis), which characterizes electron energy rather than particle count.

NAMES.name: electron_temperature_at_magnetic_axis
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Thermal energy per particle of the electron population, expressed as an energy-equivalent temperature and evaluated at the magnetic axis.
NAMES.long:
Thermal energy per particle of the electron population, expressed as an energy-equivalent temperature and evaluated at the magnetic axis. The magnetic axis is the degenerate innermost magnetic surface of the equilibrium, where the gradient of the poloidal magnetic flux vanishes; evaluation at this locus does not imply that the electron temperature has an extremum there.

For a thermal electron population with a well-defined absolute thermodynamic temperature, the energy-equivalent electron temperature is defined by:

$$
T_e = k_\mathrm{B}\,\Theta_e
$$

where $T_e$ is the electron temperature expressed as energy per particle, $\Theta_e$ is the absolute thermodynamic temperature of the electrons, and $k_\mathrm{B}$ is the Boltzmann constant.

This quantity applies specifically to the electron population at the magnetic axis and is an intensive, per-particle quantity rather than a charge-state sum, volume average, or volume-integrated electron energy. It excludes ion temperatures, radiative temperature-equivalent scales, and the total thermal energy content of the electron population.

It is the electron-specific member of the broader [temperature at the magnetic axis](name:temperature_at_magnetic_axis), which also encompasses other populations and radiative temperature interpretations. The corresponding electron temperature at another locus is [electron temperature at the outboard midplane](name:electron_temperature_at_outboard_midplane), while [thermal electron energy](name:thermal_electron_energy) denotes an integrated energy content rather than this local temperature.

NAMES.name: helium_3_density_at_magnetic_axis
NAMES.subject: helium_3
NAMES.short: Particle number density of the helium-3 ion population evaluated at the magnetic axis is the local helium-3 ion count per physical volume at that location. It is summed over all helium-3 ionic charge states.
NAMES.long:
Particle number density of the helium-3 ion population evaluated at the magnetic axis is the local helium-3 ion count per physical volume at that location. It represents helium-3 ions specifically, rather than neutral helium-3, electrons, or another plasma population.

The defining relation is

$$
n_{3,\mathrm{axis}} = \left.\frac{dN_3}{dV}\right|_{\mathrm{axis}}
$$

where $n_{3,\mathrm{axis}}$ is the helium-3 ion number density at the magnetic axis, $N_3$ is the number of helium-3 ions, and $V$ is physical volume.

The quantity is local to the magnetic axis, the innermost location of nested closed poloidal magnetic-flux surfaces where the poloidal-flux gradient vanishes. It applies to the complete helium-3 ion population at that location and is summed over all helium-3 ionic charge states; it is neither a flux-surface or volume integral nor a neutral-helium or other-species density.

This is the helium-3-specific realization of the population-independent [density at the magnetic axis](name:density_at_magnetic_axis). The unlocalized [helium-3 density](name:helium_3_density) describes the same charge-state-summed helium-3 ion population without this specified magnetic-axis locus, while [helium-4 density at the magnetic axis](name:helium_4_density_at_magnetic_axis) represents the corresponding density for a different helium isotope.

NAMES.name: helium_4_density_at_magnetic_axis
NAMES.subject: helium_4
NAMES.short: Particle number density of the helium-4 ion population evaluated at the magnetic axis is the local helium-4 ion count per physical volume at that location, summed over all helium-4 ionic charge states.
NAMES.long:
Particle number density of the helium-4 ion population evaluated at the magnetic axis is the local helium-4 ion count per physical volume at that location, summed over all helium-4 ionic charge states. It represents helium-4 ions specifically, rather than neutral helium, electrons, other isotopes, or another plasma population.

The defining relation is

$$
n_{{}^{4}\mathrm{He},\mathrm{axis}} = \left.\frac{dN_{{}^{4}\mathrm{He},\mathrm{ion}}}{dV}\right|_{\mathrm{axis}}
$$

where $n_{{}^{4}\mathrm{He},\mathrm{axis}}$ is the helium-4 ion number density at the magnetic axis, $N_{{}^{4}\mathrm{He},\mathrm{ion}}$ is the number of helium-4 ions summed over all ionic charge states, and $V$ is physical volume. The superscript $4$ identifies the helium isotope with four nucleons.

The quantity is local to the magnetic axis, the innermost location of nested closed poloidal magnetic-flux surfaces where the poloidal-flux gradient vanishes. It applies to the complete helium-4 ion population at that location and is summed over all helium-4 ionic charge states; it is neither a flux-surface or volume integral nor a density of neutral helium or another isotope.

This is the helium-4-specific realization of the population-independent [density at the magnetic axis](name:density_at_magnetic_axis), whose population is left unspecified at the parent level. It is distinguished from [helium-3 density at the magnetic axis](name:helium_3_density_at_magnetic_axis), which counts helium-3 ions rather than helium-4 ions.

NAMES.name: hydrogen_density_at_magnetic_axis
NAMES.subject: hydrogen
NAMES.short: Particle number density of the hydrogen ion population evaluated at the magnetic axis is the local hydrogen-ion count per physical volume at that location, summed over all hydrogen ionic charge states.
NAMES.long:
Particle number density of the hydrogen ion population evaluated at the magnetic axis is the local hydrogen-ion count per physical volume at that location, summed over all hydrogen ionic charge states. It represents hydrogen ions specifically, rather than electrons, neutral hydrogen, or another plasma population.

The defining relation is

$$
n_{\mathrm{H},\mathrm{axis}} = \left.\frac{dN_{\mathrm{H}}}{dV}\right|_{\mathrm{axis}}
$$

where $n_{\mathrm{H},\mathrm{axis}}$ is the hydrogen-ion number density at the magnetic axis, $N_{\mathrm{H}}$ is the number of hydrogen ions summed over all ionic charge states, and $V$ is physical volume.

The quantity is local to the magnetic axis, the innermost location of nested closed poloidal magnetic-flux surfaces where the poloidal-flux gradient vanishes. It applies to the complete hydrogen-ion population at that location and is neither a flux-surface or volume integral nor an electron or neutral density.

This is the hydrogen-specific realization of the population-independent [density at the magnetic axis](name:density_at_magnetic_axis). NAMES.name: ion_atomic_mass
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Mass parameter assigned to a specified ion species, encoding its isotope and setting the inertial scale for collisional and transport calculations.
NAMES.long:
Atomic mass is the intrinsic mass parameter assigned to one specified ion species. It identifies the ion's isotope and provides the inertial scale used in collisional and transport physics.

The mass is represented relative to the atomic mass unit by

$$
m_s = A_s m_u
$$

where $m_s$ is the atomic mass of the specified ion species, $A_s$ is its relative atomic mass, and $m_u$ is the atomic mass unit.

The scope is one ion-species definition at a time. No aggregation over separate ion species, charge states, or plasma populations is implied, and the quantity does not represent a number density, mass density, or aggregate plasma mass. This ion-specific form specializes [atomic mass](name:atomic_mass) to ions, while [neutral species atomic mass](name:neutral_species_atomic_mass) applies the same mass concept to uncharged particle species.

NAMES.name: iron_density_at_magnetic_axis
NAMES.subject: iron
NAMES.short: Particle number density of the iron ion population evaluated at the magnetic axis is the local iron-ion count per physical volume at that location, summed over all iron ionic charge states.
NAMES.long:
Particle number density of the iron ion population evaluated at the magnetic axis is the local iron-ion count per physical volume at that location. It represents iron ions specifically, rather than electrons, neutral iron, or another plasma population.

The defining relation is

$$
n_{\mathrm{Fe,axis}} = \left.\frac{dN_{\mathrm{Fe}}}{dV}\right|_{\mathrm{axis}}
$$

where $n_{\mathrm{Fe,axis}}$ is the iron-ion number density at the magnetic axis, $N_{\mathrm{Fe}}$ is the number of iron ions summed over all iron ionic charge states, and $V$ is physical volume.

The quantity is local to the magnetic axis, the innermost location of nested closed poloidal magnetic-flux surfaces where the poloidal-flux gradient vanishes. It applies to the complete ionic iron population at that location, with all iron charge states aggregated, and is neither a flux-surface or volume integral nor a neutral-iron density.

This is the iron-specific realization of the population-independent [density at the magnetic axis](name:density_at_magnetic_axis). It is distinguished from [hydrogen density at the magnetic axis](name:hydrogen_density_at_magnetic_axis), which counts hydrogen ions, and from [iron density at the internal transport barrier](name:iron_density_at_internal_transport_barrier), which is evaluated on the flux surface assigned to that barrier rather than at the magnetic axis.

NAMES.name: krypton_density_at_magnetic_axis
NAMES.subject: krypton
NAMES.short: Particle number density of the krypton ion population evaluated at the magnetic axis is the local krypton-ion count per physical volume at that location.
NAMES.long:
Particle number density of the krypton ion population evaluated at the magnetic axis is the local krypton-ion count per physical volume at that location. It represents krypton ions specifically, summed over all ionic charge states and excluding neutral krypton.

The defining relation is

$$
n_{\mathrm{Kr,axis}} = \left.\frac{dN_{\mathrm{Kr}}}{dV}\right|_{\mathrm{axis}}
$$

where $n_{\mathrm{Kr,axis}}$ is the krypton-ion number density at the magnetic axis, $N_{\mathrm{Kr}}$ is the number of krypton ions summed over ionic charge states, $V$ is physical volume, and the subscript axis denotes evaluation at the magnetic axis.

The quantity is local to the magnetic axis, the innermost location of nested closed poloidal magnetic-flux surfaces where the poloidal-flux gradient vanishes. It applies to the complete krypton-ion population at that location, with number density summed over all krypton ionic charge states; it is neither a flux-surface or volume integral nor a density of neutral krypton, electrons, or other ion species.

This is the krypton-specific realization of the population-independent [density at the magnetic axis](name:density_at_magnetic_axis). The [neon density at the magnetic axis](name:neon_density_at_magnetic_axis) has the same local locus and charge-state-summed convention but counts neon ions rather than krypton ions.

sources.parent_definition: Krypton (Kr)

NAMES.name: lithium_density_at_magnetic_axis
NAMES.subject: lithium
NAMES.short: Particle number density of the lithium ion population evaluated at the magnetic axis is the local lithium-ion count per physical volume at that location, summed over all lithium ionic charge states.
NAMES.long:
Particle number density of the lithium ion population evaluated at the magnetic axis is the local lithium-ion count per physical volume at that location, summed over all lithium ionic charge states. It represents ionized lithium specifically, rather than electrons, neutral lithium, or another plasma population.

The defining relation is

$$
n_{\mathrm{Li,axis}} = \left.\frac{dN_{\mathrm{Li}}}{dV}\right|_{\mathrm{axis}} = \left.\sum_{q\ge 1} n_{\mathrm{Li}^{q+}}\right|_{\mathrm{axis}}
$$

where $n_{\mathrm{Li,axis}}$ is the total lithium-ion number density at the magnetic axis, $N_{\mathrm{Li}}$ is the number of lithium ions, $V$ is physical volume, $q$ is the positive integer labeling a lithium ionic charge state, and $n_{\mathrm{Li}^{q+}}$ is the number density of lithium ions in charge state $q$.

The quantity is local to the magnetic axis, the innermost location of nested closed poloidal magnetic-flux surfaces where the poloidal-flux gradient vanishes. It applies to the complete ionized lithium population at that location and uses a sum over all lithium ionic charge states, not a density for one selected charge state or a sum over different chemical elements. It is neither a flux-surface nor volume integral and excludes neutral lithium.

This is the lithium-specific realization of the population-independent [density at the magnetic axis](name:density_at_magnetic_axis). It has the same local-density and magnetic-axis scope as [deuterium density at the magnetic axis](name:deuterium_density_at_magnetic_axis), but counts lithium ions rather than deuterium ions; unlike [electron density at the magnetic axis](name:electron_density_at_magnetic_axis), it does not count electrons.

sources.parent_definition: Lithium (Li)

NAMES.name: loop_voltage_at_plasma_boundary
NAMES.short: Toroidal electromotive force evaluated on the last closed flux surface that drives the conventionally signed ohmic plasma current.
NAMES.long:
The loop voltage at the plasma boundary is the toroidal electromotive force associated with the inductive electric field around the last closed magnetic-flux surface. It is the net voltage available to drive the ohmic component of the confined plasma current.

For a closed toroidal contour $C$ on the last closed flux surface, the loop voltage is defined by

$$
V_{\mathrm{loop}} = \oint_C \mathbf{E} \cdot d\boldsymbol{\ell}
$$

where $V_{\mathrm{loop}}$ is the loop voltage, $\mathbf{E}$ is the electric-field vector, $d\boldsymbol{\ell}$ is the directed line element, and $C$ is oriented in the direction of increasing toroidal angle. The quantity is a contour-integrated scalar evaluated at the plasma boundary, not a local electric-field component or an external-coil terminal voltage.

This boundary quantity represents the total loop voltage driving plasma current, including the inductive contribution associated with changing poloidal magnetic flux. It excludes no plasma-current-driving contribution merely because it is externally generated; the narrower [external loop voltage](name:external_loop_voltage) denotes only the externally generated contribution and is therefore not equivalent to the total boundary loop voltage.

The loop voltage is related to the ohmic plasma-current drive through the toroidal component of the electric field and the plasma conductivity. The right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame uses $R$ for major radius, $\phi$ for toroidal angle, and $Z$ for vertical height.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the electromotive force drives conventional plasma current in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$, counter-clockwise when viewed from above along $+\hat{Z}$.

NAMES.name: neon_density_at_magnetic_axis
NAMES.subject: neon
NAMES.short: Particle number density of the neon ion population evaluated at the magnetic axis is the local neon-ion count per physical volume at that location, summed over all ionic charge states.
NAMES.long:
Particle number density of the neon ion population evaluated at the magnetic axis is the local neon-ion count per physical volume at that location, summed over all neon ionic charge states. It represents neon ions specifically, rather than neutral neon, electrons, or another plasma population.

The defining relation is

$$
n_{\mathrm{Ne,axis}} = \sum_{q=1}^{Z_{\mathrm{Ne}}} n_{\mathrm{Ne}^{q+},\mathrm{axis}}
$$

where $n_{\mathrm{Ne,axis}}$ is the total neon-ion number density at the magnetic axis, $n_{\mathrm{Ne}^{q+},\mathrm{axis}}$ is the number density of neon ions with charge state $q$ at that location, $q$ is the positive ionic charge-state index, and $Z_{\mathrm{Ne}}$ is the atomic number of neon.

The quantity is local to the magnetic axis, the innermost location of nested closed poloidal magnetic-flux surfaces where the poloidal-flux gradient vanishes. It applies to the neon-ion population at that location and is summed over ionic charge states; neutral neon is excluded, and the quantity is neither a flux-surface nor a volume integral.

This is the neon-specific realization of the population-independent [density at the magnetic axis](name:density_at_magnetic_axis). It has the same locus and charge-state aggregation convention as [oxygen density at the magnetic axis](name:oxygen_density_at_magnetic_axis), but counts neon ions rather than oxygen ions.

NAMES.name: neutral_species_atomic_mass
NAMES.subject: neutral_species
NAMES.short: Mass parameter assigned to a specified neutral particle species, encoding its isotope or constituent composition for inertial and transport calculations.
NAMES.long:
Atomic mass is the intrinsic mass parameter assigned to one specified neutral particle species. It identifies an isotope for an atomic neutral or the constituent composition for a molecular or compound neutral, and provides the inertial scale used in collisional and transport physics.

The mass is represented relative to the atomic mass unit by

$$
m_s = A_s m_u
$$

where $m_s$ is the atomic mass of the specified neutral species, $A_s$ is its relative atomic mass, and $m_u$ is the atomic mass unit.

The scope is one neutral species definition at a time. For an atomic neutral, the definition identifies its isotope; for a molecular or compound neutral, it includes the masses of its constituents. No aggregation over separate species or plasma populations is implied, and this quantity is not a number density, particle count, or aggregate plasma mass.

This neutral-specific quantity is an instance of the broader [atomic mass](name:atomic_mass) concept. The corresponding [ion atomic mass](name:ion_atomic_mass) applies the same mass definition to an ion species rather than a neutral particle species.

NAMES.name: neutral_temperature
NAMES.subject: neutral
NAMES.short: Translational kinetic temperature, expressed as energy per particle, of a neutral population, based on random translational motion after removal of bulk flow and averaged over represented charge states when applicable.
NAMES.long:
The translational kinetic temperature quantifies the random motion of a neutral population after its bulk translational motion has been removed. It describes translational kinetic energy and excludes energy associated with internal excitation or other internal quantum states.

For an isotropic translational distribution, the energy-equivalent temperature is defined by

$$
T_n = \frac{2}{3}\left\langle \frac{1}{2}m_n\left|\mathbf{v}-\mathbf{u}_n\right|^2 \right\rangle
$$

where $T_n$ is the neutral translational temperature, $m_n$ is the mass of a neutral particle, $\mathbf{v}$ is its velocity, $\mathbf{u}_n$ is the bulk translational velocity of the neutral population, and the angle brackets denote an average over the selected particles.

The quantity applies to the selected neutral population without restricting it to cold or energetic particles or to a particular spatial region. When multiple charge states are represented, it is the density-weighted mean over all represented charge states rather than their sum. The unqualified quantity has no spatial aggregation; [volume_averaged_neutral_temperature](name:volume_averaged_neutral_temperature) is the corresponding quantity after volume averaging inside the last closed flux surface.

The [cold_neutral_temperature](name:cold_neutral_temperature) and [hot_neutral_temperature](name:hot_neutral_temperature) names restrict this common translational-temperature definition to distinct neutral populations. In contrast, [neutral_internal_state_temperature](name:neutral_internal_state_temperature) restricts the population to a specified internal quantum or excitation state.

NAMES.name: neutron_flux
NAMES.subject: neutron
NAMES.short: Total neutron production rate from fusion reactions, integrated over the plasma volume and summed across reaction channels and reacting-population classes.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the global rate at which fusion reactions produce neutrons in the plasma. It represents an integrated production rate, not a local neutron source density or a surface-crossing particle flux.

The total neutron production rate is defined by

$$
\Gamma_n = \int_{\mathcal{V}_{\mathrm{plasma}}} S_n(\mathbf{r})\,d^3\mathbf{r} = \sum_c \Gamma_{n,c}
$$

where $\Gamma_n$ is the total neutron production rate, $\mathcal{V}_{\mathrm{plasma}}$ is the plasma volume, $S_n(\mathbf{r})$ is the local volumetric neutron production rate from fusion at position $\mathbf{r}$, $d^3\mathbf{r}$ is the volume element, $c$ indexes fusion reaction channels, and $\Gamma_{n,c}$ is the volume-integrated neutron production rate for channel $c$.

The aggregation includes deuterium–deuterium, deuterium–tritium, and tritium–tritium fusion channels, with thermal, beam-thermal, and beam-beam reacting-population contributions combined within each channel. It excludes neutron production from non-fusion processes and is nonnegative as a production rate.

The reaction-specific [deuterium–deuterium neutron flux](name:deuterium_deuterium_neutron_flux) and [tritium–tritium neutron flux](name:tritium_tritium_neutron_flux) are channel-resolved components of this aggregate. The spatially resolved counterpart is the local [fusion neutron emissivity](name:emissivity_due_to_fusion), whose volume integral supplies the corresponding contribution to the total.
